dishes.title: Creole Turtle Soup
dishes.summary: A dark, rich Creole soup of turtle meat or veal braised tender in a brown stock thickened with a dark roux, sharpened with lemon and tomato, finished with chopped egg and spinach, and served with sherry poured at the table. It is a Brennan's first course, and it is in the course because making it well brings together brown stock, a roux cooked to the colour of chocolate and a long braise refined into an elegant soup.
skills: turtle meat or veal braised tender
equipment: Large roasting tin for the bones
Large stockpot, at least 8 quarts (7.5 litres)
Heavy cast-iron or enamelled pot, at least 5 quarts (4.7 litres), for the soup
Flat-edged wooden spoon for the roux

ingredients.item: Veal or beef bones, cut into pieces
Onion, carrot and celery for the stock

ingredients.note: cut into 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice, or coarsely minced

ingredients.item: Dry sherry, to serve at the table
Fine salt, black pepper and hot sauce

mise: The day before: make the brown stock so it can be chilled and defatted.
Dice the meat; chop the onion, celery, pepper and garlic (the trinity) and keep them together in a bowl.
Measure the butter and flour for the roux beside the pot.
Hard-boil the eggs: 10 minutes in simmering water, then iced water; peel and chop.
Warm the defatted stock in a saucepan.

timeline.do: Roast the bones; start the stock and simmer 6 hours.
Strain the stock and chill; lift off the fat next day.

timeline.at: Day of, T minus 2 hours 30 min
timeline.do: Brown the meat; make the dark roux.
Add the trinity, stock and seasonings; simmer 90 minutes.
Add lemon, sherry and spinach; chop eggs.
Ladle into warm bowls with egg, lemon and sherry at the table.

steps.do: Make the brown stock: roast the bones in the tin at 450°F (230°C) for 45 minutes, add the chopped onion, carrot and celery and the 2 tbsp (30 g) tomato purée and roast 15 minutes more. Transfer to the stockpot, deglaze the tin with water and add that too, then cover with the 4 quarts (3.8 litres) water.
steps.look: Deep brown, sticky bones and vegetables; the kitchen smells of roast meat.
steps.mistake: Burning the bones or the purée black, which makes a bitter stock.
steps.fix: Check at 30 minutes and turn the bones; aim for the colour of a conker.

steps.do: Bring slowly to a bare simmer, skim the grey foam, and simmer uncovered 6 hours, skimming now and then. Strain, cool quickly and refrigerate overnight. Lift off the fat.
steps.look: A clear, amber-brown stock that sets to a soft jelly when cold.
steps.mistake: Boiling the stock, which clouds it.
steps.fix: Keep the surface just trembling. A cloudy stock still tastes good in this soup.

steps.do: Heat the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the heavy pot over high heat and brown the diced meat in two batches, 5 minutes each, until well coloured. Lift it out.
steps.look: A loud sizzle and a deep brown crust on the meat; a brown film on the base of the pot.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pot, so the meat steams grey.
steps.fix: Brown in batches and let the pot reheat between them.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the 1/2 cup (115 g) butter and, when melted, the 1/2 cup (65 g) flour. Stir constantly with the flat wooden spoon, scraping the whole base, for 20 to 25 minutes until the roux is the colour of milk chocolate.
steps.look: The roux moves from blond to peanut butter to a deep, glossy brown, smelling of toasted nuts.
steps.mistake: Walking away, or turning up the heat, so black specks appear and the roux tastes burnt.
steps.fix: Stay with it. If you see black flecks or smell acrid smoke, throw it away and start again.

steps.do: Add the trinity and garlic to the hot roux all at once and stir for 5 minutes until softened.
steps.look: A loud sizzle as the vegetables hit the roux, which stops it darkening; the smell turns sweet and savoury.
steps.mistake: Adding the vegetables gradually, so the roux keeps cooking and burns.
steps.fix: Tip them in together; their water cools the roux immediately.

steps.do: Gradually whisk in 8 cups (1.9 litres) of the warm stock, a ladle at a time at first, then the rest. Add the browned meat, passata, Worcestershire, bay, thyme and cayenne.
steps.look: A smooth, brown soup with no lumps, beginning to bubble gently.
steps.mistake: Pouring cold stock into the hot roux all at once, causing lumps.
steps.fix: Use warm stock and whisk steadily. Lumps can be sieved out before the meat goes in.

steps.do: Simmer gently, uncovered, for 90 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes and skimming fat from the surface, until the meat is tender and the soup coats a spoon.
steps.look: A glossy, deep brown soup the thickness of single cream; the meat soft enough to crush against the side of the pot.
steps.mistake: Letting it catch on the bottom.
steps.fix: Stir along the base regularly and keep the heat low.

steps.do: Stir in the lemon juice, the 1/3 cup (80 ml) sherry and the spinach and simmer 5 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and hot sauce.
steps.look: The spinach wilts into dark green flecks; the soup tastes rich, then bright with lemon, with a warm sherry finish.
steps.mistake: Adding too much lemon at once.
steps.fix: Add half, taste, then the rest.

steps.do: Ladle into warm bowls and top each with a spoonful of chopped egg, a thin slice of lemon and parsley. Pour a little sherry over each bowl at the table.
steps.look: A dark soup with a bright yellow and white garnish; the sherry releases its nutty perfume as it hits the hot soup.
steps.mistake: Stirring the egg in, which turns the soup grey.
steps.fix: Garnish on top at the last moment.

dishes.science: Roasting bones and vegetables starts the Maillard reaction, browning proteins and sugars into hundreds of savoury, roasted compounds; long simmering then dissolves gelatin from the bones, giving the stock body. A dark roux develops flavour as the flour toasts, but browning breaks down some of its starch, so a dark roux thickens less than a pale one, which is why this soup uses a generous half cup of each. Cooking the trinity in the roux stops it darkening further, because the water in the vegetables drops the temperature. Simmering the diced meat lets its connective tissue soften into gelatin. Sherry added at the end keeps its aromatic, nutty compounds; boiling it long would drive them off.
dishes.plating: Warm, wide soup plates on an underplate. Ladle the soup in, then place the chopped egg in a small heap in the centre, a paper-thin lemon slice beside it and a pinch of parsley. Bring a small jug of sherry to the table and pour a teaspoon over each bowl in front of the guest.

pairing.drink: A dry Amontillado or Fino sherry, the same wine finished into the soup: nutty and savoury, it echoes the roux and the stock.
pairing.brennans: Turtle Soup: Brennan's own first course, with sherry added at the table, so cooking it at home lets you describe each element to a guest.

variations: Use beef shin in place of veal for a deeper, beefier soup.
Mock turtle soup: a mix of veal shank and calf's foot for extra gelatin.
Make the soup a day ahead; it thickens and tastes better reheated, so loosen with stock.
safety: Cool stock quickly: divide into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Reheat the soup to a full simmer, 165°F (74°C), before serving.
A dark roux is very hot, well above 300°F (150°C): stir with a long spoon and keep children clear.

dishes.title: Bouillabaisse with Rouille
dishes.summary: Marseille's fish stew: a saffron broth boiled hard to emulsify its olive oil, poured over several kinds of fish added in order of firmness, with croutons spread with rouille, a saffron and garlic emulsion. It is in the course because it breaks the rule of every other stock: this one boils violently, on purpose, and it asks you to clean several fish and time each one.
skills: a rapid boil to emulsify oil into the broth
equipment: Wide, heavy stockpot, at least 8 quarts (7.5 litres)
Second wide pan or deep sauté pan for poaching the fish
Food mill, or a large sieve and a ladle
Mortar and pestle, or a small food processor, for the rouille

ingredients.item: Mixed firm and delicate fish, filleted, skin on
ingredients.note: at least three kinds: monkfish, gurnard, John Dory, red mullet, sea bass

ingredients.item: Fish heads and frames, gills removed

ingredients.note: plus a pinch for the rouille
soaked in a little hot broth
sliced and toasted, rubbed with garlic

mise: Scale and fillet any whole fish; cut fillets into pieces about 2 inches (5 cm), keeping the kinds separate on a tray, firm to delicate. Refrigerate.
Rinse the heads and frames, removing gills and any blood.
Slice the onion, leek and fennel; crush the garlic; chop the tomatoes.
Steep the saffron in 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water.
Toast baguette slices at 375°F (190°C) for 10 minutes and rub with garlic.
Bring a kettle of water to the boil.

timeline.do: Prepare the fish and the vegetables; toast croutons.
Sweat vegetables; add frames and boil hard 25 minutes.
Pass the broth through a food mill; season.
Make the rouille.
Bring broth back to the boil; poach fish in order of firmness.
Serve broth over croutons, then the fish.

steps.do: Heat the 1/2 cup (120 ml) olive oil in the stockpot over medium heat. Add the onion, leek, fennel and garlic and sweat for 10 minutes until soft, without browning. Add the tomatoes, tomato purée, orange zest, thyme and bay and cook 5 minutes.
steps.look: Soft, glossy vegetables, the tomatoes collapsing; it smells of fennel, garlic and orange.
steps.mistake: Browning the vegetables, which makes a darker, heavier broth.
steps.fix: Medium heat and stir; add a splash of water if anything starts to colour.

steps.do: Add the fish heads and frames and stir for 5 minutes until they turn opaque and start to break up. Pour in the 8 cups (1.9 litres) boiling water, the saffron and its water, and the pastis.
steps.look: The bones turn white, the water turns orange-gold, and the kitchen smells of the sea and saffron.
steps.mistake: Using cold water, which slows everything down.
steps.fix: Use boiling water from the kettle.

steps.do: Boil hard, uncovered, over high heat for 25 minutes. It should roll violently the whole time.
steps.look: A furious, rolling boil; the oil disappears into the broth, which turns thick, cloudy and golden.
steps.mistake: Simmering gently, as for a clear stock, so the oil floats on top.
steps.fix: Turn the heat to maximum. The hard boil is what emulsifies the oil.

steps.do: Pass everything through the food mill, or press it through a sieve with a ladle, extracting as much as you can, including the softened bones and vegetables. Season with salt and a pinch of cayenne.
steps.look: A thick, opaque, saffron-orange broth with a rich body, tasting deeply of fish and fennel.
steps.mistake: Straining it gently without pressing, which gives a thin broth.
steps.fix: Press hard; the crushed solids give body.

steps.do: Make the rouille: pound the 2 garlic cloves with a pinch of salt and saffron to a paste in the mortar. Squeeze the soaked bread and add it with the egg yolk, pounding to a smooth paste. Drip in the 3/4 cup (180 ml) olive oil, stirring with the pestle, then pour in a thin stream until thick. Season with cayenne.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, rust-coloured sauce that holds its shape on a spoon; it smells strongly of garlic and saffron.
steps.mistake: Adding the oil too fast, so it splits.
steps.fix: Stop pouring and stir hard. If it breaks, start with a new yolk in a clean bowl and add the split sauce drop by drop.

steps.do: Pour half the broth into the second wide pan and bring it to a lively simmer. Add the firmest fish, such as monkfish, and poach 3 minutes.
steps.look: The monkfish pieces turn from translucent to white at the edges; the broth bubbles gently around them.
steps.mistake: Adding all the fish at once, so the delicate pieces overcook.
steps.fix: Add fish in order and keep a timer for each kind.

steps.do: Add the medium fish, such as gurnard and John Dory, and poach 2 minutes. Add the mussels if using and cover. Add the most delicate fish, such as red mullet and sea bass, skin side up, and poach 2 to 3 minutes more, until all the fish flakes and reads 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: Each piece just opaque and flaking under gentle pressure; the mussels open.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which breaks the fish into flakes.
steps.fix: Shake the pan rather than stirring. Discard any mussels that stay shut after 3 more minutes.

steps.do: Bring the remaining broth back to the boil. Serve the first course: two croutons spread with rouille in each warm soup plate, with hot broth ladled over.
steps.look: The croutons float and soak, the rouille melting into orange streaks in the broth.
steps.mistake: Lukewarm broth that cools the croutons and rouille.
steps.fix: Bring it back to a full boil just before ladling.

steps.do: Serve the second course: lift the fish carefully onto a warm platter with the slotted spoon, moisten with a ladle of broth, and bring it to the table with more croutons and rouille.
steps.look: A platter of different fish in neat pieces, glistening with saffron broth.
steps.mistake: Piling the fish into the soup plates, so it breaks up.
steps.fix: Serve the fish separately, as in Marseille.

dishes.science: Most stocks are simmered gently to keep them clear, because boiling breaks fat into tiny droplets that cloud the liquid. Bouillabaisse wants exactly that. Boiling hard breaks the olive oil into very small droplets, and gelatin and proteins dissolved from the fish bones coat those droplets and hold them suspended, making a stable, creamy emulsion; the name is often explained as boil, then lower. Fish is added in order of firmness because muscle proteins in delicate fish set and flake at lower temperatures and with less time than dense fish such as monkfish. The rouille is an emulsion too: egg yolk lecithin and the starch in the soaked bread hold olive oil in tiny droplets, while saffron gives colour and aroma.
dishes.plating: First course in wide, warm soup plates: two croutons with a thick spoonful of rouille on each, broth ladled around so the croutons float. Second course on a warm oval platter, the fish grouped by kind, skin side up, mussels in their shells around the edge, a ladle of broth over everything and a few fennel fronds.

pairing.drink: A dry Provençal rosé, especially Bandol: its body and herbal, saline character stand up to saffron and garlic without overwhelming the fish.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Tempier Bandol Rosé 2024: the classic rosé of the coast near Marseille, on the Brennan's list, made for exactly this dish.

variations: Bourride: a white fish stew thickened with aioli instead of saffron rouille.
Cioppino: the San Francisco cousin with tomato, white wine and crab.
Potato rouille: replace the egg yolk with a small boiled potato for a sturdier, egg-free version.
safety: The rouille contains raw egg yolk: use pasteurised yolk for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system, or the potato version.
Cook fish to 145°F (63°C); mussels must be alive and closed before cooking.
Pour boiling liquid carefully; a hard-boiling pot spits.

dishes.title: Arroz Negro with Allioli
dishes.summary: Catalonia's black rice: short-grain rice cooked in a wide pan with cuttlefish, a deep sofrito, a fish fumet and the cuttlefish's own ink, finished with a pounded picada and served with allioli made in a mortar from garlic and olive oil alone. It is in the course because it teaches the preparation of a whole cephalopod, a fumet made fast and clean, and an emulsion made without any egg at all.
skills: cleaning cuttlefish and saving the ink
equipment: Paella pan, about 15 inches (38 cm) across, or the widest heavy frying pan you have
Clean tea towel to rest the rice under

ingredients.item: Whole cuttlefish (or squid), with ink sacs if possible
ingredients.note: ask for the ink sacs to be kept
in case the sacs burst or are missing

ingredients.item: Bomba or other Spanish short-grain rice
Slice of bread, for the picada
Garlic clove and parsley, for the picada
Mild olive oil, for the allioli

mise: Clean the cuttlefish (step 1) and cut the body into 1/2 inch (1 cm) squares and the tentacles into short pieces; keep the ink sacs in a small bowl.
Make the fumet (step 2) so it is hot when the rice goes in.
Chop the onion and pepper finely; grate the tomatoes; mince the garlic.
Fry the bread slice in a little oil until golden; toast the almonds in the same pan.
Have the allioli garlic peeled and the oil in a jug with a fine spout.
Put the empty mortar on a folded damp cloth so it does not slide.

timeline.do: Clean the cuttlefish and save the ink.
Make the fumet (25 minutes) and strain; keep it hot.
Make the allioli in the mortar.
Brown the cuttlefish; build the sofrito slowly.
Add rice, ink and hot fumet; cook 18 minutes without stirring.
Add the picada; let the socarrat form; rest 5 minutes.
Serve from the pan with allioli and lemon.

steps.do: Clean the cuttlefish: pull the head and tentacles away from the body. Find the small silvery ink sac among the innards and cut it free carefully; put it in the bowl. Cut the tentacles off just in front of the eyes and pop out the hard beak. Remove the white cuttlebone from the body, peel off the skin and rinse.
steps.look: A clean, white body and tentacles; a small, intact, dark ink sac in the bowl. It smells clean and of the sea.
steps.mistake: Bursting the ink sac on the board, which stains everything and loses the ink.
steps.fix: Work over a tray and handle the sac gently; if it bursts, scrape what you can into the bowl and use the sachets.

steps.do: Make the fumet: warm 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the oil in the saucepan, add the fish bones and sliced onion and stir 3 minutes without colouring. Add the wine, boil 1 minute, then the 6 cups (1.4 litres) water. Simmer gently 20 to 25 minutes, skimming, then strain through the sieve. Season lightly and keep hot.
steps.look: A clear, pale stock that smells fresh and of the sea, never fishy or bitter.
steps.mistake: Simmering longer than 30 minutes, which draws out bitter flavours from fish bones.
steps.fix: Twenty-five minutes at most. Strain without pressing hard on the bones.

steps.do: Make the allioli: pound the 4 garlic cloves and salt in the mortar to a perfectly smooth, sticky paste. Add the oil a few drops at a time, turning the pestle in one direction without stopping, then in a thread as it thickens, until you have about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of thick, pale sauce.
steps.look: The paste turns creamy, then thick and opaque, like a soft mayonnaise; it smells fiercely of garlic.
steps.mistake: Adding oil too fast, so the sauce breaks into oily, separate garlic.
steps.fix: Slow down and keep turning in one direction. If it splits, pound a fresh clove of garlic in a clean mortar and add the broken sauce drop by drop. A drop of water can help it start.

steps.do: Heat the remaining oil in the paella pan over medium-high heat. Add the cuttlefish and sauté 5 minutes until it releases its liquid and starts to brown.
steps.look: The pieces first give off liquid, then it evaporates and they sizzle and turn golden at the edges.
steps.mistake: Crowding at too low a heat, so the cuttlefish stews and turns rubbery.
steps.fix: Use high heat and spread it out; cook until the liquid has gone.

steps.do: Push the cuttlefish to the edge. Add the onion and pepper to the centre and cook over medium-low heat 12 to 15 minutes, stirring, until very soft and jammy. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the grated tomato and pimentón, and cook 8 to 10 minutes until the tomato darkens and the oil separates.
steps.look: A deep brick-red, glossy, jam-like sofrito; it smells sweet and smoky.
steps.mistake: Rushing the sofrito, which gives the rice a raw, sharp taste.
steps.fix: Low and slow; it should look like jam before the rice goes in.

steps.do: Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes to coat every grain in the sofrito. Dissolve the ink from the sacs and sachets in a ladle of hot fumet and pour it over.
steps.look: Glossy grains coated in oil; the pan turns jet black as the ink goes in.
steps.mistake: Toasting the rice dry, so it burns.
steps.fix: Stir constantly for just 2 minutes, then add liquid.

steps.do: Pour in 4 1/2 cups (1.1 litres) of hot fumet, stir once to spread the rice evenly across the pan, then do not stir again. Boil hard for 8 minutes, then lower to a steady simmer for 10 minutes.
steps.look: A flat, even layer of rice in a black liquid that bubbles across the whole pan; the liquid level drops below the rice and small craters appear.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which releases starch and makes the rice creamy like risotto.
steps.fix: Leave it alone. Rotate the pan on the burner if one side bubbles more than the other.

steps.do: Pound the fried bread, almonds, picada garlic and parsley in a clean mortar with a splash of fumet to a thick paste. Dot it over the rice at the 14-minute mark.
steps.look: A coarse, green-flecked paste that smells nutty and garlicky.
steps.mistake: Adding the picada too early, so it scorches.
steps.fix: Add it in the last few minutes; it thickens and flavours the remaining liquid.

steps.do: When the liquid has gone, turn the heat up to high for 1 to 2 minutes to form the socarrat, listening carefully.
steps.look: A crackling sound like gentle rain from the base and a smell of toasted rice; a spoon at the edge meets a crisp crust.
steps.mistake: Burning the base black.
steps.fix: Listen and smell; pull it off the heat at the first sharp, smoky smell.

steps.do: Cover the pan with a clean tea towel and rest 5 minutes. Serve from the pan with a spoonful of allioli on each portion and lemon wedges.
steps.look: Separate, glossy black grains, tender with a slight bite, a crisp crust underneath, and white allioli on top.
steps.mistake: Serving it straight from the heat, when the grains are still wet.
steps.fix: The rest lets the rice finish and settle.

dishes.science: Cuttlefish ink is a suspension of melanin, the same pigment that colours skin, with proteins and savoury amino acids; it adds colour and a deep, marine flavour. A fish fumet is simmered only 20 to 25 minutes because fish bones are thin and give up their gelatin quickly, and longer cooking extracts bitter compounds. Spanish short-grain rice such as bomba absorbs a great deal of liquid while keeping its shape, and not stirring keeps its surface starch from forming a creamy sauce. The socarrat forms when the last liquid evaporates and the rice in contact with the hot metal browns through the Maillard reaction. Allioli holds oil without egg because crushed garlic releases sticky compounds and fine particles that coat and stabilise the oil droplets.
dishes.plating: Serve straight from the pan at the table, the black rice smoothed flat, the allioli in a small bowl in the centre or a spoonful on each portion, lemon wedges around the rim. Scrape some socarrat onto every plate, crust side up.

pairing.drink: A crisp Albariño or Godello from northwest Spain: saline, citrusy whites that cut through the ink and garlic and suit the cuttlefish.
pairing.brennans: Raúl Pérez ‘Ultreia’ Godello Bierzo 2021: a Spanish white on the Brennan's list with the texture to meet rich rice and the freshness to cut the allioli.

variations: Arroz a banda: the same method without ink, with a mix of fish and prawns.
Fideuà negra: replace the rice with short, thin pasta toasted in the oil first.
Squid version: use cleaned squid and ink sachets if cuttlefish is not available.
safety: The allioli is raw garlic in oil: make it on the day and refrigerate leftovers, using within 1 day.
Cook the cuttlefish until opaque throughout.
Hot paella pans are wide and heavy: lift with oven gloves and two hands.

dishes.title: Moqueca Baiana
dishes.summary: Bahia's fish stew: thick pieces of fish marinated in lime and garlic, layered raw with onions, tomatoes and peppers in a clay pot, then cooked gently in coconut milk and red dendê oil without stirring, with a pirão made from the broth thickened with cassava flour. It is in the course because it teaches building a dish in layers and holding back, and turning a broth into a second dish.
equipment: Clay pot (panela de barro) or a wide, heavy casserole with a lid, about 11 inches (28 cm)
Medium saucepan for the fish stock and pirão

ingredients.item: Firm white fish steaks or thick fillets (snapper, halibut, cod, sea bass)
ingredients.note: cut in pieces about 2 inches (5 cm)

ingredients.item: Fish head and frame, or extra fish trimmings
ingredients.note: for a quick stock; gills removed
optional; peel and save the shells for the stock
half chopped for the marinade, half to finish

mise: Marinate the fish: toss with the lime juice, crushed garlic, 1 tsp (6 g) salt and half the chopped coriander; leave 30 minutes in the fridge.
Make a quick stock: simmer the fish head and frame (and prawn shells) in the 4 cups (950 ml) water with a few onion slices for 20 minutes; strain.
Slice the onions, tomatoes and peppers into rings; slice the spring onions.
Rinse the rice and have it ready to cook.
Open the coconut milk and stir it smooth.

timeline.do: Marinate the fish; start the quick stock.
Strain the stock; slice vegetables.
Cook the rice.
Layer the moqueca and cook gently 15 minutes.
Make the pirão from the stock and moqueca broth.
Finish with dendê and coriander; serve in the pot.

steps.do: Make the stock: put the fish head, frame and any prawn shells in the saucepan with the 4 cups (950 ml) water and a few onion slices. Bring to a simmer, skim and simmer 20 minutes. Strain and season lightly.
steps.look: A pale, clean-smelling stock with a little body.
steps.mistake: Boiling it hard for an hour, which makes it bitter and cloudy.
steps.fix: Twenty minutes is enough for fish.

steps.do: Lay half the onion, tomato and pepper rings in the bottom of the clay pot in overlapping layers. Sprinkle with a little salt.
steps.look: A colourful, even bed of vegetables covering the base.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps, so the fish sits directly on the hot pot and sticks.
steps.fix: Overlap the rings to make a full bed.

steps.do: Arrange the marinated fish pieces in one layer on the vegetables, with the marinade. Tuck in the prawns if using. Cover with the remaining onion, tomato and pepper and the spring onions and chilli.
steps.look: Neat layers of vegetables, fish and vegetables again, nothing stirred, colours showing at the sides.
steps.mistake: Piling fish on top of fish, so some pieces cook before others.
steps.fix: Use a single layer of fish; a wider pot helps.

steps.do: Pour the 1 2/3 cups (400 ml) coconut milk over the whole pot. Cover and bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat, then cook 12 to 15 minutes without stirring, gently rocking the pot now and then and spooning liquid over the top.
steps.look: Small bubbles around the edges, the vegetables softening and the coconut milk turning pink from the tomatoes; it smells of lime, coconut and coriander.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which breaks the fish into flakes.
steps.fix: Rock the pot by its handles instead of stirring.

steps.do: Check the fish: the thickest piece should flake when pressed and read 145°F (63°C). Ladle 1 cup (240 ml) of the moqueca broth into the saucepan with 2 cups (480 ml) of the fish stock for the pirão. Keep the pot covered off the heat.
steps.look: Opaque fish that separates into large flakes; a pink-orange broth.
steps.mistake: Overcooking until the fish falls apart.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as it reaches 145°F (63°C); it carries on cooking.

steps.do: Make the pirão: bring the broth and stock to a simmer. Whisk in the 1/2 cup (70 g) cassava flour a little at a time and cook, whisking constantly, for 3 to 5 minutes until thick and smooth like soft polenta. Season.
steps.look: A glossy, orange, spoonable porridge that falls slowly from the whisk.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour all at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Rain it in slowly while whisking. Whisk out lumps or add more stock if too thick.

steps.do: Return the moqueca to low heat for 1 minute and drizzle the 3 tbsp (45 ml) dendê over the top in a spiral. Scatter the remaining coriander.
steps.look: The red oil marbles the surface in orange ribbons; the smell turns rich and nutty.
steps.mistake: Adding dendê at the start and boiling it, which dulls its flavour.
steps.fix: Dendê goes in at the end so its colour and aroma stay bright.

steps.do: Serve at the table in the clay pot, with rice, pirão and lime wedges. Spoon fish, vegetables and broth over the rice and pirão.
steps.look: A bubbling pot of red, yellow and green, fish in whole pieces, a bowl of orange pirão.
steps.mistake: Ladling it into bowls in the kitchen, breaking the fish.
steps.fix: Bring the pot to the table and serve gently with a wide spoon.

dishes.science: The lime marinade starts to firm the surface proteins of the fish and seasons it, but only for 30 minutes; longer and the acid toughens it. Layering puts the vegetables between the fish and the hot base, so the fish cooks in gentle, moist heat from the liquid the vegetables release, rather than by direct contact. Coconut milk is an emulsion of fat in water that thickens slightly as it reduces, and keeping the heat low stops it splitting. Dendê is red because it is rich in carotenoids, the same pigments that colour carrots; adding it at the end keeps its colour and nutty aroma. Cassava flour thickens the pirão because its starch swells and gelatinises in hot liquid.
dishes.plating: Bring the clay pot to the table on a board. In each wide bowl, a mound of white rice on one side and a spoonful of pirão on the other, with a piece of fish and its vegetables between them and broth spooned over, finished with a coriander sprig and a lime wedge.

pairing.drink: A caipirinha or a dry, fruity rosé: the caipirinha's lime and sugar echo the marinade, and a rosé has the freshness to handle coconut and palm oil.
pairing.brennans: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024: a pale, dry Provençal rosé on the Brennan's list, bright enough for a coconut fish stew.

variations: Moqueca de camarão: all prawns, cooked only 5 to 6 minutes in total.
Moqueca capixaba: the Espírito Santo style, with annatto oil instead of dendê and no coconut milk.
Vegetable moqueca: plantain, hearts of palm and peppers cooked the same way.
safety: Cook the fish to 145°F (63°C).
Clay pots crack with sudden temperature changes: heat them slowly and never put a hot pot on a cold, wet surface.

dishes.title: Banku with Grilled Tilapia and Shito
dishes.summary: Ghana's chop bar lunch: banku, a smooth, sour dough of fermented corn and cassava stirred in a pot until it stretches, beside a whole tilapia scored, marinated and grilled over charcoal, with shito, here the fresh pepper sauce ground from raw tomato, onion and chilli (in Ga the word simply means pepper; the dark fried shito is a variation). It is in the course because it joins a fermented dough that takes strength and patience to stir with live-fire cooking of a whole fish.
equipment: Two large glass or ceramic bowls for fermenting, with cloths
Heavy-based pot, at least 5 quarts (4.7 litres)
Strong, flat wooden spatula or banku stick
Charcoal grill with a lid, and a hinged fish basket if you have one
Bowl of cold water for wetting hands

ingredients.item: Fine white cornmeal or corn flour (not cornflour starch)
Grated cassava, fresh or frozen and thawed
Cold water, for cooking the banku
Scotch bonnet chilli, for the marinade
Ripe tomatoes, for the pepper sauce
Red onion, for the pepper sauce
Fresh hot chillies (kpakpo shito or Scotch bonnet)
Fine salt, for the pepper sauce

mise: Three days ahead: start fermenting the corn dough. Two days ahead: start fermenting the cassava.
On the day, blend the marinade: onion, ginger, garlic, Scotch bonnet, stock cube, oil and salt to a paste.
Rinse the fish, pat dry, and check the gills and scales are fully removed.
Light the charcoal in a chimney 30 minutes before grilling.
Have a bowl of cold water and four squares of cling film ready for shaping the banku.

timeline.do: Mix the corn dough with water and leave covered at room temperature.
Mix the cassava with a little water and leave covered; knead the corn dough once.
Score and marinate the fish; light the charcoal at T minus 60 minutes.
Blend the pepper sauce; start the banku.
Grill the fish 8 to 10 minutes a side.
Shape the banku into balls and wrap.
Serve the fish with banku, pepper sauce and sliced vegetables.

steps.do: Day 1: mix the 3 cups (450 g) cornmeal with enough lukewarm water to make a stiff, sticky dough like wet clay, about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml). Cover with a cloth and leave at room temperature, ideally 75 to 85°F (24 to 29°C), for 3 days, kneading once a day.
steps.look: By day 2 small bubbles appear and it smells mildly sour; by day 3 it smells clearly sour, like yoghurt and bread.
steps.mistake: Sealing it airtight or keeping it in a cold room, so it barely ferments.
steps.fix: Cover with a cloth only and keep it warm. A grey film on top can be scraped off; pink, orange or fuzzy mould means start again.

steps.do: Day 2: mix the squeezed cassava with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water, cover and leave 2 days beside the corn dough.
steps.look: The cassava softens slightly and smells faintly sour.
steps.mistake: Leaving cassava wet and sloppy.
steps.fix: Squeeze it dry before fermenting.

steps.do: Score the fish: make three diagonal cuts on each side through the skin to the bone, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Rub the marinade into the cuts, the cavity and all over the skin. Marinate 1 hour in the fridge.
steps.look: Deep, even slashes; the paste packed into every cut and the cavity.
steps.mistake: Shallow scoring, so the thickest part stays raw while the outside chars.
steps.fix: Cut right down to the bone; it lets heat and flavour reach the centre.

steps.do: Make the pepper sauce: blend or grind the tomatoes, red onion, chillies and salt to a coarse, fresh sauce. Taste and adjust the heat.
steps.look: A bright red, slightly chunky sauce, fresh and fiery, smelling of raw onion and chilli.
steps.mistake: Blending to a thin, frothy liquid.
steps.fix: Pulse briefly, or use a grinding stone as in Ghana.

steps.do: Start the banku: put the corn dough and cassava dough in the pot with the 3 3/4 cups (900 ml) cold water and squeeze them through your fingers until no lumps bigger than a grain of rice remain.
steps.look: A smooth, thin, chalky white slurry, like single cream.
steps.mistake: Starting with hot water, which makes lumps that never dissolve.
steps.fix: Always dissolve in cold water first; push lumps through a sieve if needed.

steps.do: Set the pot over medium heat and stir without stopping with the flat spatula, scraping the base and corners, for 8 to 10 minutes until the mixture thickens and turns from white to glossy and translucent.
steps.look: The mixture suddenly thickens, drags on the spatula and turns shiny; it smells of sour bread.
steps.mistake: Stopping stirring, so it scorches on the base and tastes bitter.
steps.fix: Stir constantly. If it catches, move to a clean pot without scraping the bottom.

steps.do: Lower the heat and keep beating, pressing the paste against the side of the pot and folding it back, for 15 to 20 minutes, adding the 1 tsp (6 g) salt halfway. Wet the spatula if it sticks.
steps.look: A smooth, elastic mass that pulls away from the pot in one piece and stretches when lifted.
steps.mistake: Stopping too early, so the banku tastes raw and floury.
steps.fix: Keep beating until it is smooth and no longer tastes of raw flour.

steps.do: Grill the fish: spread the hot coals for medium-high direct heat, oil the grill bars or fish basket well, and lay the fish on. Grill 8 to 10 minutes a side with the lid on, turning once, until the skin is charred and blistered and the flesh at the thickest point flakes from the bone and reads 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: Crackling, dark-blistered skin, the slashes opening to show white flesh; it smells smoky and spicy.
steps.mistake: Turning the fish too early, so the skin sticks and tears.
steps.fix: Wait until it releases. Use a fish basket or two spatulas to turn it.

steps.do: Shape the banku: wet your hands and the spatula in cold water, scoop a quarter of the hot banku and roll it into a smooth ball by turning it in a wet bowl. Wrap each ball in cling film.
steps.look: Four smooth, glossy, slightly springy balls, too hot to hold for long.
steps.mistake: Shaping with dry hands, so it sticks.
steps.fix: Keep dipping your hands in cold water. Work quickly before the banku sets.

steps.do: Serve each person a ball of banku and half a fish with a bowl of pepper sauce and sliced onion, tomato and cucumber. Eat with the right hand: pinch off banku, dip it in the pepper sauce and take some fish.
steps.look: A charred, steaming fish, pale banku, red pepper sauce.
steps.mistake: Letting banku go cold, when it turns rubbery.
steps.fix: Serve within 10 minutes of shaping, still warm.

dishes.science: Fermentation sours the corn: lactic acid bacteria naturally present on the grain eat its sugars and produce lactic acid, which gives banku its tang and lowers the pH enough to suppress spoilage organisms. Cassava adds amylopectin, a branched starch that makes the dough stretchy and smooth instead of crumbly. Cooking gelatinises the starches: the granules absorb water and swell, so the slurry thickens suddenly and turns translucent, and long beating makes the paste smooth and elastic. Scoring the fish lets heat reach the thick centre at the same speed as the thin tail and lets the marinade in, while the hot coals char the skin through the Maillard reaction and caramelisation.
dishes.plating: Serve on a large plate or in a wide bowl: one whole fish laid diagonally, a ball of banku beside it, the pepper sauce in a small bowl or spooned beside the fish, and slices of onion, tomato and cucumber fanned along the other side.

pairing.drink: An ice-cold Ghanaian lager or sobolo, a hibiscus drink with ginger: cold and refreshing, either soothes the chilli and cuts the sour banku.

variations: Grill the fish under a very hot overhead grill (broiler) in the kitchen, 7 to 8 minutes a side, if you have no charcoal.
Kenkey: the fermented corn dough wrapped in corn husks and boiled, a cousin of banku.
Shito, the dark, fried pepper sauce of dried shrimp and chilli, served alongside for contrast.
safety: Cook the fish to 145°F (63°C) at the thickest part next to the bone.
Discard any ferment with pink, orange or fuzzy mould.
Never eat cassava raw; it must be cooked thoroughly, as it is here.
Use the charcoal grill outdoors only, and keep children away from hot coals.

dishes.title: Lahpet Thoke (Burmese Tea Leaf Salad)
dishes.summary: Myanmar's tea leaf salad: green tea leaves soaked, rinsed and fermented in the jar, dressed with garlic, lime and oil, then tossed at the table with shredded cabbage, tomato and a heap of crisp, fried and toasted things. It is in the course because it teaches fermenting leaves, frying several kinds of crunch to the right colour, and balancing sour, salty and oily as you serve.
skills: frying beans, garlic and lentils for crunch
balancing sour, salty and oily at the table
equipment: Clean glass jar, about 1 pint (500 ml), with a lid
Small weight or a small bag of water to press the leaves
mise: A week ahead: soak and ferment the tea leaves.
Soak the split peas overnight, drain and dry very well on a towel for 1 hour.
Slice the frying garlic thinly and evenly.
Shred the cabbage finely and soak it in iced water for crispness, then drain and dry.
Line trays with kitchen paper for the fried things.
Pound or blend the dried shrimp coarsely.

timeline.do: Soak and rinse the tea leaves; pack with salt in a jar to ferment.
Ferment at room temperature, pressing down daily.
Soak the split peas overnight.
Make the tea leaf dressing; fry split peas and garlic; toast peanuts and sesame.
Arrange everything on a platter.
Toss at the table and serve at once.

steps.do: Put the tea leaves in a bowl, pour over 2 cups (480 ml) boiling water and steep 5 minutes. Drain, cover with cold water, swirl and drain again. Repeat the cold rinse 4 or 5 times over 2 hours, tasting a leaf each time.
steps.look: The leaves unfurl into large, soft green leaves; the bitterness fades with each rinse until they taste grassy and only gently bitter.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rinses, so the salad is harsh and astringent.
steps.fix: Keep rinsing until a leaf tastes pleasant to chew.

steps.do: Squeeze the leaves firmly to remove water, remove any hard stems, chop them roughly and toss with the 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt. Pack tightly into the clean jar, press down hard and weigh them down so they sit in their own juice. Cover loosely.
steps.look: A dense, dark green mass, slightly wet, pressed flat under the weight.
steps.mistake: Leaving air pockets or leaves sticking up above the liquid, where mould can grow.
steps.fix: Press down firmly and keep everything below the weight.

steps.do: Ferment at room temperature, 68 to 75°F (20 to 24°C), for 5 to 7 days, pressing down once a day.
steps.look: The leaves darken to olive green, soften further and smell pleasantly sour and tea-like.
steps.mistake: Fermenting in a hot spot, which turns them mushy and over-sour.
steps.fix: Keep them cool; check the smell daily. Discard if you see fuzzy or coloured mould.

steps.do: Make the dressing: pound or blend the 3 garlic cloves, ginger and chillies to a paste. Squeeze the fermented leaves and mix them with the paste, the 3 tbsp (45 ml) lime juice, 2 tbsp (30 ml) fish sauce and 1/3 cup (80 ml) peanut oil. Rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A glossy, dark green, oily relish that tastes sour, salty, hot and gently bitter.
steps.mistake: Too little oil, which leaves it dry and harsh.
steps.fix: The oil is part of the dish; add more if it looks dry.

steps.do: Heat the 2 cups (480 ml) frying oil in the saucepan to 300°F (150°C). Fry the sliced garlic, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until pale golden, then lift onto paper at once.
steps.look: Garlic slices turning evenly pale gold, sizzling gently; they smell sweet and nutty.
steps.mistake: Frying until brown, which makes the garlic bitter as it carries on cooking.
steps.fix: Lift them out while still lighter than you want; they darken on the paper.

steps.do: Raise the oil to 350°F (175°C). Fry the dried split peas in two batches for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on paper and salt lightly.
steps.look: A lively sizzle that quietens as the water leaves them; they turn golden and rattle when stirred.
steps.mistake: Wet split peas, which spit violently in the hot oil.
steps.fix: Dry them thoroughly first and add them slowly, standing back.

steps.do: Toast the peanuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, then the sesame for 2 minutes, shaking constantly. Fry the dried shrimp briefly in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the garlic oil until crisp.
steps.look: Golden peanuts that crack between your teeth; sesame popping and smelling nutty.
steps.mistake: Leaving the sesame unattended; it burns in seconds.
steps.fix: Shake the pan constantly and tip seeds out as soon as golden.

steps.do: Arrange the platter in sections around the tea leaf dressing in the centre: cabbage, tomato wedges, fried garlic, split peas, peanuts, sesame, shrimp, chillies and lime.
steps.look: A colourful platter of separate piles, each crunchy element dry and crisp.
steps.mistake: Mixing everything in the kitchen, so the crunch softens before eating.
steps.fix: Keep it separate until the moment of serving.

steps.do: At the table, take some of each into a bowl, add the tea leaves, squeeze over lime, toss and taste: it should be sour, salty, oily, crunchy and gently bitter all at once. Adjust with fish sauce, lime or chilli.
steps.look: A tossed salad glistening with oil, full of crunch, tasting of everything at once.
steps.mistake: Serving it pre-mixed and limp.
steps.fix: Toss only what will be eaten at once; leave the rest for another round.

dishes.science: Rinsing tea leaves washes out much of their caffeine and tannins, the bitter, astringent polyphenols. Packing the leaves with salt and pressing them under their own juice lets lactic acid bacteria grow while keeping out air, which encourages spoilage moulds; the acid they produce sours and preserves the leaves and softens them. The crunchy elements all depend on removing water: frying drives water out of split peas and garlic as steam, then the surface dries and browns, and toasting does the same for peanuts and sesame. Garlic is fried at a lower temperature because its sugars brown quickly and turn bitter. The dish balances sour lime, salty fish sauce, oil that carries flavour, and the bitterness of tea.
dishes.plating: Use a large round platter or a lacquered segmented tray. The dark tea leaves sit in the centre, with each crunchy element in its own neat pile around it like the spokes of a wheel, colours alternating, lime wedges on the rim. Toss in front of the guests.

pairing.drink: Hot, plain green tea, the Burmese way, or an off-dry Pinot Gris whose texture and gentle sweetness balance the sour and bitter notes.

variations: Quick version: use bought fermented tea leaves (lahpet) from an Asian shop and skip the fermenting.
Add fried broad beans or crispy chickpeas for more crunch.
Vegetarian: replace the fish sauce with soy and leave out the dried shrimp.
safety: Heat oil only in a pan less than half full; dry the split peas so they do not spit, and never leave hot oil alone.
Discard fermented leaves showing fuzzy or coloured mould, or smelling rotten rather than sour.
This salad contains peanuts and sesame: ask your guests about allergies before serving.

dishes.title: Bossam with Fresh Kimchi
dishes.summary: Pork belly simmered with doenjang, coffee and aromatics until tender enough to slice cleanly, served with a fresh kimchi made that morning, salted cabbage leaves, a fermented shrimp sauce and garnishes for wrapping. It is in the course because it asks for two things done the same day: a fresh kimchi seasoned by taste and a braise that leaves the meat moist, with a clean slice and no strong pork smell.
skills: simmering pork belly with doenjang and coffee
equipment: Large pot with lid, big enough to cover the pork with liquid

ingredients.item: Skin-on pork belly, in one or two slabs

ingredients.note: plus 2 tbsp (30 g) for the dipping sauce

ingredients.item: Garlic cloves, minced, for the kimchi
Fresh ginger, grated, for the kimchi
Lettuce leaves, sliced garlic and green chillies

mise: Cut the cabbage in half lengthways, then quarter it; separate a few outer leaves to salt whole for wrapping.
Dissolve 2 tbsp (35 g) of the salt in 2 cups (480 ml) water.
Mince the kimchi garlic and grate the ginger; cut the spring onions.
Wash and dry the lettuce; slice the garlic and chillies thinly.
Make the shrimp dipping sauce: 2 tbsp (30 g) salted shrimp, a pinch of gochugaru, a few drops of sesame oil and a little chopped spring onion.

timeline.do: Salt the cabbage quarters and wrapping leaves.
Rinse and drain the cabbage.
Start simmering the pork belly.
Make the fresh kimchi seasoning and toss the cabbage.
Lift the pork and rest it 10 minutes.
Slice the pork and build the platter.

steps.do: Salt the cabbage: lift the layers of each quarter and sprinkle the remaining coarse salt between them, mostly on the thick white stems, then pour the salted water over. Leave 1 1/2 hours, turning the quarters every 30 minutes. Salt the whole wrapping leaves the same way.
steps.look: The thick white stems bend without snapping; the leaves are limp and glossy and water has pooled in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Salting too long, so the cabbage turns soggy and salty.
steps.fix: Test after an hour by bending a stem; stop as soon as it bends.

steps.do: Rinse the cabbage three times in cold water, gently squeeze, and drain cut side down in the colander for 30 minutes.
steps.look: Supple, pale leaves that taste seasoned but not salty.
steps.mistake: Not rinsing enough, so the kimchi is too salty.
steps.fix: Taste a leaf after rinsing; rinse again if salty.

steps.do: Put the pork belly in the pot with the doenjang, coffee, onion, garlic, ginger, spring onion whites, bay, peppercorns and soju, and add water to cover by 1 inch (2.5 cm). Stir to dissolve the doenjang. Bring to the boil, skim, cover and simmer gently for 50 to 60 minutes.
steps.look: A dark, earthy-smelling broth with gentle bubbles; the pork turns firm and grey-brown.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which tightens the meat and makes it dry.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer with the lid on.

steps.do: Make the kimchi seasoning: mix the 3 tbsp (15 g) gochugaru, 2 tbsp (30 ml) fish sauce, 1 tbsp (15 g) chopped salted shrimp, minced garlic, ginger and sugar into a paste. Add the spring onions and radish if using.
steps.look: A thick, brick-red paste that smells hot, garlicky and of the sea.
steps.mistake: A dry paste that will not coat the leaves.
steps.fix: Add 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) water to loosen it.

steps.do: Tear or cut the drained cabbage quarters into bite-size pieces. With gloves on, toss them in the seasoning, rubbing it into every leaf. Finish with the sesame oil and seeds. Taste and adjust with fish sauce or sugar.
steps.look: Glossy red leaves, evenly coated, crisp, tasting hot, salty, sweet and fresh.
steps.mistake: Too little seasoning, so it tastes of plain cabbage.
steps.fix: Fresh kimchi should be bold; add more paste until every leaf is red.

steps.do: Test the pork: push a chopstick into the thickest part. It should slide in with little resistance. Lift the pork onto a board and rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: The chopstick enters smoothly; no pink juices run; it smells savoury, not porky.
steps.mistake: Undercooking, so the meat is chewy and hard to slice.
steps.fix: Simmer 10 to 15 minutes more and test again.

steps.do: Slice the pork across the grain into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, each with a layer of skin, fat and meat.
steps.look: Neat slices showing clean stripes of skin, fat and meat, moist and holding together.
steps.mistake: Slicing hot from the pot, so the layers fall apart.
steps.fix: Rest first; use a sharp knife in long strokes.

steps.do: Arrange the pork overlapping on a platter with the fresh kimchi, salted cabbage leaves, lettuce, garlic and chillies, ssamjang and the shrimp sauce. To eat, lay a cabbage or lettuce leaf in your palm, add pork, kimchi, a dab of sauce, garlic and chilli, wrap and eat in one bite.
steps.look: A generous platter with the pork fanned in the middle and everything for wrapping around it.
steps.mistake: Too much in one wrap, so it falls apart.
steps.fix: Small wraps, one bite each.

dishes.science: Pork belly is layered muscle and fat with plenty of connective tissue. Simmering below the boil lets collagen slowly turn to gelatin, so the meat becomes tender and moist while staying in one piece for slicing; a hard boil tightens the muscle fibres and drives out moisture. Doenjang and coffee add savoury and bitter compounds that cover the stronger aromas of pork. Salting the cabbage draws out water by osmosis, softening the stems so they bend without breaking and seasoning the leaves. Fresh kimchi is eaten before fermentation begins, so its taste is bright and sharp rather than sour; salted shrimp brings concentrated savoury flavour because its proteins have been broken down into amino acids over months in salt.
dishes.plating: A large platter: the pork slices fanned in overlapping rows in the centre, skin side up. The fresh kimchi in a mound at one end, salted cabbage leaves folded at the other, lettuce, garlic and chilli slices in small heaps, and the sauces in little bowls on the platter or beside it.

pairing.drink: Chilled soju or a cloudy makgeolli rice wine: soju's clean bite or makgeolli's soft sourness refresh after rich pork and fiery kimchi.

variations: Spicy radish salad (musaengchae) instead of cabbage kimchi.
Pressure cooker: cook the pork 25 minutes at high pressure with a natural release.
Use leftover pork in kimchi fried rice the next day.
safety: Pork belly should be simmered until tender, well past 145°F (63°C).
Refrigerate leftover pork and fresh kimchi within 2 hours; fresh kimchi keeps 3 to 4 days and begins to sour.
Wear gloves when mixing the kimchi seasoning; chilli burns skin and eyes.

dishes.title: Tafelspitz
dishes.summary: Vienna's boiled beef: a whole rump cap held for hours below the boil with marrow bones, root vegetables and a charred onion, served in two courses, first the clear amber broth with marrow on toast, then the sliced beef with apple horseradish, a chive sauce and crisp rösti. It is in the course because one pot must yield a broth of perfect clarity and meat that is tender yet sliceable, with two cold sauces made to match.
skills: simmering beef rump for hours below the boil
equipment: Large stockpot, at least 8 quarts (7.5 litres)
Dry cast-iron frying pan for charring the onion
Clean tea towel for squeezing potatoes
Non-stick or cast-iron frying pan, about 10 inches (25 cm), for the rösti
Small bowls and a whisk for the sauces
Warm soup plates and dinner plates

ingredients.item: Beef rump cap (tafelspitz), also sold as top sirloin cap or picanha, fat cap on
Beef marrow bones, cut in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces
Black peppercorns, bay leaves and a sprig of lovage or celery leaves

ingredients.note: boiled in their skins the day before and chilled

mise: The day before: boil the potatoes in their skins for 15 minutes until just tender, cool and refrigerate.
Char the onion halves cut side down in a dry cast-iron pan over high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until black.
Rinse the marrow bones in cold water.
Peel and cut the vegetables in large pieces.
Grate the apples into the lemon juice and stir in the horseradish; season with a pinch of salt and sugar.
Hard-boil 2 eggs for 10 minutes, cool, and take out the yolks.

timeline.do: Boil and chill the potatoes for rösti.
Char the onion; put the bones in cold water and bring to a simmer, skimming.
Add the beef to the trembling broth; hold just below a simmer.
Add the vegetables and aromatics.
Make the apple horseradish and chive sauce; grate and cook the rösti.
Strain and season the broth; slice the beef.
Serve the broth with marrow toast, then the beef with sauces and rösti.

steps.do: Put the marrow bones in the stockpot with the 4 quarts (3.8 litres) cold water. Bring slowly to a bare simmer over medium heat, about 30 minutes, skimming off the grey foam as it rises.
steps.look: Grey scum gathers on the surface and is lifted off until the liquid looks clear; small bubbles break only at the edge.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which churns the scum back in and clouds the broth.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and skim patiently; clarity is decided in this first half hour.

steps.do: Lower the beef into the hot liquid, fat side up. When it returns to a tremble, hold it at 185 to 195°F (85 to 90°C), uncovered, skimming every 15 minutes, for 2 hours.
steps.look: The surface shivers but never bubbles; the beef turns grey-brown and firms.
steps.mistake: Letting it bubble, so the meat tightens and dries and the broth clouds.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer; set the heat at the lowest that holds the temperature.

steps.do: Add the charred onion, carrots, celeriac, leek, parsley root, peppercorns, bay and lovage. Continue at the same gentle heat for another 1 to 1 1/2 hours until a carving fork slides into the beef and out without lifting it.
steps.look: The broth turns a deep, clear amber from the burnt onion; it smells of beef, root vegetables and celery.
steps.mistake: Adding the vegetables at the start, so they disintegrate and cloud the broth.
steps.fix: Add them in the final 90 minutes only.

steps.do: Make the chive sauce: soak the bread in the milk, then squeeze it. Mash the egg yolks with the mustard and bread to a paste, then whisk in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) oil in a thin stream and the vinegar. Fold in the chives and season.
steps.look: A thick, pale, creamy sauce flecked with green, tasting sharp and herbal.
steps.mistake: Adding the oil too fast, so it looks oily and loose.
steps.fix: Whisk in slowly; a spoonful of broth can bring it back together.

steps.do: Make the rösti: peel the cold potatoes and grate them on the coarse side of the box grater. Season with salt. Heat 3 tbsp (40 g) of the clarified butter in the frying pan over medium heat, add the potato and press lightly into a cake 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. Cook 12 to 15 minutes until deep golden underneath.
steps.look: A gentle, steady sizzle; the edge turns golden and crisp and the cake slides when the pan is shaken.
steps.mistake: Pressing hard and turning the heat up, so the rösti is dense and burnt outside, raw inside.
steps.fix: Medium heat, light pressure and patience.

steps.do: Slide the rösti onto a plate, invert the pan over it and flip it back in. Add the remaining butter around the edge and cook 10 minutes more until golden.
steps.look: A crisp, golden, lacy cake on both sides, tender inside.
steps.mistake: Flipping with a spatula, which breaks it.
steps.fix: Use the plate method; patch any break with a press of the spatula.

steps.do: Lift out the beef and keep it warm, covered, in a little broth. Strain the broth through the muslin-lined sieve. Season with the salt. Scoop the marrow from the bones.
steps.look: A crystal-clear, amber broth with a few golden fat beads on top.
steps.mistake: Pressing the vegetables through the sieve, which clouds the broth.
steps.fix: Let it drain; do not press.

steps.do: First course: ladle the hot broth into warm soup plates with a few pieces of the cooked carrot. Serve with toast spread with the marrow, salted and peppered.
steps.look: Steaming, clear amber broth; marrow melting into the warm toast.
steps.mistake: Lukewarm broth that loses its aroma in the bowl.
steps.fix: Bring it back to a bare simmer before serving.

steps.do: Second course: slice the beef across the grain into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Arrange on warm plates with a ladle of broth over, the rösti in wedges, and the apple horseradish and chive sauce beside.
steps.look: Moist, rosy-grey slices with a little edge of fat, glistening with broth.
steps.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which makes stringy slices.
steps.fix: Find the grain and cut across it; a sharp carving knife in long strokes.

dishes.science: Clarity comes from temperature and skimming. When cold water heats slowly, soluble proteins from the bones and meat coagulate into foam that rises and can be removed; boiling would break those particles into fine specks and churn fat into an emulsion, both of which cloud the broth. Holding the beef at 185 to 195°F (85 to 90°C) converts its collagen to gelatin over hours while keeping the muscle fibres from contracting as hard as they would at a boil, so it stays moist and sliceable. The charred onion adds colour and a deep, slightly bitter, caramelised flavour from browning reactions on its cut surface. Horseradish heat comes from compounds released when the root's cells are broken by grating; lemon slows the reaction and holds the heat.
dishes.plating: Broth in warm, wide soup plates with a few carrot coins, marrow toast on a side plate. For the beef: three slices overlapping on a warm plate, a ladle of broth poured over to keep them moist, a wedge of rösti, and spoonfuls of apple horseradish and chive sauce side by side at the edge, never on the meat.

pairing.drink: A Grüner Veltliner, Austria's own white: peppery and crisp, it meets horseradish and chive and cuts through the rich broth.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Alte Reben’ Grüner Veltliner 2023: an Austrian Grüner on the Brennan's list, the classic Viennese partner for Tafelspitz.

variations: Add Frittaten: thin pancakes rolled and cut into ribbons, warmed in the broth.
Spinach purée as a third accompaniment, made with a little of the broth.
Leftover beef: slice cold and dress with vinegar, oil and onion for Rindfleischsalat.
safety: Cool leftover broth and beef quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Grating fresh horseradish releases fumes that sting the eyes: grate near an open window and keep your face back.

dishes.title: Hünkar Beğendi
dishes.summary: A tender lamb and tomato braise served on a smoky aubergine purée enriched with béchamel and kaşar cheese, a dish of the Ottoman palace kitchens. It is in the course because it is a refined variation on a mother sauce: aubergines charred over open flame, folded into a béchamel cooked properly, and a braise reduced to a glossy sauce to sit on top.
skills: a béchamel with the smoked flesh and kaşar cheese
equipment: Gas hob, barbecue or a very hot overhead grill (broiler) for charring the aubergines
Heavy casserole or saucepan with lid, for the lamb
Medium heavy saucepan for the béchamel

ingredients.note: cut in 1 inch (2.5 cm) cubes, some fat left on

ingredients.item: Green Turkish pepper or green pepper

ingredients.note: in a bowl of 4 cups (950 ml) water

ingredients.item: Kaşar or another mild melting cheese (young pecorino, gruyère)

mise: Cube the lamb and pat it dry.
Chop the onion and pepper, mince the garlic, grate the tomatoes.
Make the lemon water in a bowl.
Warm the milk.
Grate the cheese.
Line the hob around the burner with foil to catch aubergine drips.

timeline.do: Brown the lamb, build the braise and simmer covered 90 minutes.
Char the aubergines; peel and soak the flesh in lemon water.
Make the béchamel; fold in the aubergine and cheese.
Uncover the lamb and reduce the sauce.
Spread the begendi on a platter and spoon the lamb on top.

steps.do: Heat the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and 1 tbsp (15 g) butter in the casserole over high heat and brown the lamb in two batches, 5 to 6 minutes each, until deep brown on several sides. Lift out.
steps.look: Loud sizzle, a dark brown crust on the meat and a brown film forming on the pan base.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the lamb releases liquid and stews grey.
steps.fix: Brown in batches; let the pan reheat between them.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion and pepper and cook 8 minutes until soft and golden, scraping up the browned bits. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the 2 tbsp (30 g) tomato paste and stir 2 minutes until it darkens.
steps.look: The paste turns from bright red to brick red and smells sweet and roasted.
steps.mistake: Burning the tomato paste, which turns it bitter.
steps.fix: Keep stirring and lower the heat if it sticks hard.

steps.do: Return the lamb with its juices, add the grated tomatoes, the 2 cups (480 ml) hot water, thyme, pul biber and 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 75 to 90 minutes until the lamb is tender.
steps.look: A gentle bubble under the lid; the lamb softens until a piece crushes against the side of the pot.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the lamb.
steps.fix: Keep the bubbles small. Add a splash of water if it gets dry.

steps.do: Char the aubergines: prick each a few times with a fork and lay them directly on a gas flame on high, turning with tongs every 2 to 3 minutes, for 12 to 15 minutes until the skin is black and blistered all over and the flesh collapses.
steps.look: The skin crackles and blackens, the aubergine slumps and leaks juice; the kitchen smells strongly of smoke.
steps.mistake: Taking them off while still firm, so the flesh is raw and not smoky.
steps.fix: Keep going until they are completely soft right to the stem end.

steps.do: Put the aubergines on a board, slit them open and scoop out the flesh with a spoon, leaving the black skin. Drop the flesh straight into the lemon water and leave 10 minutes. Drain and squeeze out as much water as possible, then mash with a fork.
steps.look: Pale, smoky flesh, flecked with a few black bits, which stays light rather than turning grey.
steps.mistake: Leaving the flesh in the air, so it darkens.
steps.fix: Lemon water stops the browning; squeeze it well so the purée is not watery.

steps.do: Make the béchamel: melt the 3 tbsp (45 g) butter in the saucepan over medium heat, add the 3 tbsp (25 g) flour and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes without browning. Whisk in the warm milk gradually and cook 5 minutes, whisking, until thick and smooth.
steps.look: A white roux that smells like baked pastry; then a smooth, glossy sauce that coats the back of a spoon thickly.
steps.mistake: Adding cold milk all at once, which forms lumps.
steps.fix: Use warm milk and add it gradually. Whisk or sieve out any lumps.

steps.do: Stir the mashed aubergine into the béchamel and cook 3 to 4 minutes, beating with a wooden spoon. Add the grated cheese and stir until melted and stretchy. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, smoky purée the colour of pale coffee, glossy and slightly stretchy from the cheese.
steps.mistake: Watery purée, because the aubergine was not squeezed.
steps.fix: Cook a few minutes longer to drive off water.

steps.do: Uncover the lamb and simmer 10 to 15 minutes to reduce the sauce until thick and glossy and clinging to the meat. Taste for salt.
steps.look: A rich, red sauce that coats the lamb, oil beginning to glisten at the edges.
steps.mistake: Serving a thin, watery stew that floods the purée.
steps.fix: Reduce until the sauce is thick.

steps.do: Spread the hot begendi on a warm platter or plates, making a well in the centre. Spoon the lamb and its sauce into the well and scatter with parsley.
steps.look: Pale, smoky purée around a glossy red braise, parsley bright green on top.
steps.mistake: Mixing the two together.
steps.fix: Lamb on top, never stirred in.

dishes.science: Charring over a flame burns the aubergine skin and steams the flesh inside it; smoke compounds from the burning skin, especially phenols, soak into the soft flesh, giving the dish its smoky character. Aubergine flesh browns quickly in air because an enzyme oxidises its phenolic compounds; lemon juice lowers the pH and slows that enzyme. The béchamel thickens because flour starch, separated by butter in the roux, absorbs milk and swells as it heats; cooking the roux briefly removes the raw flour taste without browning it. Cheese adds fat and proteins that melt into the sauce. Searing the lamb first creates browned flavours through the Maillard reaction, and slow, covered simmering converts its connective tissue to gelatin.
dishes.plating: Use a warm platter or wide plates. Spread the begendi in a smooth round with the back of a spoon, lifting it slightly at the edge to form a rim. Spoon the lamb into the centre so the red sauce pools inside the pale ring, finish with parsley and a pinch of pul biber over the purée edge.

pairing.drink: A medium-bodied southern French or Turkish red: its spice and soft tannin meet the lamb braise and stand up to the smoky aubergine.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023: a spicy, generous Rhône red on the Brennan's list that suits lamb in tomato.

variations: Beef: use chuck steak cubes and braise 2 hours.
Chicken: thighs browned and braised 35 minutes in the same sauce.
Vegetarian: serve the begendi with a mushroom and chickpea braise.
safety: Char aubergines with long tongs and watch for dripping juices that can flare on a gas burner.
Cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; reheat the braise to 165°F (74°C).

dishes.title: Chelo Kebab Koobideh with Tahdig
dishes.summary: Iran's national dish: lamb mince kneaded with grated onion until it clings to wide flat skewers, grilled over hot coals and served on chelo, long-grain rice parboiled then steamed with saffron over a golden crust called tahdig, which is lifted out whole. It is in the course because both halves need technique: mince that holds to metal without cracking, and rice that steams fluffy above a crust that releases cleanly.
skills: kneading lamb mince until it clings to wide skewers
chelo rice steamed with a golden tahdig
equipment: Flat, wide kebab skewers, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide, at least four
Charcoal grill with two bricks or a rack to suspend the skewers above the coals
Box grater and a clean tea towel
Large non-stick pot with a tight lid, about 9 inches (23 cm), for the rice
Clean tea towel to wrap the lid
Mortar and pestle for the saffron
Large flat platter for inverting the tahdig

ingredients.item: Lamb shoulder mince, about 20% fat (or half lamb, half beef)

ingredients.note: ground with a pinch of sugar

ingredients.item: Fine salt, for soaking and parboiling
Unsalted butter, for the tahdig and topping
Raw onion, fresh herbs (basil, mint) and flatbread

mise: Rinse the rice in cool water 5 or 6 times until it runs clear, then soak in water with 1 tbsp (17 g) salt for 2 hours.
Grind the saffron with a pinch of sugar in the mortar, pour on the 1/4 cup (60 ml) hot water and steep 15 minutes.
Grate the onion on the coarse side of the grater and wring it in a tea towel until no more juice comes out; discard the juice.
Wrap the lid of the rice pot in a clean tea towel, tying the corners on top so they cannot hang near the flame.
Light the charcoal 40 minutes before grilling and set up bricks so the skewers can rest over the coals without touching the grate.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice; steep the saffron.
Knead the kebab mince 10 minutes; chill 1 hour.
Shape the kebabs on skewers; chill.
Parboil the rice and drain; build the tahdig layer and start steaming.
Light the coals.
Grill the kebabs and tomatoes.
Invert the tahdig; serve rice, kebabs, tomatoes and sumac together.

steps.do: Put the lamb, wrung onion pulp, 2 tsp (10 g) salt, pepper and turmeric in the large bowl. Knead firmly with one hand, pushing and folding, for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The mince changes from loose crumbs to a sticky, pale, tacky paste that stretches when pulled and sticks to your upturned palm.
steps.mistake: Stopping after 2 minutes, so the meat falls off the skewers.
steps.fix: Knead the full time. Test: a handful should cling to your palm held upside down.

steps.do: Cover the bowl and chill the kneaded mixture in the fridge for 1 hour, until firm and cold.
steps.look: Firm, cold mince that is easier to shape.
steps.mistake: Shaping warm, soft meat, which slides down the skewer.
steps.fix: Chill until it feels firm and cold.

steps.do: Bring 3 quarts (2.8 litres) water and 2 tbsp (33 g) salt to a rolling boil. Drain the soaked rice and add it. Boil 5 to 7 minutes, stirring gently once, until the grains are soft outside with a firm, white dot in the centre. Drain in the sieve and rinse briefly with lukewarm water.
steps.look: Long, separate grains that bend when pressed but still have a slight bite in the middle.
steps.mistake: Overboiling, so the rice turns mushy and breaks.
steps.fix: Test a grain every minute after 4 minutes.

steps.do: Make the tahdig layer: put the 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil, 1 tbsp (15 g) butter and 2 tbsp (30 ml) saffron water in the non-stick pot over medium heat. Mix 1 cup (about 150 g) of the parboiled rice with the 3 tbsp (45 g) yoghurt and spread it evenly over the base, pressing it flat.
steps.look: A sizzling, golden layer of rice flat against the base of the pot.
steps.mistake: Too little fat, so the crust sticks.
steps.fix: Be generous with the oil; the crust fries in it.

steps.do: Heap the remaining rice on top in a pyramid, not touching the sides. Poke 5 or 6 holes to the bottom with the handle of a wooden spoon. Dot with 1 tbsp (15 g) butter and drizzle with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water.
steps.look: A mound of rice with small steam holes.
steps.mistake: Pressing the rice down, which makes it heavy.
steps.fix: Pile it loosely so steam can circulate.

steps.do: Cook 10 minutes on medium heat until you hear a steady sizzle, then cover with the towel-wrapped lid, turn the heat to low and steam 45 to 50 minutes.
steps.look: Steam rising through the holes, then quiet; a toasty smell. The grains on top turn fluffy and separate.
steps.mistake: Heat too high, so the crust burns before the rice steams.
steps.fix: Medium-low heat; the smell should be toasted, never burnt.

steps.do: Shape the kebabs: with wet hands, take about 3 1/2 oz (100 g) of mince and squeeze it around a flat skewer, pressing it into an even layer about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick and 8 inches (20 cm) long. Pinch along its length with thumb and finger every 1 inch (2.5 cm) to make ridges, and press the ends tight to the metal.
steps.look: A long, even, ridged kebab firmly attached at both ends.
steps.mistake: Thick spots and thin spots, so it cooks unevenly and breaks.
steps.fix: Wet your hands and smooth it evenly; reshape if it slips.

steps.do: Grill: rest the skewers over very hot coals so the meat hangs about 3 inches (8 cm) above them without touching the grate. Turn every 30 seconds for the first 2 minutes, then every minute, for 5 to 6 minutes in total, until browned with charred ridges and the centre reads 160°F (71°C). Grill the tomatoes alongside.
steps.look: Sizzling fat dripping into the coals, the meat firming and browning evenly all around; tomatoes blistering.
steps.mistake: Leaving the skewers still at the start, so the soft underside slides off into the fire.
steps.fix: Turn constantly at first until the surface sets all round.

steps.do: Brush the kebabs with the melted butter mixed with the remaining saffron water as they come off. Slide the meat off the skewers using a piece of flatbread to grip it.
steps.look: Glossy, golden kebabs that smell of saffron and butter, the ridges still crisp.
steps.mistake: Pulling the meat off with a fork, which breaks it.
steps.fix: Grip with bread and slide in one firm movement.

steps.do: Spoon some of the steamed rice from the top into a bowl and mix it with a little saffron water for golden rice. Then put a platter over the pot and invert it confidently so the tahdig comes out whole. Serve rice, golden rice, kebabs and tomatoes with sumac, raw onion, herbs and bread.
steps.look: A golden, glassy rice crust that crackles; fluffy white and saffron rice above it.
steps.mistake: Inverting timidly, so the crust breaks.
steps.fix: Run a spatula round the edge first, then invert in one motion. If it sticks, set the pot on a damp cloth for 2 minutes.

dishes.science: Salt and long kneading draw myosin, a muscle protein, out of the meat fibres into a sticky film that binds the mince and glues it to the metal skewer; when heated, that protein sets like glue. Onion juice is discarded because its water and enzymes weaken the bond and make the kebab slide. About 20 percent fat keeps the kebab moist and helps it hold as it shrinks. Persian rice is parboiled so its outer starch softens while the core stays firm, then steamed gently so the grains finish cooking separately and lengthen. The tahdig forms at the bottom as starch and yoghurt proteins fry in fat, browning through the Maillard reaction into a crisp crust.
dishes.plating: Use a large oval platter: the tahdig in shards or one golden disc at one end, a mound of white rice topped with saffron rice and a pat of butter in the middle, two kebabs laid long beside it with grilled tomatoes at the tips. Sumac in a bowl to sprinkle over the rice, herbs and onion on the side.

pairing.drink: Doogh, a chilled, lightly salted yoghurt drink with dried mint, sometimes sparkling: tangy and cool beside rich, charred lamb and buttered rice.

variations: Kabab barg: thin strips of marinated lamb loin on the same skewers.
Joojeh kabab: chicken thighs marinated in saffron, lemon and yoghurt.
No flat skewers: shape the mince into long logs on a tray and cook under a very hot overhead grill (broiler), turning once.
safety: Cook minced lamb to 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
Flat metal skewers become extremely hot: use oven gloves or a cloth to turn them.
Light charcoal outdoors only.
