dishes.title: Kibbeh Maqliyeh (Fried Kibbeh)
dishes.summary: Torpedo-shaped Lebanese kibbeh with a thin shell of fine bulgur and lean lamb, hollowed by finger, filled with spiced lamb, onions and pine nuts, and fried until deep brown. It is in the course because shaping kibbeh is a skill cooks spend years refining: a shell thin and even enough to fry crisp, sealed so it never bursts in the oil.
skills: a fine bulgur and lean lamb shell
hollowing by finger into thin torpedoes
equipment: Meat grinder or a butcher willing to mince twice
Bowl of iced water for your hands
Heavy deep saucepan or Dutch oven for frying
Lid that fits the frying pan, kept nearby

ingredients.item: Lean lamb leg, all fat and sinew removed, minced twice
Minced lamb shoulder, for the filling
Onion, finely diced, for the filling
Fine salt and black pepper, for the filling
Sunflower or other neutral oil, for frying
Plain yoghurt, lemon wedges and a chopped salad

mise: Rinse the bulgur in a sieve, squeeze it dry in your fist and leave it in a bowl to swell for 10 minutes.
Keep the lean lamb in the coldest part of the fridge until you need it.
Dice the filling onion; grate the shell onion.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes until golden.
Fill a bowl with iced water for your hands.
Set up the frying station: pot no more than half full of oil, thermometer, spider and rack.

timeline.do: Soak the bulgur; cook and cool the filling.
Make the shell dough in the processor; chill 15 minutes.
Shape and fill about 20 kibbeh; chill on a tray.
Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C).
Fry in batches 4 to 5 minutes; drain on a rack.
Serve hot with yoghurt, lemon and salad.

steps.do: Make the filling: heat the 3 tbsp (40 g) samneh in the frying pan over medium heat, cook the diced onion 6 to 8 minutes until soft and golden, then add the shoulder mince and cook, breaking it up, 6 to 8 minutes until browned and the fat runs. Stir in the pine nuts, allspice, pomegranate molasses, salt and pepper. Cool completely.
steps.look: Golden, crumbly, glistening mince with pine nuts, tasting sweet, sour and warmly spiced.
steps.mistake: Using warm filling, which softens the shell and makes it tear.
steps.fix: Spread on a plate and chill to cool quickly.

steps.do: Make the shell: process the very cold lean lamb, grated onion, spices and salt to a smooth paste. Add the soaked bulgur and process again in bursts, adding iced water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time, until the dough is smooth, cold and holds together like soft clay.
steps.look: A pinkish, smooth, slightly sticky dough that takes a fingerprint without cracking.
steps.mistake: Letting it warm in the processor, so the fat smears and it turns greasy.
steps.fix: Process in short bursts and add iced water; chill 15 minutes if it feels warm.

steps.do: Wet your hands in iced water. Take a piece of dough the size of a walnut, about 1 1/2 oz (40 g), and roll it into an oval.
steps.look: A smooth, cold oval with no cracks at the edges and a slightly tacky surface.
steps.mistake: Dry hands, so the dough sticks and tears.
steps.fix: Dip your hands in iced water between every kibbeh.

steps.do: Hold the oval in one palm and push the index finger of your other hand into one end. Rotate the dough around your finger while pressing it against your palm, so the walls thin out evenly until the shell is no thicker than a coin and about 3 inches (8 cm) long.
steps.look: A hollow, even cup with thin walls you can almost see light through at the edges.
steps.mistake: Thick walls at the bottom, which stay raw while the outside burns.
steps.fix: Rotate steadily and press gently all the way round; patch any hole with a pinch of dough.

steps.do: Fill the shell with 1 heaped tsp of filling, about 1/2 oz (15 g), without packing it. Bring the open edges together, pinch to seal, and roll the end between your palms to a point, making a torpedo. Smooth any cracks with a wet finger.
steps.look: A sealed torpedo with tapered ends and a smooth surface.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the seam splits in the oil.
steps.fix: Fill loosely; seal and smooth the seam completely.

steps.do: Lay the kibbeh on a tray and chill 15 minutes while the oil heats to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: Firm, cold torpedoes that hold their pointed shape when picked up.
steps.mistake: Frying soft, warm kibbeh, which deform.
steps.fix: Chill them longer until they are firm.

steps.do: Fry 4 or 5 at a time, lowering them gently with the spider, for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep brown all over and floating. The shell should read 160°F (71°C) in the thickest part.
steps.look: A steady sizzle, the kibbeh rising to the surface and turning an even mahogany; it smells of warm spice and roasted lamb.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding, which drops the oil temperature and makes them oily.
steps.fix: Small batches; let the oil recover to 350°F (175°C) between them.

steps.do: Drain them standing on end on the rack for 2 minutes, then serve hot with yoghurt, lemon wedges and salad.
steps.look: Crisp, dark shells that crack when bitten, revealing a juicy, spiced filling.
steps.mistake: Draining flat on paper, so the base turns soggy.
steps.fix: Stand them on end on a rack.

dishes.science: Fine bulgur is wheat that has been boiled, dried and cracked, so it hydrates quickly from the meat's moisture. Its starch and the lamb's proteins, worked in the processor with salt, form a cohesive dough that can be stretched thin. The shell meat must be lean because fat melts in the fryer, turns to steam and can burst the seam. Iced water keeps the paste cold so the remaining fat does not smear and make the shell greasy. At 350°F (175°C) the outside dries and browns quickly through the Maillard reaction, forming a crisp crust that limits oil absorption, while heat passes through a thin shell fast enough to cook it through before the outside burns.
dishes.plating: Serve on a warm platter, the kibbeh stacked in a loose pyramid or standing upright in a row, with a bowl of thick yoghurt, lemon wedges and a fresh, sharp salad such as fattoush beside them. Cut one in half to show the filling.

pairing.drink: Arak diluted with iced water, or a Lebanese red: arak's anise freshness cuts the fried crust, and a Lebanese red's spice matches the allspice and lamb.
pairing.brennans: Château Musar Bekaa Valley 2003: the famous Lebanese red on the Brennan's list, a natural match for kibbeh's spice and lamb.

variations: Kibbeh bil sanieh: press half the shell dough into a tray, add the filling, cover with the rest, score and bake.
Kibbeh nayyeh: the raw version, made only with the freshest lamb and served at once.
Pumpkin kibbeh: a vegetarian shell of pumpkin and bulgur with a chickpea and spinach filling.
safety: Cook the lamb shell to 160°F (71°C) at the thickest point.
Fill the pot no more than half full of oil, keep a lid nearby, and never leave hot oil unattended.
This dish contains pine nuts: ask your guests about allergies before serving.

dishes.title: Chiles en Nogada
dishes.summary: Puebla's September dish: whole poblano chillies charred and peeled, stuffed with a picadillo of pork, fruit, almonds and spices, covered in a cool, fresh walnut sauce and scattered with pomegranate seeds and parsley. It is in the course because it combines the stuffed-chilli skills with a fruit and meat filling balanced between sweet and savoury and a delicate raw walnut sauce that must be smooth and pale.
equipment: Gas hob or a very hot overhead grill (broiler) for charring
Bowl and cling film or a plastic bag for steaming the chillies
Large frying pan or casserole for the picadillo

ingredients.note: straight and smooth for easier peeling

ingredients.item: Queso fresco or mild fresh goat's cheese
Pork mince (or half pork, half beef)
Apple, pear and peach (or ripe plantain)
ingredients.note: peeled and cut in 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice

ingredients.item: Candied citron or candied pineapple, chopped

mise: The night before: soak the walnuts in the 1 cup (240 ml) milk in the fridge.
In the morning, peel the thin brown skins from the walnuts with a small knife or your nails; it is slow but makes the sauce white and not bitter.
Peel and dice the fruit, keeping the apple and pear in water with a squeeze of lime so they do not brown.
Chop onion and garlic; peel and chop the tomatoes.
Seed the pomegranate by tapping halves over a bowl with a wooden spoon.
Pick the parsley leaves.

timeline.do: Soak walnuts in milk.
Peel the walnuts; make and chill the nogada.
Char, steam and peel the chillies; slit and seed them.
Cook the picadillo and let it cool to warm.
Stuff the chillies.
Cover with nogada, pomegranate and parsley; serve at room temperature.

steps.do: Make the nogada: drain the peeled walnuts and put them in the blender with the queso fresco, crema, 1/2 cup (120 ml) milk, sherry, sugar, cinnamon and salt. Blend 2 minutes until very smooth. It should pour slowly, like double cream. Chill.
steps.look: A pale ivory, completely smooth sauce, tasting gently sweet, nutty and fresh.
steps.mistake: Leaving the walnut skins on, which turns the sauce grey and bitter.
steps.fix: Peel them all. If bitter, add a little more cheese and sugar.

steps.do: Char the chillies directly on a gas flame on high or under a very hot grill, turning with tongs every minute or so, for 6 to 8 minutes until the skin is blistered and black all over but the flesh is not cooked through.
steps.look: Blackened, blistered skin that crackles; the chilli is still firm enough to hold its shape.
steps.mistake: Charring too long, so the flesh becomes soft and tears when stuffed.
steps.fix: Take each chilli off as soon as all sides are blistered.

steps.do: Put the hot chillies in a bowl, cover tightly with cling film and steam 10 minutes. Then rub off the charred skin with your fingers and a damp cloth, without rinsing.
steps.look: The skin slips off easily, revealing glossy dark green flesh.
steps.mistake: Rinsing under the tap, which washes away the smoky flavour.
steps.fix: Wipe with a damp cloth; a few black flecks are fine.

steps.do: Make a slit down one side of each chilli from just below the stem to 1/2 inch (1 cm) from the tip. Carefully cut out the seed pod and scrape away the veins, keeping the stem and the chilli whole.
steps.look: An intact chilli with an open pocket, no seeds inside.
steps.mistake: Tearing the chilli by cutting too long a slit.
steps.fix: A tear can be closed with a toothpick after stuffing.

steps.do: Make the picadillo: heat the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the large pan over medium heat, add the onion and cook 5 minutes until soft, then the garlic for 1 minute. Add the pork and cook, breaking it up, 8 minutes until it loses its pink and reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: Fine, evenly browned mince with no pink, the onion soft and sweet smelling.
steps.mistake: Leaving big lumps of mince.
steps.fix: Break it up thoroughly with a wooden spoon.

steps.do: Add the tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until they collapse. Add the drained fruit, raisins, almonds, citron, cinnamon and cloves and cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the fruit is just tender but holds its shape and the mixture is moist but not wet. Season.
steps.look: A glossy, jewel-like filling: cubes of fruit, raisins and almonds through the meat, tasting sweet, savoury and gently spiced.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the fruit turns to mush.
steps.fix: Stop when a piece of apple is tender but still a cube.

steps.do: Let the picadillo cool until warm, then spoon it into each chilli through the slit, filling generously so the chilli looks plump. Close the edges over the filling.
steps.look: Plump, glossy green chillies, slightly gaping to show the filling.
steps.mistake: Stuffing with hot filling, which makes the nogada split later.
steps.fix: Warm, not hot. The dish is served at room temperature.

steps.do: Lay the chillies on the plates. Spoon the cold nogada over each so it covers it completely, leaving the stem showing. Scatter generously with pomegranate seeds and parsley leaves.
steps.look: Green chilli under white sauce, scattered with red seeds and green leaves.
steps.mistake: Heating the nogada, which thickens it and makes it grainy.
steps.fix: Serve the sauce cool, straight from the fridge.

dishes.science: Charring blisters and burns the chilli's tough outer skin while steam forms beneath it; covering the hot chillies traps that steam so the skin separates cleanly from the flesh. Walnut skins are rich in tannins, bitter and astringent compounds that also turn grey in a sauce; soaking in milk softens the skins for peeling, and milk proteins bind some tannin. The nogada is raw, an emulsion of walnut oil and cheese fat in milk held by proteins; heating it would make the proteins clump and the sauce grainy. The picadillo balances sugars from fruit with savoury browned meat, and cooking the fruit briefly keeps its pectin intact so the pieces hold their shape.
dishes.plating: A white plate to show the colours. Lay one chilli diagonally across the centre, stem at the top left. Spoon the nogada over to cover it fully in a smooth white blanket, then scatter pomegranate seeds thickly across it and tuck three or four parsley leaves along its length: green, white and red.

pairing.drink: A pale cream or dry Amontillado sherry: the nogada carries sherry, and its nutty, gently sweet character matches the walnuts and fruit.
pairing.brennans: Barbadillo ‘Pale Cream’ Sherry NV: a lightly sweet sherry on the Brennan's list that mirrors the sherry and walnuts in the nogada.

variations: Capeados: dip the stuffed chillies in a whipped egg batter and fry before saucing, the older Puebla style.
Vegetarian picadillo: mushrooms, potato and plantain in place of pork.
Pecan nogada: if fresh walnuts are not in season, use fresh pecans, peeled the same way.
safety: Cook the pork mince to 160°F (71°C).
Keep the nogada chilled below 40°F (4°C) until serving and discard after 2 hours at room temperature.
This dish contains walnuts and almonds: ask your guests about allergies before serving.
Wear gloves when seeding chillies and do not touch your eyes.

dishes.title: Kerala Sadya
dishes.summary: The vegetarian feast of Kerala served on a banana leaf: red rice, dal with ghee, sambar, avial, a cabbage thoran, olan in coconut milk, a beetroot pachadi, papadams, pickle and banana chips, ending with a milk payasam. It is in the course because cooking eight dishes for one leaf is a lesson in planning, timing and tempering, each dish finished with spices bloomed in hot oil, and in serving in a set order.
skills: planning a dozen dishes on a banana leaf: avial, thoran, sambar, olan, pachadi, payasam
equipment: Four large pieces of banana leaf, or large plates
Large heavy pot for the rice
Pressure cooker or heavy saucepan for the dal
Five medium heavy saucepans or kadais
Small tempering pan (tadka pan) or a small frying pan
Blender or spice grinder for coconut pastes
Deep pan and thermometer for frying papadams

ingredients.item: Mixed vegetables for sambar: drumstick, okra, aubergine, shallots, tomato

ingredients.note: soaked in 1/2 cup (120 ml) warm water and strained

ingredients.item: Mixed vegetables for avial: carrot, green beans, yam, raw banana, cucumber or ash gourd
ingredients.us: 4 cups, cut in 2 inch (5 cm) batons

ingredients.item: Short-grain rice or broken rice, for payasam
Bought mango or lime pickle, banana chips and jaggery-coated banana chips

mise: Write the order of work on a card and tape it up; read it before each dish.
Soak the rice; soak and strain the tamarind.
Cut every vegetable before you light the stove: sambar vegetables in chunks, avial vegetables in batons, cabbage shredded, ash gourd sliced, beetroot grated.

Make three coconut pastes in the blender: for avial, 1 cup (100 g) coconut, 2 green chillies, 1 tsp (3 g) cumin, ground coarse with a splash of water; for pachadi, 1/2 cup (50 g) coconut, 1 green chilli and 1 tsp (3 g) mustard seeds, ground smooth; keep the remaining coconut for thoran.
Set out a small bowl for each tempering: 1 tsp (3 g) mustard seeds, 1 dried chilli and a sprig of curry leaves per dish.
Wash and dry the banana leaves; wipe with a damp cloth.

timeline.do: Start the payasam on the lowest heat; cook the dals.
Cook the rice; build the sambar.
Make the avial and olan.
Make the pachadi and thoran.
Finish the payasam; temper the dal.
Fry papadams; reheat the hot dishes.
Lay the leaves and serve in order, rice and dal first.

steps.do: Start the payasam: put the 5 cups (1.2 litres) milk and the rinsed rice in the heavy saucepan and bring to the boil, then simmer on the lowest heat for 90 minutes to 2 hours, stirring every 10 minutes and scraping the base, until reduced by about half and pale gold. Stir in the sugar and cardamom and cook 10 minutes more.
steps.look: Milk thickening slowly to a creamy, ivory-gold consistency with very soft rice; it smells of caramelised milk and cardamom.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat to hurry, so the milk catches and tastes burnt.
steps.fix: Low heat and regular scraping; if it catches, pour into a clean pan without scraping.

steps.do: Cook the dals: pressure-cook the moong dal with 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) water and a pinch of turmeric for 2 whistles (or simmer 25 minutes) until soft; mash and salt. Separately cook the toor dal with 2 cups (480 ml) water and turmeric for 3 whistles (or simmer 40 minutes) and mash.
steps.look: Two pots of soft, creamy dal that fall apart when stirred.
steps.mistake: Undercooking the toor dal, so the sambar is grainy.
steps.fix: Cook until it collapses completely when pressed.

steps.do: Cook the rice: drain the soaked matta rice and boil in 10 cups (2.4 litres) salted water for 25 to 30 minutes until tender, then drain like pasta. Keep covered.
steps.look: Plump, separate, reddish grains, tender with a slight chew.
steps.mistake: Cooking it like basmati by absorption, which leaves matta rice hard.
steps.fix: Boil in plenty of water and drain.

steps.do: Make the sambar: simmer the sambar vegetables in 3 cups (720 ml) water with salt for 10 minutes, add the tamarind water and sambar powder and simmer 8 minutes, then stir in the mashed toor dal and simmer 5 minutes. Temper: heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) coconut oil, add 1 tsp (3 g) mustard seeds, and when they pop add a dried chilli and curry leaves; pour over the sambar.
steps.look: A thick, tangy, orange-brown stew; the mustard seeds crackle and the curry leaves hiss and turn glossy in the oil.
steps.mistake: Adding the tempering ingredients to cold oil, so they never pop and taste raw.
steps.fix: Wait until the oil shimmers and a test seed pops instantly.

steps.do: Make the avial: cook the avial vegetables with turmeric, salt and 1/2 cup (120 ml) water, covered, 10 to 12 minutes until just tender, adding the hardest ones first. Stir in the coarse coconut paste and cook 3 minutes, then fold in 1/2 cup (120 g) yoghurt off the heat. Drizzle with 2 tbsp (30 ml) raw coconut oil and curry leaves.
steps.look: Batons of vegetable that hold their shape, coated in a thick, pale, coconut-yoghurt sauce; it smells of fresh coconut oil.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which breaks the vegetables into mush.
steps.fix: Fold gently and do not boil after the yoghurt goes in.

steps.do: Make the olan: simmer the sliced ash gourd and 2 slit green chillies in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) thin coconut milk with salt for 8 minutes until translucent. Add the cooked beans and the 1/2 cup (120 ml) thick coconut milk and warm through without boiling. Finish with 1 tbsp (15 ml) raw coconut oil and curry leaves.
steps.look: A pale, delicate, ivory stew with translucent slices; no spices, just coconut and chilli.
steps.mistake: Boiling the thick coconut milk, which splits it.
steps.fix: Warm gently after the thick milk is added.

steps.do: Make the beetroot pachadi: cook the grated beetroot with a pinch of salt and 1/4 cup (60 ml) water for 6 to 8 minutes until soft and dry. Stir in the smooth mustard-coconut paste and cook 2 minutes. Cool, then fold in 1 cup (240 g) yoghurt. Temper with mustard seeds, dried chilli and curry leaves in 1 tsp (5 ml) coconut oil.
steps.look: A vivid magenta, creamy pachadi, tangy and gently pungent from the raw mustard.
steps.mistake: Adding yoghurt to the hot beetroot, so it splits.
steps.fix: Always cool the beetroot completely first.

steps.do: Make the thoran: heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) coconut oil in a kadai, pop 1 tsp (3 g) mustard seeds, add a dried chilli, curry leaves and 1/2 tsp (1 g) cumin, then the cabbage, 2 chopped green chillies, turmeric and salt. Stir-fry 5 minutes, then add the remaining grated coconut and toss 3 minutes more.
steps.look: Bright, tender-crisp cabbage flecked with yellow and white coconut, dry, not wet.
steps.mistake: Covering the pan, so the cabbage steams to a soggy heap.
steps.fix: Cook uncovered over medium-high heat and keep tossing.

steps.do: Finish the parippu (dal): reheat the mashed moong dal, adding water to a thick, pourable consistency, and stir in 2 tbsp (30 g) ghee.
steps.look: A golden, glossy dal with ghee pooling on top, smelling buttery.
steps.mistake: Too thick to pour over the rice.
steps.fix: Add hot water until it pours slowly.

steps.do: Fry the payasam garnish: fry the cashews in 1 tbsp (15 g) ghee until golden, add the raisins until they puff, and pour over the payasam.
steps.look: Golden cashews and plump raisins floating on the creamy payasam.
steps.mistake: Burning the cashews in hot ghee.
steps.fix: Medium heat; they colour fast.

steps.do: Fry the papadams: heat the frying oil to 375°F (190°C) and fry each for 3 to 5 seconds until it puffs and blisters. Drain on paper.
steps.look: Instant puffing and bubbling into crisp, pale rounds.
steps.mistake: Oil too cool, so they turn leathery.
steps.fix: Test one; it should puff within 2 seconds.

steps.do: Lay each banana leaf with the tip pointing to the guest's left. Serve in order: a pinch of salt, pickle, banana chips and the sweet chips at the top left; thoran, avial, olan and pachadi along the top of the leaf; papadam at the bottom left; then a mound of rice in the lower centre, with dal and ghee poured over first, followed by sambar for the second helping, and payasam to finish.
steps.look: A full, colourful leaf with each dish in its own place, rice at the centre of it all.
steps.mistake: Putting everything down at once in random places.
steps.fix: Follow the order: the sides first, then rice with dal and ghee, then sambar, then payasam.

dishes.science: Each dish is finished with a tempering: whole spices fried in hot fat. Mustard seeds contain compounds that only become aromatic and lose their harshness when the seeds are heated until they pop; curry leaves release aromatic oils that dissolve in the fat, which then carries their flavour through the dish. Coconut milk is an emulsion of coconut fat and water held by proteins; boiling breaks it, so the thick milk is added at the end. Yoghurt curdles if heated quickly because its proteins tighten and squeeze out whey, which is why it goes into avial and pachadi off the heat. Payasam thickens and turns golden as water evaporates and milk sugars and proteins brown slowly through the Maillard reaction.
dishes.plating: The banana leaf is the plate. Lay it with the narrow tip to the guest's left. Small dishes go along the upper half from left to right, with crisp papadam at the lower left and the rice mounded in the lower centre. Payasam is served last, poured onto the leaf or in a small cup. Use your right hand to mix each dish with rice.

pairing.drink: Sambharam, a thin spiced buttermilk with ginger, green chilli and curry leaves: cool and sour, it aids a long meal and soothes the chilli.

variations: Pineapple pachadi: ripe pineapple cooked with a pinch of sugar in place of beetroot.
Ada pradhaman: a payasam of rice flakes with jaggery and coconut milk.
A smaller sadya for weekdays: rice, dal, sambar, thoran and one pachadi.
safety: Refrigerate leftover dishes with yoghurt and coconut milk within 2 hours; reheat cooked dishes to 165°F (74°C).
Mustard seeds spit as they pop: stand back and have the next ingredient ready.
Fry papadams in a pan no more than half full of oil and never leave it.

dishes.title: Bún Bò Huế
dishes.summary: Huế's spicy beef noodle soup: a long pork and beef bone broth perfumed with lemongrass and fermented shrimp paste, poured over thick round rice noodles with sliced beef shank and pork hock, lit up with annatto chilli oil and served with herbs and lime. It is in the course because it layers flavours deliberately: a clear bone broth, a pungent ferment tamed by settling, and a flavoured oil made separately and added at the end.
skills: a pork and beef bone broth
equipment: Large stockpot, at least 10 quarts (9.5 litres)
Second large pot for blanching bones
Dry frying pan or gas flame for charring
Small saucepan for the chilli oil
Heavy knife or meat mallet for bruising lemongrass
Small bowl for dissolving shrimp paste

ingredients.item: Pork neck bones or knuckle bones
Pork hock, cut in rounds 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick

ingredients.note: bruised and tied in a bundle

ingredients.item: Neutral oil, for the chilli oil
Thick round rice noodles (bún bò Huế)
Bean sprouts, shredded banana blossom or cabbage
Herbs: mint, Thai basil, Vietnamese coriander, coriander

mise: Char the onion and ginger halves cut side down in a dry pan for 8 to 10 minutes until blackened.
Bruise 6 lemongrass stalks with the back of a heavy knife and tie them in a bundle.
Dissolve the shrimp paste in 1 cup (240 ml) water, stir and leave to settle for 30 minutes.
Mince the lemongrass, garlic and shallots for the chilli oil.
Soak the noodles in warm water for 30 minutes if the packet suggests it.
Wash the herbs and bean sprouts; slice onions and spring onions.

timeline.do: Blanch the bones, hock and shank; rinse.
Start the broth with lemongrass and charred aromatics.
Remove the shank when tender; chill it for slicing.
Add the settled shrimp paste liquid; season.
Make the annatto chilli oil.
Cook the noodles; slice the shank; prepare garnishes.
Assemble bowls and ladle on boiling broth.

steps.do: Blanch: put the bones, hock and shank in the second pot, cover with cold water and bring to a hard boil for 5 minutes. Drain and rinse each piece under running water, scrubbing off the grey scum. Wash the pot.
steps.look: Heavy grey foam on the surface; after rinsing, clean meat and bones with no scum.
steps.mistake: Skipping the blanch, which gives a murky, gamy broth.
steps.fix: Always blanch and rinse; it is the key to a clear broth.

steps.do: Put the cleaned bones, hock and shank in the stockpot with the 5 quarts (4.7 litres) water, the lemongrass bundle, charred onion and ginger. Bring to a boil, lower to a gentle simmer and skim.
steps.look: Small bubbles and a clean-smelling broth that turns lightly golden.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil that clouds the broth.
steps.fix: Keep the surface just bubbling and skim often in the first 30 minutes.

steps.do: After 1 1/2 to 2 hours, lift out the beef shank when a chopstick slides in easily. Plunge it into cold water for 10 minutes, then wrap and refrigerate to firm for slicing.
steps.look: Tender shank that holds together; the cold bath stops it darkening and drying.
steps.mistake: Leaving the shank in for the full time, so it falls apart.
steps.fix: Check it after 90 minutes.

steps.do: Pour the settled shrimp paste liquid into the broth, leaving the gritty sediment behind in the bowl. Add the fish sauce, rock sugar and salt. Continue simmering 1 1/2 hours more, until the hock is tender.
steps.look: The broth turns slightly cloudy pink-gold and smells pungent, then mellows into a savoury, lemongrass-scented depth.
steps.mistake: Pouring in the sediment, which makes the broth gritty and harsh.
steps.fix: Pour slowly and leave the bottom 2 tbsp (30 ml) in the bowl.

steps.do: Make the annatto chilli oil: heat the 1/3 cup (80 ml) oil with the annatto seeds over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until deep red, then strain out the seeds. Return the oil to the pan, add the minced lemongrass, garlic and shallots and fry 3 minutes until fragrant and pale gold, then stir in the chilli flakes off the heat.
steps.look: The oil turns brilliant red-orange; the lemongrass sizzles gently and smells sweet and citrusy.
steps.mistake: Burning the annatto, which turns bitter and brown.
steps.fix: Low heat only; strain as soon as the oil is deep red.

steps.do: Taste the broth and adjust: it should be savoury, slightly sweet and fragrant with lemongrass, with a gentle funk from the shrimp paste. Remove the lemongrass, onion and ginger. Stir 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the chilli oil into the broth.
steps.look: A rich, slightly cloudy broth with a red sheen on the surface.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning, because the noodles will dilute the flavour.
steps.fix: Season boldly; the broth must carry plain noodles.

steps.do: Cook the noodles: boil in plenty of water according to the packet, usually 12 to 15 minutes for thick noodles, until tender but still chewy. Drain and rinse under hot water.
steps.look: Thick, white, slippery noodles that are tender right through.
steps.mistake: Undercooking thick noodles, which leaves a hard centre.
steps.fix: Taste one; it should be tender with a slight bounce.

steps.do: Slice the chilled shank thinly across the grain, about 1/8 inch (3 mm). Cut the hock into serving pieces.
steps.look: Thin, neat slices showing the marbling of tendon and meat.
steps.mistake: Slicing the shank warm, so it shreds.
steps.fix: Slice it cold with a sharp knife.

steps.do: Assemble: divide the noodles among the bowls, top with shank slices, hock and sliced onion and spring onion. Bring the broth to a rolling boil and ladle about 2 cups (480 ml) into each bowl. Add chilli oil to taste.
steps.look: Steaming bowls with a red, glossy broth, noodles and meat visible, onions wilting.
steps.mistake: Using broth that is merely hot, so the bowl is lukewarm.
steps.fix: Always ladle at a full boil; warm the bowls with hot water first.

steps.do: Serve with the bean sprouts, banana blossom, herbs, lime wedges and fresh chillies on a plate for each person to add.
steps.look: A heaped plate of green herbs and pale sprouts beside each bowl.
steps.mistake: Adding all the herbs in the kitchen, so they wilt.
steps.fix: Let each person add them at the table.

dishes.science: Blanching removes blood and surface proteins that would otherwise form fine particles and cloud the broth. Long, gentle simmering dissolves collagen from pork hock and bones into gelatin, giving body. Lemongrass contains citral and other aromatic oils that dissolve slowly into the hot broth. Fermented shrimp paste is rich in free amino acids and pungent volatile compounds formed during months of fermentation; dissolving and settling it removes the sandy sediment, and simmering softens its sharpest notes. Annatto seeds are coated in a red pigment called bixin that dissolves in fat rather than water, so heating them in oil colours it deeply; frying lemongrass and garlic in that oil adds aroma that floats on the soup's surface.
dishes.plating: Deep, wide bowls warmed with hot water. Noodles in a neat nest, shank slices fanned on one side, a piece of hock on the other, a scatter of onions and spring onions in the middle, then the boiling broth ladled around so the surface shines red. A plate of herbs, sprouts, banana blossom and lime alongside.

pairing.drink: An ice-cold Vietnamese lager with a squeeze of lime: crisp and cold against the chilli oil and pungent broth.

variations: Add chả Huế, a peppery pork roll, sliced into the bowls.
Pressure cooker broth: 45 minutes at high pressure after blanching.
Add cubes of pork blood cake, the traditional addition, if you can buy it from a Vietnamese butcher.
safety: Simmer the broth until the meat is tender, well past safe temperatures, and bring it back to a rolling boil before serving.
Cool leftover broth quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Annatto oil splashes stain: use an apron and keep it away from your face.

dishes.title: Tonkotsu Ramen
dishes.summary: A bowl of five separate components: an opaque pork bone broth boiled hard for twelve hours until it turns creamy, a soy tare, rolled chashu pork braised until tender, soft-boiled eggs marinated overnight, and fresh noodles, assembled to order. It is in the course because it breaks the clear-stock rule on purpose, and because a ramen bowl is a lesson in managing several preparations across two days and bringing them together in a minute.
skills: a pork bone broth boiled hard to emulsify
equipment: Large stockpot, at least 12 quarts (11 litres), or a pressure cooker
Heavy saucepan with a lid for the chashu
Saucepan for eggs and a bowl of iced water
Large pot for noodles and a noodle strainer

ingredients.note: ask the butcher to split them

ingredients.item: Pork neck bones or back bones
Onion, garlic and ginger, for the broth
ingredients.us: 1 onion, 1 head garlic, 2 inch (5 cm) ginger

ingredients.item: Skinless pork belly, in one rectangular piece
Fresh ramen noodles, thin and straight
Wood ear mushrooms (kikurage), soaked and sliced
Pickled red ginger (beni shoga) and toasted sesame seeds

mise: Two days ahead: blanch and scrub the bones and start the broth.
Roll and tie the pork belly into a tight log with string at 1 inch (2.5 cm) intervals.
Make the tare: warm soy, mirin, sake and kombu to just below a simmer, turn off the heat, add the bonito, steep 10 minutes and strain.
Have a kettle of boiling water beside the broth for topping up.
On serving day, set out everything for assembly in order: bowls, tare, toppings, noodles, broth.

timeline.do: Blanch, scrub and start boiling the bones hard; top up hourly.
Braise the chashu; boil and marinate the eggs in the cooled braising liquid.
Keep the broth at a hard boil; add aromatics in the last hour; strain and chill.
Reheat the broth to a boil; slice the chashu; halve the eggs.
Warm the bowls; put on the noodle water.
Cook the noodles; assemble each bowl in under a minute.

steps.do: Blanch: put the trotters and bones in the second pot, cover with cold water, bring to a hard boil and boil 15 minutes. Drain, then scrub every piece under running water, removing dark blood, clots and scum.
steps.look: Clean, pale bones with no dark marrow or scum on the surface.
steps.mistake: Skipping the scrub, which makes the broth grey and smell unpleasant.
steps.fix: Scrub thoroughly; it is messy but essential.

steps.do: Return the clean bones to the large pot, cover by 2 inches (5 cm) with fresh water, and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Keep it at a hard, rolling boil with the lid slightly ajar, topping up with boiling water every hour to keep the bones covered, for 10 to 12 hours.
steps.look: A violent boil the whole time; after 3 or 4 hours the broth turns milky, then creamy and opaque, and smells rich and porky.
steps.mistake: Simmering gently, which gives a clear broth instead of a creamy one.
steps.fix: Keep it boiling hard. Never leave the pot unattended or overnight on the hob.

steps.do: In the last hour, add the halved onion, garlic, ginger and spring onion greens to the broth.
steps.look: The smell becomes sweeter and more rounded, with garlic and ginger over the pork.
steps.mistake: Adding aromatics at the start, where they break down and taste stewed.
steps.fix: Add them only in the final hour.

steps.do: Make the chashu: put the tied pork belly in the heavy saucepan with the 1/2 cup (120 ml) each of soy, mirin and sake, the 1/4 cup (50 g) sugar and 1 cup (240 ml) water. Bring to a simmer, cover with a lid slightly ajar, and simmer very gently 2 1/2 to 3 hours, turning every 30 minutes, until a skewer slides in easily.
steps.look: A glossy, dark brown log; the liquid reduces and smells sweet and savoury.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the pork.
steps.fix: Keep the bubbles tiny and turn the log often so it colours evenly.

steps.do: Make the eggs: lower the eggs into boiling water and cook exactly 6 1/2 minutes. Transfer to iced water for 5 minutes and peel carefully. Put them in a zip-lock bag with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the cooled chashu liquid and marinate in the fridge 8 to 24 hours.
steps.look: Peeled eggs with set whites and yolks that will be jammy; after marinating, a golden-brown outside.
steps.mistake: Peeling warm eggs, which tear.
steps.fix: Chill them fully first. Crack all over and peel under water.

steps.do: Cool the chashu in its liquid, then refrigerate overnight. Strain the broth through the fine sieve, pressing on the solids. You should have about 2 1/2 quarts (2.4 litres). Cool quickly and refrigerate.
steps.look: A creamy, opaque broth that sets to a jelly in the fridge; firm chashu that slices cleanly.
steps.mistake: Leaving the hot broth to cool slowly at room temperature.
steps.fix: Divide into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

steps.do: On serving day, reheat the broth to a rolling boil and whisk well, as fat and collagen separate in the fridge. Season with a little salt only if needed; the tare does the seasoning.
steps.look: A smooth, creamy, steaming broth that re-emulsifies when boiled and whisked.
steps.mistake: Serving it without boiling, so it looks greasy and separated.
steps.fix: Boil hard for 2 minutes and whisk until creamy again.

steps.do: Slice the chashu into rounds 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, removing the string. If you have a blowtorch, sear the slices until the edges caramelise. Halve the eggs lengthways.
steps.look: Neat spirals of pork with a lacquered edge; eggs with orange, jammy yolks.
steps.mistake: Thin, broken slices from warm pork.
steps.fix: Slice it cold from the fridge.

steps.do: Fill the bowls with boiling water to warm them. Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a rolling boil for the noodles.
steps.look: Bowls too hot to hold comfortably, and a fierce, rolling boil in the noodle pot.
steps.mistake: Cold bowls, which cool the broth at once.
steps.fix: Warming bowls is part of the recipe.

steps.do: Empty the bowls and put 2 tbsp (30 ml) tare in each. Cook the noodles for the time on the packet, usually 60 to 90 seconds, while you ladle 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) boiling broth into each bowl and whisk with the tare.
steps.look: A creamy, golden-brown, steaming broth in every bowl.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the noodles while assembling.
steps.fix: Start the noodles and ladle the broth at the same time.

steps.do: Drain the noodles very well, shaking hard, and fold them into each bowl in a neat pile. Top quickly with chashu, egg, wood ear, spring onions, nori, beni shoga and sesame. Serve at once.
steps.look: A bowl with each topping in its own place, noodles just visible, steam rising.
steps.mistake: Wet noodles that dilute the broth, or slow assembly so the noodles go soft.
steps.fix: Shake the strainer firmly. Eat within minutes.

dishes.science: Tonkotsu broth is milky because it is boiled hard. The vigorous boil breaks rendered pork fat into tiny droplets, and gelatin from trotters and collagen-rich bones, along with dissolved proteins, coats those droplets and holds them in suspension, forming an emulsion that looks like cream. A gentle simmer would leave the fat floating and the broth clear. Blanching and scrubbing first removes blood and impurities that would otherwise turn the broth grey. The chashu is braised gently so its connective tissue turns to gelatin without the muscle tightening. Marinating eggs draws soy, sugar and mirin into the white by diffusion, while the 6 1/2 minute boil leaves the yolk partly set and jammy.
dishes.plating: Deep, warmed ramen bowls. Noodles folded in a neat pile, chashu slices overlapping on one side, egg halves cut side up beside them, wood ear and spring onions in small clusters, nori standing upright at the back against the rim, a pinch of red ginger for colour. Serve with a soup spoon and chopsticks.

pairing.drink: An ice-cold Japanese lager or a dry junmai sake: crisp and cold to cut through the rich, fatty broth.

variations: Pressure cooker broth: 90 minutes at high pressure after blanching, then boil hard uncovered 30 minutes to emulsify.
Black garlic oil (mayu): garlic fried slowly in sesame oil until black, then blended, drizzled on top.
Shio tare: replace the soy tare with a salt and kombu tare for a paler bowl.
safety: Never leave a pot boiling unattended or overnight on the hob; turn it off and resume the next day if needed.
Cool broth and chashu quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat broth to a rolling boil.
Ramen eggs have jammy yolks: boil 9 minutes for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Keep marinated eggs refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

dishes.title: Crubeens (Irish Pig's Trotters)
dishes.summary: Pig's trotters simmered for hours until the meat and skin fall from the bone, boned out, pressed with their own jelly, chilled, cut into fingers, crumbed and fried until crisp outside and melting inside, served with mustard. It is in the course because it is nose-to-tail cooking at its most practical: turning a cheap, bony cut into something elegant through simmering, boning out, pressing and frying.
equipment: Loaf tin, 9 by 5 inches (23 by 13 cm), lined with cling film
Second loaf tin or a piece of card wrapped in foil and weights, for pressing

ingredients.item: Bay leaves, thyme and black peppercorns
English mustard, pickled onions or gherkins, and soda bread

mise: Check the trotters for stray hairs and singe them off with a gas flame or shave with a disposable razor.
Rinse the trotters well under cold water.
Line the loaf tin with cling film, leaving plenty overhanging.
Chop the parsley and shallot.
Set out the crumbing station: flour, beaten egg, breadcrumbs, then a tray.

timeline.do: Simmer the trotters 3 to 3 1/2 hours.
Bone out the trotters while warm; reduce some stock.
Season, press into the tin and chill overnight under weight.
Unmould, cut into fingers, crumb and chill.
Fry until deep golden and hot through.
Serve with mustard, pickles and bread.

steps.do: Put the trotters in the stockpot, cover with cold water, bring to the boil, boil 5 minutes and drain. Rinse them and the pot.
steps.look: Grey scum on the water; clean trotters after rinsing.
steps.mistake: Skipping the blanch, which leaves the stock cloudy and strong.
steps.fix: Always blanch and rinse them first.

steps.do: Return the trotters to the clean pot with the vegetables, herbs, peppercorns, vinegar and enough fresh water to cover by 2 inches (5 cm). Bring to a simmer, skim, and simmer gently, partly covered, 3 to 3 1/2 hours until the meat and skin are completely soft and the bones come away when pulled.
steps.look: The skin turns translucent and wobbly, the toes pull away easily, and the stock becomes sticky between your fingers.
steps.mistake: Undercooking, so the skin is rubbery and the meat clings to the bone.
steps.fix: Keep simmering and test every 30 minutes after 3 hours.

steps.do: Lift the trotters onto a tray and leave until cool enough to handle but still warm, about 20 minutes. Strain the stock and boil 2 cups (480 ml) of it in the small saucepan until reduced to about 1/2 cup (120 ml).
steps.look: A syrupy, sticky reduction that coats a spoon and sets on a cold plate.
steps.mistake: Letting the trotters go cold, when the gelatin sets and the bones stick.
steps.fix: Bone them while warm; reheat briefly in the stock if they set.

steps.do: Wearing gloves, pick all the meat, skin and soft tissue off the bones, discarding every bone, the hard nails and any gristle. Feel through the meat twice for the many small bones.
steps.look: A pile of soft, sticky meat and skin, with a heap of small bones discarded.
steps.mistake: Missing tiny bones, which spoil the finished dish.
steps.fix: Spread the meat on a tray and press through it with your fingers.

steps.do: Chop the meat and skin roughly, about 1/2 inch (1 cm), and mix with the mustard, parsley, shallot, plenty of salt and pepper and 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the reduced stock. Taste: it should be well seasoned, as it will be served cold inside.
steps.look: A sticky, glistening mixture flecked with green parsley and specks of mustard seed.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning; chilled food needs more salt.
steps.fix: Season more than tastes right warm.

steps.do: Pack the mixture into the lined tin, pressing it into the corners. Pour over the rest of the reduced stock, fold the cling film over, set the second tin or weighted card on top, and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: A level, tightly packed block under a weight.
steps.mistake: Not pressing firmly, so the block crumbles when cut.
steps.fix: Press hard and use heavy weights such as tins of tomatoes.

steps.do: Unmould the set block and cut it into fingers about 3 by 1 inch (8 by 2.5 cm). Dredge each in flour, then dip in egg, then press into the breadcrumbs, covering all sides. Chill 20 minutes.
steps.look: Neat, even fingers with a complete, dry crumb coat.
steps.mistake: Gaps in the coating, which let the filling leak and spit in the oil.
steps.fix: Coat thoroughly; double dip in egg and crumbs if needed.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C) in the heavy saucepan, no more than half full. Fry the fingers 4 or 5 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and the centre reads 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: A steady sizzle and an even golden crust; inside, the jelly melts so the centre is soft and molten.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, so the crumb burns before the middle warms through.
steps.fix: Keep it at 350°F (175°C) and check the centre with a probe.

steps.do: Drain on the rack for 1 minute and serve hot with English mustard, pickled onions or gherkins and buttered soda bread.
steps.look: Golden, crisp fingers that crack open to a soft, rich, savoury centre.
steps.mistake: Draining on paper, so the bottom steams soft.
steps.fix: Use a rack and serve immediately.

dishes.science: Trotters are mostly skin, tendon and small bones, which are rich in collagen. Hours of simmering convert that collagen into gelatin, which dissolves into the stock and makes the meat soft and sticky. Reducing the stock concentrates the gelatin so that, when chilled, it sets the pressed meat into a firm block; pressing removes air and binds the pieces together. When the crumbed fingers are fried, the coating dries and browns through the Maillard reaction, while heat travels inward and melts the gelatin back to liquid, so the centre turns soft and molten. The coating is a barrier that keeps the melting interior from leaking into the oil, which is why it must be complete.
dishes.plating: A warm plate or a board lined with paper. Stack three or four fingers in a loose criss-cross, with one cut open to show the soft centre, a generous spoonful of English mustard at the side, pickled onions or gherkins, and a slice of buttered soda bread.

pairing.drink: A pint of Irish stout: its roasted bitterness and creamy body are the classic partner for rich, fried pork.

variations: Traditional crubeens: serve the simmered trotters whole and hot, with vinegar and soda bread, without boning or frying.
Pan-fry the fingers in butter in a frying pan instead of deep-frying.
Add chopped ham hock to the trotter meat for more meatiness.
safety: Cool the cooked meat and stock quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Fry the fingers until the centre reaches 165°F (74°C).
Fill the pan no more than half full of oil, keep a lid nearby and never leave it unattended.

dishes.title: Tortellini in Brodo
dishes.summary: Tiny filled pasta from Emilia, folded by hand around a filling of pork loin, mortadella, prosciutto and Parmigiano, cooked and served in a clear, golden capon broth. It is the Christmas lunch of Bologna and Modena, and it is in the course because it tests two things at the highest standard: a broth of perfect clarity and flavour, and hundreds of small, even, well-sealed tortellini made from a sheet rolled thin by hand.
skills: a pork, prosciutto, mortadella and Parmigiano filling
equipment: Large stockpot, at least 8 quarts (7.5 litres)
Long thin rolling pin (mattarello), about 32 inches (80 cm), or a pasta machine
Pastry wheel or sharp knife and a ruler

ingredients.note: or 3 lb (1.4 kg) chicken wings and backs

ingredients.item: Pork loin, in 1 inch (2.5 cm) cubes

mise: Start the broth first thing; it needs at least 3 hours.
Cube the pork loin; chop the mortadella and prosciutto; grate the Parmigiano.
Clear a large, smooth wooden board and dust it lightly with flour.
Dust two trays with semolina for the finished tortellini.
Have a damp tea towel ready to cover the dough and the cut squares.

timeline.do: Start the broth at a bare tremble, skimming.
Brown the pork; make and chill the filling.
Make the pasta dough and rest it 30 minutes.
Roll, cut and fold tortellini in batches, keeping the sheet covered.
Strain and defat the broth; season.
Bring the broth to a gentle simmer and cook the tortellini 3 to 4 minutes.
Serve in warm bowls with Parmigiano at the table.

steps.do: Make the broth: put the capon, beef shin and whole vegetables in the stockpot with the 4 quarts (3.8 litres) cold water. Bring slowly to 190 to 194°F (88 to 90°C), never a rolling boil, skimming off all the foam. Hold at that temperature, uncovered, for 3 to 4 hours, skimming every 30 minutes.
steps.look: Grey foam rising and being lifted off, then a clear, pale-gold broth that trembles at the surface; it smells of roast chicken and beef.
steps.mistake: Boiling, which churns fat and protein into the broth and clouds it.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer and the lowest flame. Clarity cannot be added later.

steps.do: Make the filling: brown the pork cubes in the butter over medium-high heat for 6 to 8 minutes until golden and cooked through to 145°F (63°C). Cool, then mince finely with the mortadella and prosciutto in the food processor. Mix in the Parmigiano, egg and nutmeg. Chill.
steps.look: A smooth, pinkish paste that holds a fingerprint without weeping; it smells of cured pork, cheese and nutmeg.
steps.mistake: A wet, loose filling, which makes the pasta soggy and hard to seal.
steps.fix: If wet, add a little more Parmigiano; chill to firm it.

steps.do: Make the pasta: mound the 2 1/3 cups (300 g) flour on the board, make a well, break in the 3 eggs, beat them with a fork and gradually draw in flour from the walls. Knead 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, yellow dough that springs back slowly when pressed.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the dough fights the pin and shrinks.
steps.fix: Rest under an upturned bowl for the full 30 minutes.

steps.do: Roll a quarter of the dough at a time, keeping the rest covered: with the long pin, roll from the centre outward, turning the dough a quarter turn often and stretching it over the pin, until it is about 1/32 inch (0.7 mm) thick and you can see the grain of the board through it. With a machine, roll to the second-thinnest setting.
steps.look: A thin, even, slightly translucent sheet with a velvety surface that holds broth.
steps.mistake: A thick sheet, which makes heavy, doughy tortellini.
steps.fix: Keep rolling until the board shows through; work fast so it does not dry.

steps.do: Cut the sheet into squares of 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) with the pastry wheel and ruler. Cover with the damp cloth.
steps.look: Neat, even squares of the same size, with clean edges and no torn corners.
steps.mistake: Cutting more squares than you can fill before they dry.
steps.fix: Cut one strip at a time.

steps.do: Put a chickpea-sized ball of filling, about 1/16 oz (2 g), on each square. Fold one corner over to the opposite corner to make a triangle, pressing out air from the filling towards the edges and sealing firmly.
steps.look: A small triangle, tightly sealed, with no air bubble around the filling.
steps.mistake: Trapped air, which expands in the broth and splits the seal.
steps.fix: Press from the filling outward. If the edges are dry, touch them with a damp fingertip.

steps.do: Hold the triangle with the long side towards your fingertip, wrap it around the tip of your little finger, and pinch the two corners together firmly, then fold the top point back slightly so the tortellino stands like a little ring. Set it on the semolina tray. Repeat, making at least 120 for four people (the dough and filling make about twice that) and freezing the extra.
steps.look: Uniform little rings with a raised navel shape, standing up on the tray.
steps.mistake: Loose pinches that open in the broth.
steps.fix: Press the corners hard; a dab of water helps them stick.

steps.do: Strain the broth through the muslin-lined sieve, then chill or skim off as much fat as possible. Season with salt. You should have about 2 1/2 quarts (2.4 litres).
steps.look: A clear, golden broth, with only a few small beads of fat.
steps.mistake: Pressing the solids, which clouds it.
steps.fix: Let it drip through without pressing.

steps.do: Bring 2 quarts (1.9 litres) of broth to a gentle simmer, add the tortellini and cook 3 to 4 minutes, until they float and the pinched part has lost its chalky centre.
steps.look: Tortellini rising to the surface, the pasta turning soft and slightly translucent at the edges; the broth stays clear.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which bursts the tortellini and clouds the broth with flour.
steps.fix: A bare, trembling simmer only.

steps.do: Ladle the tortellini and broth into warm bowls, about 30 tortellini and 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of broth each. Serve with grated Parmigiano at the table.
steps.look: Small golden rings floating in a clear, steaming broth.
steps.mistake: Too few tortellini or too much broth.
steps.fix: Serve in wide, warm bowls; Parmigiano on the side.

dishes.science: A clear broth depends on temperature: below a boil, proteins released from the meat coagulate slowly into large clumps that rise as foam and can be skimmed off, while fat stays in a separate layer. A rolling boil breaks both into fine particles and droplets and emulsifies them into the liquid, making it cloudy. Long, gentle cooking dissolves gelatin from the capon's bones and skin, giving body. The pasta is egg and flour only: egg proteins and wheat gluten form a strong, elastic sheet that can be rolled very thin. Rolling by hand stretches the dough and leaves a slightly rough surface that holds broth, while trapped air expands with heat, which is why air must be pressed out before sealing.
dishes.plating: Use warm, wide, shallow soup bowls. Ladle in the tortellini first so they lie in a single layer, then the broth so they float. Serve at once with a bowl of freshly grated Parmigiano and a small spoon so each guest adds their own.

pairing.drink: A dry Lambrusco di Sorbara, lightly sparkling and served cool: its bright acidity and bubbles refresh after the rich filling, as Emilians drink it.

variations: Tortellini panna e prosciutto: drained tortellini tossed in cream and prosciutto, a richer non-broth version.
Cappelletti: larger squares with a cheese and meat filling, from Romagna.
Freeze uncooked tortellini on the tray, then bag; cook from frozen, adding 1 minute.
safety: Cook the pork for the filling to 145°F (63°C) before mincing; the raw egg in the filling cooks in the broth.
Cool the broth quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Freeze any tortellini you will not cook within a day.

dishes.title: Xiaolongbao
dishes.summary: Shanghai soup dumplings: a pork skin and chicken aspic set firm overnight and folded with seasoned pork into thin wrappers rolled thicker at the centre, gathered in eighteen pleats and steamed until the jelly melts into hot soup inside. It is in the course as the summit of dumpling craft, judged by the even pleats, the thinness of the skin and whether it arrives at the table unbroken.
skills: a thin wrapper rolled with a thicker centre
equipment: Shallow dish or loaf tin for setting
Small, thin rolling pin, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) across
Bamboo steamer with lid and a wok or saucepan underneath
Baking paper cut into small squares, or napa cabbage leaves

ingredients.item: Pork skin, scraped clean of fat

mise: The day before: blanch the pork skin and wings and simmer the aspic; chill overnight.
On the day, dice 10 oz (300 g) of the set aspic into 1/4 inch (5 mm) cubes and keep them cold.
Mince the ginger for the filling; cut the ginger matchsticks and soak them in the vinegar.
Cut baking paper into 2 inch (5 cm) squares, or line the steamer with cabbage leaves.
Fill the wok with water to just below the steamer and have more boiling water ready.

timeline.do: Blanch skin and wings; simmer the aspic 3 hours; strain and chill.
Make the filling; fold in the diced aspic; chill.
Make the dough; rest 30 minutes.
Roll wrappers and pleat the dumplings in batches.
Bring the steamer water to a hard boil.
Steam the first batch 8 minutes.
Serve straight from the basket with vinegar and ginger.

steps.do: Make the aspic: blanch the pork skin and wings in boiling water for 3 minutes, drain and rinse. Put them in the saucepan with the 6 3/4 cups (1.6 litres) water, ginger, spring onions and wine and simmer at a bare tremble for 3 hours, until reduced by about half. Strain and chill overnight.
steps.look: A sticky, golden stock that sets firm by morning; a cut cube holds clean edges and does not wobble.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which clouds the stock, or under-reducing, so it barely sets.
steps.fix: If it is soft, melt and reduce by a third, then chill again.

steps.do: Make the filling: put the pork in a bowl with the soy, wine, sugar, pepper, sesame oil and minced ginger. Stir hard in one direction for 3 minutes until sticky. Fold in the diced aspic gently and chill at least 30 minutes.
steps.look: A sticky, cohesive paste with jelly cubes throughout, cold to the touch.
steps.mistake: Stirring the aspic in hard, which melts and breaks it.
steps.fix: Fold it in last, gently, and keep the filling cold.

steps.do: Make the dough: mix the 2 cups (250 g) flour and salt, add the 1/2 cup (125 ml) warm water and knead 8 minutes until smooth and firm. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, firm, matt dough that springs back slowly.
steps.mistake: A soft, sticky dough, which tears with soup inside.
steps.fix: Knead in a little flour if sticky; the dough should feel firm.

steps.do: Roll the dough into a log and cut pieces of 0.35 oz (10 g). Keep them covered. Flatten each with your palm and roll the edge only with the small pin, rotating the disc, to a round 3 1/4 inches (8 cm) across: thin at the rim, noticeably thicker in the centre.
steps.look: A disc with a thin, frilly edge and a slightly domed, thicker centre.
steps.mistake: Rolling the centre thin, so the base bursts while steaming.
steps.fix: Roll from the edge inward and stop before the middle.

steps.do: Hold a wrapper in your left palm and put about 0.7 oz (20 g) of cold filling in the centre. With your right thumb and forefinger, pinch a small fold at the edge and keep pleating around the rim, rotating the dumpling with your left thumb, making 16 to 18 small pleats.
steps.look: Fine, even pleats spiralling up to the top, the filling enclosed.
steps.mistake: Floury rims that will not stick, or pleats that are too large.
steps.fix: Keep the rim free of flour; use small, quick pleats close together.

steps.do: Gather the pleats at the top and twist them closed into a small knot. Set each dumpling on a paper square in the steamer, 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Keep made dumplings covered.
steps.look: A neat little purse with a swirl of pleats and a tiny closed top.
steps.mistake: Leaving a hole at the top, which lets the soup boil out.
steps.fix: Twist firmly to seal; a small knob of dough on top is fine.

steps.do: Set the basket over a hard rolling boil, put the lid on and steam the dumplings for exactly 8 minutes.
steps.look: The skins turn translucent; when you nudge the basket, the dumplings sag and you can see the soup moving inside.
steps.mistake: Steaming longer than 9 minutes, which stretches the skin until it leaks.
steps.fix: Set a timer and pull them at 8 minutes.

steps.do: Serve at once in the basket with the vinegar and ginger. To eat, lift a dumpling by its top knot onto a soup spoon, bite a small hole, sip the soup, then eat the dumpling with a little vinegar and ginger.
steps.look: A dumpling sagging heavily in the spoon, full of hot, clear soup.
steps.mistake: Biting straight in and burning your mouth.
steps.fix: Show guests the spoon-and-sip method; the soup is very hot.

dishes.science: The soup begins as a solid. Long simmering of pork skin and chicken wings converts their collagen into gelatin, which dissolves in the stock and sets into a firm jelly when cold. Diced and folded into the filling, the jelly can be wrapped like any solid, then melts at about 95°F (35°C) as the dumpling steams, turning to broth inside the sealed skin. The dough is made with warm water, which partly gelatinises the flour's starch and weakens the gluten slightly, giving a dough that rolls thin without springing back but stays strong. The wrapper is rolled thicker in the centre because the base carries the weight of the soup, while the many pleats concentrate extra dough at the top, where it is not needed.
dishes.plating: Serve in the bamboo basket set on a plate, the dumplings in a neat ring with the paper squares underneath. A small dish of black vinegar with ginger matchsticks and a soup spoon for each guest.

pairing.drink: Hot jasmine or oolong tea, the classic partner: clean and fragrant, it refreshes between rich, soupy bites.

variations: Crab xiaolongbao: replace a quarter of the pork with picked crab meat and a little crab roe.
Freeze pleated dumplings on a tray, then bag; steam from frozen 10 to 11 minutes.
Pan-fried soup buns: the same filling in a yeasted dough, fried and steamed in a pan.
safety: Cook the filling to 160°F (71°C); 8 minutes over a hard boil does this for 20 g dumplings.
The soup inside is boiling hot: warn guests and use a spoon.
Cool and refrigerate the aspic within 2 hours of making it.

dishes.title: Chicken Pastilla
dishes.summary: The great pie of Fes: chicken braised with onions, saffron, ginger and cinnamon, the sauce set with eggs, layered with sweet toasted almonds inside many sheets of buttered pastry, baked crisp and dusted with icing sugar and cinnamon. It is in the course because it balances sweet and savoury with precision and assembles several preparations in a crisp case, a showpiece of Moroccan cooking.
skills: braising chicken with saffron and cinnamon
equipment: Heavy casserole or tagine-style pot with lid
Round baking tin or ovenproof frying pan, 10 inches (25 cm) across

ingredients.item: Bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks, skin on
Neutral oil, for frying the almonds
Icing sugar and ground cinnamon, to finish

mise: Grate the onions on the coarse side of the box grater.
Crush the saffron and steep it in 2 tbsp (30 ml) warm water.
Chop the coriander and parsley.
Beat the 6 eggs in a bowl.
Thaw the phyllo in its packet; keep it under a damp cloth once opened.
Melt the butter for brushing.

timeline.do: Braise the chicken with onions and spices for about 1 hour.
Fry and grind the almonds with sugar and cinnamon.
Shred the chicken; reduce the sauce; set the eggs in it; cool.
Assemble the pastilla.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes at 375°F (190°C).
Rest, invert if needed, and decorate with icing sugar and cinnamon.

steps.do: Heat the 4 tbsp (55 g) butter and 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the casserole over medium heat. Add the chicken, grated onions, all the braise spices, saffron water, salt, pepper and herbs. Stir well and cook 10 minutes, turning the chicken, until the onions soften and smell sweet.
steps.look: The onions turn translucent and golden-yellow from the turmeric and saffron; the kitchen smells of warm spice.
steps.mistake: High heat, which browns and burns the onions before they soften.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium; this is a gentle, aromatic braise.

steps.do: Add the 1 cup (240 ml) water, cover and simmer gently 50 to 60 minutes, turning the chicken twice, until it is falling from the bone and reads well above 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: Very tender chicken and a thick, golden onion sauce.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry and catch.
steps.fix: Check halfway and add a splash of water if needed.

steps.do: Fry the almonds: heat the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the almonds, stirring, 5 to 7 minutes until golden throughout. Drain, cool, then pulse in the food processor with the icing sugar and cinnamon to a coarse crumb. Add the orange flower water.
steps.look: Golden almonds that smell toasted; a sandy, sweet crumb.
steps.mistake: Grinding to a paste, which turns oily.
steps.fix: Pulse in short bursts and stop at coarse sand.

steps.do: Lift out the chicken and shred the meat, discarding skin and bones. Boil the sauce uncovered over medium-high heat, stirring, for 10 to 15 minutes until reduced to about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) and thick.
steps.look: A thick, glossy onion sauce; the bubbles become large and slow.
steps.mistake: A thin, watery sauce, which makes the pastry soggy.
steps.fix: Keep reducing; the sauce should hold a trail across the pan.

steps.do: Lower the heat and pour in the beaten eggs. Stir slowly and constantly for 4 to 5 minutes until they set into soft, moist curds bound with the sauce. Tip into a sieve set over a bowl to drain off any liquid, and cool.
steps.look: Soft, golden, scrambled-egg curds mixed through the onion; no liquid pooling.
steps.mistake: Cooking the eggs dry, or leaving liquid in them.
steps.fix: Pull them off while still moist and drain well.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush the tin with melted butter. Lay 6 sheets of phyllo in it, each brushed with butter, overlapping like the petals of a flower so they cover the base and hang well over the sides.
steps.look: A buttered, layered pastry case with a wide overhang all round.
steps.mistake: Letting the sheets dry and crack.
steps.fix: Keep the stack under a damp cloth and work quickly.

steps.do: Sprinkle half the almond mixture over the base. Spread the egg mixture over it, then the shredded chicken, then the rest of the almonds.
steps.look: Even layers right to the edges: almonds, golden eggs, chicken, then almonds again.
steps.mistake: Piling filling into the middle, so the pie is uneven.
steps.fix: Spread each layer right to the edges.

steps.do: Fold the overhanging sheets over the filling, brushing with butter. Lay the remaining 6 sheets on top, each buttered, and tuck the edges down and under the pie all round. Brush the top with egg yolk to seal and then with butter.
steps.look: A neat, round, sealed parcel with a smooth, buttery top.
steps.mistake: Loose edges that let filling escape.
steps.fix: Tuck them firmly down the sides with a spatula.

steps.do: Bake 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden and crisp. For an even colour, invert onto a buttered tray halfway through and finish the other side.
steps.look: A crackling, glossy, golden crust; it smells of butter, cinnamon and almonds.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the pastry is pale and soft.
steps.fix: Bake until truly golden; the inside is already cooked.

steps.do: Rest 10 minutes. Dust the top heavily with icing sugar through the sieve, then draw lines of cinnamon in a lattice using a teaspoon or a paper strip as a guide. Cut into wedges with a serrated knife.
steps.look: A white top with a fine brown lattice; the crust shatters as it is cut, revealing layers.
steps.mistake: Dusting while very hot, so the sugar melts.
steps.fix: Wait 10 minutes before decorating.

dishes.science: The braise builds flavour slowly: grated onions break down and release sugars that caramelise lightly, while saffron and turmeric dissolve in the fat and colour the sauce. Reducing the sauce concentrates flavour and removes water that would soften the pastry. Eggs set in the sauce as their proteins unfold and bond between about 145 and 165°F (63 and 74°C); stirring makes soft curds that bind the onions. Frying the almonds deepens their flavour through the Maillard reaction, and the sugar and cinnamon give the sweet note that defines pastilla. Phyllo bakes crisp because each layer is separated by butter, which fries it as water in the dough turns to steam.
dishes.plating: Serve whole on a round platter at the table for the effect, then cut into wedges with a serrated knife. Each wedge on a warm plate, lattice side up, with a small salad of orange segments and mint to the side.

pairing.drink: Moroccan mint tea or an aromatic, off-dry Pinot Gris: sweet mint or a soft white with stone fruit both bridge the sugar and spice.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: a rich, gently spicy Alsace white on the Brennan's list that suits sweet and savoury together.

variations: Seafood pastilla: prawns, white fish and vermicelli with chermoula, with no sugar on top.
Individual pastillas: make small parcels in muffin tins and bake 20 minutes.
Pigeon pastilla: the classic Fes version, with braised pigeon in place of chicken.
safety: Cook the chicken until it falls from the bone, well past 165°F (74°C).
Cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; reheat in a 350°F (175°C) oven to 165°F (74°C).
This dish contains almonds: ask your guests about allergies before serving.

dishes.title: Coulibiac (Kulebyaka)
dishes.summary: The Russian fish pie: salmon, dill rice, mushrooms and hard-boiled eggs layered between thin crêpes that absorb the juices, wrapped in puff pastry, vented, decorated and baked until golden, served in thick slices with lemon butter. It is in the course because it is an exercise in managing moisture: every layer is prepared to stop the pastry from going soggy, and the fish must be cooked through inside a closed case.
skills: salmon, rice, mushrooms and eggs layered with crêpes to absorb juice
equipment: Small non-stick frying pan for crêpes, about 8 inches (20 cm)
Medium saucepan with lid for rice
Large baking tray lined with baking paper
Sharp knife and small cutters for decoration
Small saucepan for the lemon butter

ingredients.item: Salmon fillet, centre cut, skinless and pin-boned
All-butter puff pastry, homemade or bought
Unsalted butter, for the mushrooms and rice

ingredients.note: plus a little for the pan
beaten with a pinch of salt

ingredients.item: Fine salt, black pepper and lemon zest
Unsalted butter, for the lemon butter

mise: Hard-boil the 3 eggs for 10 minutes, cool in iced water, peel and slice.
Chop the mushrooms, shallots and dill.
Pat the salmon dry, check again for pin bones and season it with salt, pepper and lemon zest.
Whisk the crêpe batter and rest it 20 minutes.
Line the baking tray; keep the pastry chilled until you roll it.

timeline.do: Cook the dill rice and spread it to cool.
Cook the mushroom duxelles until dry; cool. Make 4 thin crêpes.
Roll the pastry and assemble the coulibiac.
Decorate, vent, egg wash and chill 30 minutes.
Bake 35 to 45 minutes until the salmon reaches 140°F (60°C).
Rest 10 minutes; make the lemon butter.
Slice thickly and serve with lemon butter.

steps.do: Cook the rice: melt 1 tbsp (15 g) butter in the saucepan, stir in the rice for 1 minute, add the 1 cup (240 ml) hot stock, cover and simmer on low 15 minutes. Rest 5 minutes, fold in half the dill, season and spread on a tray to cool.
steps.look: Fluffy, separate grains flecked with dill, dry to the touch.
steps.mistake: Wet, sticky rice, which makes the pastry soggy.
steps.fix: Spread it out to steam off moisture and cool completely.

steps.do: Make the duxelles: melt 2 tbsp (30 g) butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat, add the shallots for 2 minutes, then the mushrooms. Cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring, until all their liquid has evaporated and they form a dry, dark paste. Season and cool.
steps.look: Mushrooms release water, then it boils off and the mixture sizzles again and darkens; it smells deeply savoury.
steps.mistake: Stopping while wet, which floods the pie with liquid.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until a spoon drawn through the pan leaves a dry trail.

steps.do: Make the crêpes: heat the small pan over medium heat with a little butter, pour in 3 tbsp (45 ml) batter and swirl to coat thinly. Cook 1 minute until set and lightly golden, flip for 20 seconds. Make 4 thin crêpes and stack them.
steps.look: Thin, lacy, pale golden crêpes, about 8 inches (20 cm) across.
steps.mistake: Thick crêpes that add stodge.
steps.fix: Use less batter and swirl quickly.

steps.do: Divide the pastry in two pieces, one slightly larger. Roll the smaller to a rectangle about 14 by 8 inches (35 by 20 cm) and 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and lay it on the lined tray. Roll the larger to about 16 by 10 inches (40 by 25 cm) and keep it chilled.
steps.look: Two even sheets with sharp edges, still cold.
steps.mistake: Warm, sticky pastry that stretches out of shape.
steps.fix: Chill the sheets 10 minutes if they soften.

steps.do: Lay two crêpes on the base pastry, leaving a 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) border. Spread half the rice over them, then half the duxelles. Set the salmon on top, sprinkle with the remaining dill, cover with the egg slices, the rest of the duxelles, then the rest of the rice. Lay the last two crêpes over the top, tucking them down the sides.
steps.look: A neat, compact, loaf-shaped stack wrapped in crêpes.
steps.mistake: Leaving the salmon exposed to the pastry, so juices soak it.
steps.fix: The crêpes must form a jacket around the filling.

steps.do: Brush the border with egg wash, drape the larger sheet over the filling, and press the edges together firmly. Trim to a 1 inch (2.5 cm) rim and crimp it with a fork or your fingers.
steps.look: A smooth, tight parcel with no air pockets and a neat, sealed edge.
steps.mistake: Trapped air, which balloons and splits the pastry.
steps.fix: Smooth the top sheet down over the filling from the centre outward before sealing.

steps.do: Cut two holes about 1/2 inch (1 cm) wide in the top for steam. Decorate with leaves or a lattice cut from the trimmings. Brush everything with egg wash, avoiding the cut edges. Chill 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
steps.look: Two neat vents and decorations glued with egg wash; the pastry firm and cold.
steps.mistake: Egg wash dripping down the sides, sealing the layers so they do not rise.
steps.fix: Brush thinly and wipe drips.

steps.do: Bake 35 to 45 minutes until deep golden. Push the probe through a vent into the centre of the salmon: it is done at 140°F (60°C), and will rise to about 145°F (63°C) while resting.
steps.look: A tall, golden, crisp pastry; steam escaping through the vents; it smells of butter and dill.
steps.mistake: Pale pastry with an underdone centre, or overcooked dry fish.
steps.fix: If the pastry browns before the fish is done, cover it loosely with foil.

steps.do: Rest the coulibiac on the tray for 10 minutes. Meanwhile melt the 6 tbsp (85 g) butter with the 2 tbsp (30 ml) lemon juice, salt and pepper and keep warm.
steps.look: Golden, gently bubbling lemon butter that smells nutty and sharp.
steps.mistake: Slicing at once, so the layers slump.
steps.fix: Rest it so the layers settle.

steps.do: Slice thickly with the serrated knife using a gentle sawing motion, and serve each slice with lemon butter spooned beside it.
steps.look: Clean slices showing distinct layers of pastry, crêpe, rice, mushroom, pink salmon and yellow egg.
steps.mistake: Pressing down with a straight knife, which crushes the layers.
steps.fix: Saw gently and let the knife do the work.

dishes.science: Coulibiac is a moisture problem solved in layers. Salmon releases juices as its proteins tighten in the heat; uncontained, those juices soak the pastry and stop it crisping. The crêpes are a sponge: they absorb the juices before they reach the pastry. The rice is cooked and cooled dry, and the mushrooms are cooked until their water has evaporated, so neither adds liquid. Puff pastry rises because water in its butter-separated layers turns to steam and pushes them apart; it needs a hot oven to set quickly. The fish is protected inside the case, so it cooks gently and evenly, and carryover heat raises its temperature by a few degrees during the rest.
dishes.plating: Bring the whole coulibiac to the table on a long board for the moment, then slice. Lay each thick slice on its side on a warm plate so the layers face the guest, spoon lemon butter beside it, and add a few dill sprigs and a lemon wedge.

pairing.drink: A white Burgundy or Chablis: Chardonnay's richness meets salmon and butter, while its acidity cuts the pastry.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Meursault 2022 (375 ml): a rich white Burgundy on the Brennan's list that partners salmon in pastry and butter sauce.

variations: Brioche coulibiac: wrap in an enriched brioche dough instead of puff pastry, as was done classically.
Add a layer of buttered spinach to keep the salmon moist.
Individual coulibiacs: four small parcels baked 25 to 30 minutes.
safety: Cook the salmon to 145°F (63°C); take it out at 140°F (60°C) and rest it, checking the temperature rises.
Cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; reheat slices in a 350°F (175°C) oven to 165°F (74°C).
Cool the rice quickly and refrigerate if not using within 1 hour.
