dishes.title: Melton Mowbray Pork Pie
dishes.summary: A raised pork pie in the Melton Mowbray manner: a hot water crust shaped by hand around a jar, filled with hand-chopped seasoned pork, baked free-standing and filled through the lid with stock that sets to jelly. It is in the course because it is a British art of pastry and charcuterie together: a pastry worked while warm, a filling seasoned only with salt and pepper, and a jelly that seals the meat.
skills: a hot water crust raised by hand
filling with stock that sets to jelly
equipment: Straight-sided jar or a pie dolly, about 5 inches (13 cm) across
Large mixing bowl and wooden spoon
Sharp knife and board for hand-chopping
Small funnel or a piping nozzle

ingredients.item: Egg yolk and milk, for the wash
Pork or chicken stock, well flavoured

mise: Wrap the outside of the jar in cling film and dust it lightly with flour.
Cut the chilled pork shoulder and belly into 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice by hand, keeping a third of the belly slightly coarser.
Cut a strip of baking paper about 4 inches (10 cm) wide and long enough to wrap the pie, and a length of string.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Soak the gelatine in cold water just before making the jelly.

timeline.do: Chop and season the filling; chill.
Make the hot water crust and raise the case around the jar.
Fill, lid and crimp the pie; collar it with paper.
Bake 30 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then about 75 minutes at 350°F (175°C).
Cool 1 hour; pour in the cool jelly through the hole.
Chill overnight to set.
Serve cold in wedges with pickle and mustard.

steps.do: Make the filling: put the diced shoulder and belly in a bowl with the salt, white and black pepper and mace and mix well with your hands for 1 minute until slightly sticky. Fry a small piece to taste for seasoning. Chill.
steps.look: A coarse, pink, well-seasoned mixture that just holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Mincing it fine, which makes a dense, sausage-like filling.
steps.fix: Chop by hand for the classic open texture.

steps.do: Make the hot water crust: mix the 3 cups (375 g) flour and salt in the bowl. Heat the lard and 2/3 cup (150 ml) water in the saucepan until the lard melts and the water just boils. Pour it into the flour and stir with the wooden spoon, then knead briefly when cool enough to handle, to a smooth, warm dough.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, pliable dough, warm to the touch and slightly glossy.
steps.mistake: Letting the dough go cold, when it cracks and cannot be shaped.
steps.fix: Work it warm. Keep the portion you are not using covered and warm in the bowl.

steps.do: Cut off a quarter of the dough for the lid and keep it warm and covered. Flatten the rest into a thick disc, set the floured jar in the centre, and push and coax the pastry up its sides with your hands, turning the jar, until the walls are an even 3/8 inch (1 cm) thick and about 3 inches (8 cm) high.
steps.look: An even, smooth-walled case standing around the jar.
steps.mistake: Thin patches near the base, which leak during baking.
steps.fix: Press the base and lower walls a little thicker. Patch thin spots with dough while warm.

steps.do: Let the case cool and firm for 10 minutes, then twist and lift the jar out gently, peeling away the cling film.
steps.look: A free-standing pastry case that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Pulling the jar out while the pastry is still soft, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Wait until the walls feel firm and cool.

steps.do: Pack the filling into the case, pressing it into the edges and doming it slightly in the middle. Roll the reserved dough into a lid, brush the rim of the case with egg wash, set the lid on, and pinch and crimp the edges together firmly. Cut a 1/2 inch (1 cm) hole in the centre.
steps.look: A full, slightly domed pie with a crimped edge and a neat steam hole.
steps.mistake: Leaving air gaps, which leave holes in the slice.
steps.fix: Press the meat down firmly as you fill.

steps.do: Wrap the paper strip around the pie and tie it loosely with string to support the walls. Brush the lid with egg wash.
steps.look: A neat paper collar holding the pie walls straight and upright, tied without denting them.
steps.mistake: Tying too tightly, which dents the soft pastry.
steps.fix: Snug but loose; it only stops the walls bowing.

steps.do: Bake on the tray at 400°F (200°C) for 30 minutes, then lower to 350°F (175°C) for 60 to 75 minutes. Remove the collar for the last 20 minutes, brush the sides with egg wash and return until golden all over. The centre should read 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: A deep golden, glossy crust; juices bubbling up through the hole; it smells of baked pork and pepper.
steps.mistake: Pale sides, or pulling it before the centre is cooked.
steps.fix: Use the probe through the hole; bake until golden and 160°F (71°C).

steps.do: Cool the pie 1 hour. Make the jelly: squeeze the soaked gelatine and dissolve it in the warm stock, then cool until it is just pourable, the thickness of egg white. Pour it slowly through the hole with the funnel, a little at a time, letting it soak in, until the pie will take no more.
steps.look: The jelly disappears into the gap between meat and pastry, then rises to the hole.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot jelly, which softens the crust and leaks out.
steps.fix: Use cool, syrupy jelly and pour in stages.

steps.do: Refrigerate overnight so the jelly sets. Serve cold, cut into wedges with a sharp knife, with English mustard and pickle or piccalilli.
steps.look: A clean slice: golden crust, a layer of clear jelly, then pale grey pork with a coarse texture.
steps.mistake: Slicing warm, when the jelly runs.
steps.fix: Chill thoroughly; slice straight from the fridge.

dishes.science: Hot water crust works differently from other pastry. Pouring boiling water and melted lard into flour partly gelatinises the starch and coats the flour in fat, so very little gluten forms; the warm dough is soft and mouldable like clay and sets firm as it cools, which is why the case can stand on its own. In the oven the lard keeps it crisp and sturdy rather than flaky. The meat shrinks as its proteins contract and release juices, leaving a gap under the crust. Jelly fills that gap: gelatin from the stock sets when cold, sealing the meat from air, keeping it moist and helping the pie keep. A Melton Mowbray pie uses uncured pork, which is why the meat is grey, not pink.
dishes.plating: Serve on a wooden board, the whole pie with one wedge cut and pulled slightly away to show the layers of crust, jelly and meat. Mustard and piccalilli in small pots, pickled onions and a few watercress sprigs beside.

pairing.drink: A pint of English bitter or a crisp cider: malt and gentle bitterness, or apple acidity, both cut through lard pastry and rich pork.

variations: Gala pie: add a line of hard-boiled eggs through the middle of the filling in a loaf-shaped pie.
Pork and apple: add 1 diced apple and a little sage to the filling.
Small pies: make six individual pies around a small jar, baking 45 to 55 minutes.
safety: Bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C).
Add the jelly only once the pie has cooled for 1 hour, then refrigerate promptly; keep the pie at 40°F (4°C) or below and eat within 4 days.
Hot lard and water burn: pour carefully and stir with a wooden spoon before touching the dough.

dishes.title: Pâté en Croûte
dishes.summary: The summit of French charcuterie: a cured forcemeat of pork, liver and ham with pistachios, baked in a pastry-lined hinged mould to a precise internal temperature, filled with aspic through chimneys, chilled for a day and sliced clean. It is in the course because it brings together curing, forcemeat, pastry and aspic, and is judged by one thing: a slice with no gaps.
skills: a pastry lining a hinged mould
equipment: Hinged pâté en croûte mould, about 12 by 3 inches (30 by 8 cm), or a loaf tin
Digital scale reading to 0.01 g for the curing salt
Meat grinder with a 1/4 inch (6 mm) plate, chilled
Two small tubes of rolled foil or card for chimneys
Long thin knife or electric knife for slicing

ingredients.item: Chicken livers, trimmed of green spots and sinew
Curing salt number 1 (pink salt, 6.25% sodium nitrite)
ingredients.note: weigh exactly: 0.25 percent of the meat

ingredients.item: Egg yolk and water, for the wash
Cornichons, Dijon mustard and dressed leaves

mise: Weigh the meat and calculate the salts from that weight; weigh the curing salt on the precise scale and label it.
Chill the grinder parts and bowls in the freezer for 1 hour.
Grease the mould lightly with butter.
Roll two tubes of foil about 2 inches (5 cm) long for the chimneys.
Soak the gelatine in cold water just before making the aspic.

timeline.do: Cure the diced meats with salts, Madeira and spices for 12 hours in the fridge.
Make the pastry and chill it at least 1 hour.
Grind, mix and test the forcemeat; line the mould; fill and lid.
Bake 20 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then at 325°F (160°C) until the centre reads 165°F (74°C).
Cool 1 hour, then chill overnight.
Pour in the cool aspic in stages; chill 24 hours more.
Unmould, slice with a thin knife and serve with cornichons and mustard.

steps.do: Toss the pork, back fat, livers and ham with the 1 tbsp (18 g) fine salt, the 1/2 tsp (3 g) curing salt, Madeira, white pepper and quatre épices. Cover and refrigerate 12 hours.
steps.look: The cubes turn deep pink and feel tacky, clinging to each other.
steps.mistake: Guessing the curing salt by volume; too much is dangerous.
steps.fix: Weigh it on a scale that reads to 0.01 g and mix it evenly through the fine salt first.

steps.do: Make the pastry: rub the 14 tbsp (200 g) cold butter into the 4 cups (500 g) flour and salt until it looks like coarse gravel. Add the 1/2 cup (120 ml) iced water and bring it together into a firm dough with no dry patches. Wrap and chill at least 1 hour.
steps.look: A firm, smooth dough with small flecks of butter.
steps.mistake: Overworking, which makes the pastry tough and shrink.
steps.fix: Mix only until it holds.

steps.do: Grind the cured meats through the chilled 1/4 inch (6 mm) plate into a chilled bowl. Beat in the 2 eggs and the pistachios with a wooden spoon for 1 minute until sticky. Fry a teaspoon and taste for salt and spice.
steps.look: A coarse, pink forcemeat studded with green pistachios, cold and sticky; the test piece is well seasoned and springy.
steps.mistake: Letting the mixture warm, so the fat smears and it turns greasy.
steps.fix: Keep everything cold. If it warms, chill 20 minutes.

steps.do: Roll two thirds of the pastry to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and line the mould, pressing it into the corners and leaving 3/4 inch (2 cm) hanging over the top. Patch any thin spots.
steps.look: Pastry lining every surface evenly with no cracks or holes.
steps.mistake: Holes or thin spots, where the juices and later the aspic will leak.
steps.fix: Press patches on firmly and seal with egg wash.

steps.do: Pack the forcemeat into the lined mould in layers, pressing into the corners to remove air, and level the top slightly domed.
steps.look: A tightly packed, level filling with no air pockets.
steps.mistake: Loose filling, which leaves gaps in the slice.
steps.fix: Press firmly in layers and tap the mould on the worktop.

steps.do: Brush the overhang with egg wash, fold it over the filling, and lay the rolled-out lid on top, pressing the edges to seal. Cut two holes about 5/8 inch (15 mm) across in the lid and insert the foil chimneys. Decorate with pastry trimmings and brush all over with egg wash.
steps.look: A neat, sealed top with two chimneys standing up.
steps.mistake: Forgetting the chimneys, so steam bursts the crust.
steps.fix: Insert them firmly; they let steam out and the aspic in later.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 minutes, then lower to 325°F (160°C) and bake about 1 hour 15 minutes, until a probe through a chimney reads 165°F (74°C) in the centre.
steps.look: A deep golden crust; juices bubbling up the chimneys; it smells of roast pork, Madeira and butter.
steps.mistake: Taking it out by time alone.
steps.fix: Trust the probe, not the clock; cover with foil if it browns too fast.

steps.do: Cool the pâté in its mould for 1 hour at room temperature, then refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: The filling shrinks slightly, leaving a gap under the crust.
steps.mistake: Adding the aspic while the pâté is hot.
steps.fix: Chill it fully overnight first.

steps.do: Make the aspic: squeeze the gelatine and dissolve it in the warm stock. Cool it until syrupy, the thickness of egg white. Pour through the chimneys with the funnel in three or four stages, letting each soak in, until the gap is full. Chill 24 hours.
steps.look: The aspic disappears into the gaps, then rises to the top of the chimneys.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot aspic, which melts the fat and runs out of the seams.
steps.fix: Pour it cool and syrupy, a little at a time.

steps.do: Unmould the pâté and slice it with a long, thin knife dipped in hot water and wiped between slices, about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Serve with cornichons, mustard and dressed leaves.
steps.look: Clean slices: a golden crust, a thin line of clear aspic, then a pink forcemeat with green pistachios and ham.
steps.mistake: Sawing with a blunt knife, which crumbles the crust.
steps.fix: A hot, sharp knife and long, single strokes.

dishes.science: Curing does three jobs. Salt dissolves muscle proteins so the forcemeat binds; sodium nitrite in curing salt keeps the meat pink, adds the cured flavour and inhibits the bacterium that causes botulism, which is why it is weighed to the hundredth of a gram, because too much is toxic. As the pâté bakes its proteins contract and shed liquid and fat, so the forcemeat shrinks away from the crust that has already set. Aspic fills that gap: gelatin dissolved in stock sets when cold, sealing the meat from air so it stays moist and keeps longer. Baking to a measured 165°F (74°C) cooks the pork and liver safely without overshooting, which would dry the forcemeat.
dishes.plating: Use a long, cold plate. Lay one slice flat in the centre so the cross-section faces up, two cornichons fanned beside it, a small spoonful of Dijon mustard and a little heap of dressed bitter leaves. A slice of toasted bread on the side.

pairing.drink: A Beaujolais cru, served slightly cool: bright red fruit and gentle tannin cut the fat of the forcemeat and pastry, the classic bistro partner.
pairing.brennans: Marcel Lapierre Morgon 2023: a Beaujolais cru on the Brennan's list, the textbook wine for charcuterie and pâté.

variations: Game pâté en croûte: replace half the pork shoulder with venison or duck, and the ham with diced duck breast.
Add a central garnish of seared duck breast or foie gras laid along the middle of the forcemeat.
Terrine: bake the same forcemeat without pastry in a bain-marie to 165°F (74°C).
safety: Curing salt is toxic in excess: weigh it precisely, label it clearly and store it out of reach of children.
Bake until the centre reaches 165°F (74°C), the poultry standard, because the forcemeat holds chicken liver.
Keep the finished pâté refrigerated at 40°F (4°C) or below and eat within 1 week.
Keep the forcemeat below 40°F (4°C) while grinding and mixing.

dishes.title: Seared Scallops with Black Pudding and Cauliflower Purée
dishes.summary: Hand-dived scallops opened from the shell, seared hard in seconds and set on a silky cauliflower purée with crisp black pudding, sharp apple and brown butter. It is in the Chef course because three components must be finished at the same moment, and the scallop leaves no margin: thirty seconds too long and it is rubber.
skills: a silky purée passed through a sieve
dishes.serves: 4 as a starter, 2 as a main
equipment: Heavy stainless or carbon steel frying pan, 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm)
Second smaller non-stick pan for the black pudding
Oyster or short, stiff, blunt-tipped knife and a thin flexible knife
Blender (a jug blender gives a smoother purée than a stick blender)
Fine sieve and a flexible scraper or ladle to push through it
Kitchen paper, a tray and a wire rack
Fish slice or thin offset spatula
Squeeze bottle or small spoon for plating
Tongs or a tablespoon for basting

ingredients.item: Large scallops in the shell, or dry-packed shucked scallops
ingredients.note: ask for dry scallops: wet-packed ones are soaked in phosphate and will not brown
cut into even 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces
2 tbsp (30 g) for the purée, 3 tbsp (40 g) for brown butter
a firm sausage that will slice

ingredients.item: Crisp green apple, such as Granny Smith
ingredients.note: cut into fine matchsticks at the last minute
half for the apple, half for the brown butter

ingredients.item: Neutral oil with a high smoke point (rapeseed, sunflower or grapeseed)

mise: Cut the cauliflower into even 1 inch (2.5 cm) florets so they cook at the same rate.
Open and clean the scallops (step 1 and 2), then lay them on kitchen paper on a tray, uncovered, in the fridge for at least 30 minutes.
Skin the black pudding and cut it into 8 rounds about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick.
Put the 3 tbsp (40 g) butter for the brown butter in a small pan beside the stove; put a sieve over a bowl for the purée.
Warm four plates in a low oven at 140°F (60°C).
Cut the apple last, into matchsticks, and toss with half the lemon juice.

timeline.do: Open and clean the scallops; dry them on paper in the fridge.
Simmer the cauliflower; blend and pass the purée; keep it warm, covered.
Slice the black pudding; warm the plates; cut the apple.
Fry the black pudding; keep warm.
Make the brown butter; heat the scallop pan.
Sear the scallops, baste, rest 30 seconds.
Plate and serve at once.

steps.do: To open a scallop, hold it flat shell up in a folded towel, hinge towards you. Slide the blade of a stiff knife between the shells at the side of the hinge and sweep it flat against the inside of the top shell to cut the muscle. Lift off the top shell.
steps.look: The top shell comes away cleanly with the round white muscle still attached to the bottom shell, and the shell smells of clean sea, never of sulphur.
steps.mistake: Levering the shells apart with the knife tip, which snaps the blade or shatters the shell and cuts into the meat.
steps.fix: Keep the blade flat and scrape along the shell rather than prising; a shell that will not open after three sweeps is a dead scallop and is thrown away.

steps.do: Slide a thin spoon or knife under the frill (the skirt) and lift everything off the shell. Pull away the skirt, the dark stomach and the coral, then peel off the small, tough side muscle on the edge of each white disc. Rinse each disc for 2 seconds under cold water and pat dry.
steps.look: Twelve clean, ivory discs about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across with no grit and no rough strip on the side.
steps.mistake: Soaking the scallops in water to clean them, which waterlogs them so they cannot brown.
steps.fix: Rinse fast and dry on paper; the coral can be kept, fried 20 seconds, and served alongside.

steps.do: Lay the scallops on fresh kitchen paper on a tray, uncovered, and refrigerate for 30 to 60 minutes, turning once. They are ready when the surface looks matte and feels tacky rather than wet.
steps.look: A dull, slightly tacky surface with no bead of moisture.
steps.mistake: Searing straight from the shell or the packet, which steams the surface grey.
steps.fix: Change the paper and give them another 15 minutes, or blot every face again just before cooking.

steps.do: Put the cauliflower, milk, water, 2 tbsp (30 g) butter and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt in a saucepan, bring to a simmer, cover and cook on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes until a floret crushes against the side of the pan with no resistance.
steps.look: Florets that collapse under a spoon; the milk smells sweet and gently cooked, never scorched.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which catches the milk on the base and gives a burnt, brown flavour to a white purée.
steps.fix: Keep it to a lazy simmer; if the base catches, tip the florets into a clean pan without scraping and carry on.

steps.do: Lift the cauliflower into the blender with a slotted spoon, add 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the cooking milk and blend on high for a full 2 minutes, adding milk a spoonful at a time until it turns like a vortex. Push it through the fine sieve with a scraper, season with salt and white pepper, cover and keep warm.
steps.look: A glossy purée that holds a soft peak on a spoon and runs off it slowly, smooth on the tongue with no fibre.
steps.mistake: Too much liquid at the start, which gives a soup that cannot hold a shape on the plate.
steps.fix: Simmer a thin purée in a wide pan over low heat, stirring, for 3 to 5 minutes to drive off water.

steps.do: Fry the black pudding rounds in the dry non-stick pan over medium heat for about 2 minutes a side, pressing gently once with a spatula, until the faces crisp. Drain on paper and keep warm on a tray in the low oven.
steps.look: A dark crisp crust with a soft, crumbly centre; it smells of toasted oats and warm spice.
steps.mistake: Turning it too early or too often, which makes it crumble.
steps.fix: Leave it alone until it releases by itself; a crumbled round is still served, piled as a crumb beside the purée.

steps.do: Melt the 3 tbsp (40 g) butter in the small pan over medium heat and cook, swirling, for 3 to 4 minutes until it foams, the foam subsides and the milk solids turn hazelnut brown. Take it off the heat and add the remaining lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
steps.look: Brown flecks on the base, a nutty smell like toasted hazelnuts, and the hiss slows as the water cooks out.
steps.mistake: Walking away at the foaming stage; brown butter turns black within 20 seconds.
steps.fix: Pour it into a cold cup the moment it browns; if it burns, start again, as burnt butter is bitter.

steps.do: Heat the heavy pan over high heat for 2 minutes, add the oil and wait until it shimmers and the first wisp of smoke rises. Season the scallops with fine salt on one side only, just before they go in.
steps.look: Oil that ripples like heat haze; a scallop edge touched to it sizzles loudly at once.
steps.mistake: Salting the scallops early, which draws water to the surface.
steps.fix: Salt in the last minute; if beads of water appear, blot them off.

steps.do: Lay the scallops salted side down in a clock pattern, starting at 12 o'clock, with a 1 inch (2.5 cm) gap between them. Do not move them for 90 seconds to 2 minutes until a deep golden crust has formed and each releases from the pan.
steps.look: A steady, loud sizzle; the bottom third turns opaque up the sides; the crust is the colour of dark honey.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan or nudging the scallops, which drops the heat and stops the crust.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches in a 10 inch (25 cm) pan; if one sticks, give it 15 seconds more and it will release.

steps.do: Turn each scallop in the same clock order, add a knob of butter from the brown butter pan or 1 tbsp (15 g) fresh, and baste for 30 to 45 seconds. Lift them out when the sides are opaque but the centre still has a translucent band, about 115 to 120°F (46 to 49°C) in the middle.
steps.look: Springy, like a relaxed muscle at the base of your thumb; the centre band glistens.
steps.mistake: Cooking both sides as long as the first, which drives the centre to 140°F (60°C) and squeezes the scallop dry and rubbery.
steps.fix: Lift them early; carry-over heat finishes them while they rest 30 seconds on paper. An overcooked scallop cannot be saved, so serve it sliced thinly with extra brown butter.

steps.do: Plate on the warm plates: spoon 2 tbsp (30 ml) purée on each and drag it into a swoosh with the back of the spoon. Set two pieces of black pudding and three scallops crust side up along it, scatter the apple and chives, spoon over the brown butter and finish each scallop with flaky salt.
steps.look: Three distinct elements, glossy crust upward, the purée still warm and the brown butter pooling, not flooding.
steps.mistake: Plating on cold plates, so the purée stiffens and the butter sets.
steps.fix: Always warm the plates; if the purée has thickened while waiting, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm milk.

dishes.science: A good sear is the Maillard reaction: amino acids and sugars on a dry surface react above about 285°F (140°C) to form hundreds of browned flavour compounds. Water caps a surface at 212°F (100°C), so any moisture must boil off before browning starts, which is why the scallops are dried uncovered. Scallop muscle is mostly myosin and actin; myosin sets around 120°F (49°C), giving a tender, just-firm texture, while actin contracts near 150°F (66°C) and squeezes out juice, which is the rubbery stage. Scallops are naturally sweet from glycogen and the amino acid glycine, so they brown faster than most flesh. The purée is smooth because blending ruptures the cell walls and the sieve removes fibre, while milk proteins and butter fat coat the particles for gloss.
dishes.plating: Use a wide, warm white plate. Drag the purée in a single confident arc across the lower third. Place three scallops, crust up, at even intervals along the arc and tuck two crisp black pudding rounds between them. Pile a small nest of apple matchsticks at one end for height, scatter chives sparingly, and spoon brown butter over each scallop so a few drops fall on the plate. Wipe the rim before it leaves the kitchen.

pairing.drink: An unoaked Chablis or a lean Albariño: high acidity cuts the richness of black pudding and brown butter, and the saline minerality echoes the scallop's sweetness from the sea.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Louis Michel ‘Montmains’ Chablis Premier Cru 2023 (375 ml): a steely Chablis on the Brennan's list that would sharpen the brown butter and frame the scallop's sweetness.

variations: Swap the black pudding for crisp pancetta or chorizo, cooked the same way.
Replace the cauliflower with a celeriac or Jerusalem artichoke purée, cooked in milk the same way.
Add a few drops of reduced apple cider, simmered to a syrup, around the plate for sweetness and acid.
safety: Buy scallops from a fishmonger who keeps them on ice and sells them for eating lightly cooked; a translucent centre is a choice made only with very fresh, cold scallops. Food safety guidance for fish is 145°F (63°C) for anyone who wants them fully cooked.
Keep scallops below 40°F (4°C) until cooking and use within a day of buying.
Hold the knife point away from the hand holding the shell and grip the shell in a folded towel.
Black pudding is sold cooked; fry it until hot right through.

dishes.title: Sashimi Moriawase from a Whole Fish
dishes.summary: A platter of raw fish cut three ways from a whole fish you fillet yourself, with a block of tuna and salmon, set on shredded daikon with shiso and fresh wasabi. It is here because nothing tests knife skill, cleanliness and judgement of freshness more nakedly than raw fish, where every ragged cut and every warm minute shows.
skills: breaking a whole fish into loins
equipment: Deba (heavy, single-bevelled filleting knife) or a sturdy filleting knife
Yanagiba (long sashimi knife) or the longest, sharpest slicing knife you own
Whetstone, 1000 and 6000 grit, and a cloth
Large cutting board, plus a second board kept clean for slicing
Fish scaler or the back of a knife
Japanese mandoline or a peeler for daikon

ingredients.item: Whole sea bream (madai) or black sea bass, sold for raw eating
ingredients.note: clear bright eyes, red gills, firm flesh, smells of seawater

ingredients.item: Tuna block (akami or chu-toro), sold for raw eating
ingredients.note: a rectangular saku block with straight grain

ingredients.item: Salmon fillet, skinless, sold for raw eating
ingredients.note: farmed salmon raised for raw consumption

ingredients.item: Fresh wasabi root, or good wasabi paste
ingredients.note: grated on sharkskin or the finest grater
for lightly curing the bream skin side

mise: Sharpen both knives on the stone and wipe them; a dull knife tears raw fish.
Fill a bowl with iced water and set out kitchen paper, cling film and a clean board.
Put the serving platter in the fridge to chill.
Peel the daikon, cut it into 3 inch (8 cm) lengths and cut it into long fine threads; soak in iced water.
Keep every block of fish in the fridge on ice until you are ready to cut it.

timeline.do: Sharpen knives; prepare daikon and chill the platter.
Scale, gut and rinse the whole fish.
Fillet three pieces; remove pin bones and the belly bones.
Scald the bream skin and chill the fillets in iced water; dry and wrap.
Chill all fish 20 minutes more to firm.
Slice tuna, salmon and bream; grate wasabi.
Arrange and serve straight away.

steps.do: Scale the bream over a sink lined with a bag, scraping from tail to head with the scaler, including along the belly and near the fins. Cut off the head behind the pectoral fin with the deba, slit the belly from vent to head, pull out the guts and scrape out the dark blood line along the spine with a spoon. Rinse in cold water for no more than 30 seconds and dry completely inside and out.
steps.look: A clean cavity with no blood line; the skin feels smooth with no scales catching your fingertip.
steps.mistake: Leaving the blood line or rinsing the fish for minutes, which washes out flavour and leaves the flesh soft.
steps.fix: Scrape the blood line with a small brush or spoon and rinse it fast; dry with paper immediately.

steps.do: Fillet into three pieces (sanmai oroshi). Lay the fish with its back towards you and cut along the back from head end to tail just above the dorsal fin, keeping the blade on the bones, in long strokes 1/2 inch (1 cm) deep each pass. Turn it and cut along the belly side from tail to head. Free the fillet over the spine with the blade flat against the bones. Turn the fish over and repeat.
steps.look: Two fillets, a skeleton with almost no flesh on it, and smooth cut surfaces with no ragged steps.
steps.mistake: Sawing back and forth with short strokes, which leaves a torn surface and wastes flesh.
steps.fix: Use long, smooth strokes the full length of the blade and let the bones guide it. Scrape the frame with a spoon to make nakaochi for a hand roll.

steps.do: Lay each fillet skin side down. Slice away the thin belly bones with a shallow cut, then run your fingertip down the centre line to find the pin bones and pull each out with tweezers, pulling towards the head. Cut each fillet in two along the centre line, discarding the narrow strip of bones.
steps.look: Four clean loins, two back (thicker) and two belly, with no bone under your fingertip.
steps.mistake: Pulling pin bones towards the tail, which tears the flesh.
steps.fix: Pull with the direction of the bone, towards the head; a stubborn bone is loosened by pressing down beside it with a finger.

steps.do: Make matsukawa (pine bark) skin: lay the bream loins skin side up on a board set across the sink, cover with a clean cloth, sprinkle a pinch of salt and pour about 2 cups (480 ml) of just-boiled water over the skin. Plunge the loins at once into the iced water for 1 minute, then dry well.
steps.look: The skin shrinks, curls slightly and turns tight and glossy with fine ridges like bark; the flesh underneath stays raw and pink-white.
steps.mistake: Pouring water slowly or leaving it out of the ice, which cooks the flesh beneath the skin.
steps.fix: Work fast and get it into ice within 3 seconds; if the edges have turned opaque, trim them away.

steps.do: Wrap each loin, the tuna and the salmon tightly in kitchen paper and then in cling film, and chill for 20 to 30 minutes to firm the flesh for slicing.
steps.look: Firm, cold flesh that holds its shape when pressed.
steps.mistake: Slicing warm or soft fish, which smears and tears.
steps.fix: If the fish feels soft, give it 10 more minutes in the coldest part of the fridge.

steps.do: Slice the tuna hirazukuri: lay the block on the clean board with the grain running diagonally. Place the heel of the yanagiba on the far edge and pull the knife towards you in one long stroke, using the whole blade, to cut slices 3/8 inch (1 cm) thick. Slide each slice to the right with the knife, stacking them like dominoes.
steps.look: Clean, glassy faces on each slice and straight edges; the slice falls away with no tearing.
steps.mistake: Pressing down or sawing, which crushes the flesh and leaves ridges.
steps.fix: Keep the pressure light and let the length of the blade do the work; wipe the knife with a damp cloth between every few slices.

steps.do: Slice the salmon sogizukuri: hold the knife at a 45 degree angle and cut slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick on the bias, pulling towards you in one stroke, so each slice shows a wide face with the white fat lines.
steps.look: Broad slices with fat lines that run in neat parallel stripes.
steps.mistake: Cutting straight down, which gives small, thick pieces.
steps.fix: Lower the angle of the blade until it is nearly flat against the board.

steps.do: Slice the bream with its skin on in hirazukuri slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, or for usuzukuri (paper thin) lay the skinless belly loin flat and cut almost horizontally into slices 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick so that the plate shows through.
steps.look: Bream skin forming a crisp rim on each slice; usuzukuri slices so thin they are translucent.
steps.mistake: Trying to cut usuzukuri with a dull knife, which shreds it.
steps.fix: Hone the knife again; if you cannot get thin slices, serve the bream hirazukuri instead.

steps.do: Grate the wasabi in small circles on a sharkskin grater or the finest grater, and let it sit 2 minutes to develop its heat. Drain the daikon, spin or squeeze it dry, and pile it in small mounds on the chilled platter.
steps.look: Fluffy, pale green wasabi with a fresh, sweet heat and fine, crisp, dry daikon threads.
steps.mistake: Grating wasabi too early, so it loses its heat within 15 minutes.
steps.fix: Grate it last; use paste only if fresh root is not available.

steps.do: Arrange the sashimi in groups of odd numbers (3 or 5 slices) leaning against the daikon mounds and the shiso leaves, tuna at the back, salmon and bream in front. Add lemon half-moons and the wasabi. Serve at once with soy sauce in small dishes.
steps.look: A platter with height at the back, colour contrast between red tuna, orange salmon and white bream, and every slice glistening and cold.
steps.mistake: Leaving the platter at room temperature for more than 20 minutes before eating.
steps.fix: Serve within 10 minutes of slicing; any left over goes back into the fridge and is eaten that day.

dishes.science: Raw fish is safe and delicious only when it is very fresh, very cold and free of parasites. After death, enzymes and bacteria break muscle proteins and fats down, producing trimethylamine (the fishy smell), so the clock starts the moment the fish dies. Chilling slows these reactions, and firm, cold flesh slices cleanly because the collagen and fat are stiff. A long single-bevelled knife cuts in one pulled stroke without tearing the muscle fibres, so the slices keep a glassy surface and release less juice. The matsukawa scald shrinks the collagen in the skin, making it tender enough to eat raw, while the ice stops heat reaching the flesh. Freshly grated wasabi is hot because cell damage lets an enzyme make allyl isothiocyanate, which fades within about 15 minutes.
dishes.plating: Use a chilled flat platter or a cedar board. Set three small mounds of daikon across the back, each fronted by a shiso leaf, and lean the sashimi against them in odd-numbered groups, each cut stacked like fallen dominoes. Keep colours apart and cut faces turned to the guest. Place the wasabi in a neat cone, the lemon in overlapping half-moons, and leave space between groups. A few drops of soy go on the side, never on the fish.

pairing.drink: A chilled junmai ginjo sake or a crisp, low-alcohol Muscadet: clean acidity and gentle umami sit alongside raw fish without overwhelming its delicate flavours.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de l’Écu ‘Orthogneiss’ Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine 2022: a saline, mineral Muscadet from the Brennan's list whose precision suits raw fish.

variations: Make a hand roll (temaki) with the spoon-scraped meat from the frame, sushi rice and nori.
Use mackerel cured for 30 minutes in salt then 20 minutes in rice vinegar (shime saba) in place of the bream.
Serve the bream usuzukuri with ponzu, grated daikon and spring onion instead of soy.
safety: Buy only fish sold for raw consumption, and ask whether it has been frozen to kill parasites: the US FDA standard is -4°F (-20°C) or below for 7 days, or -31°F (-35°C) until solid then held at -31°F (-35°C) for 15 hours. Tuna and salmon farmed for raw eating are the common exceptions.
Keep all fish at or below 40°F (4°C) right up to slicing, use a separate clean board for slicing, and eat within the day.
Raw fish is not advised for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with a weak immune system.
Sashimi knives are extremely sharp: always pull the blade towards you along the board, never towards your hand, and lay the knife down with the edge away from you.

dishes.title: Suquet de Peix
dishes.summary: A Catalan fisherman's stew in which potatoes cook in a stock made from the frame of the fish you fillet, thickened at the end with a picada of pounded almonds, fried bread, garlic and parsley. It belongs at Chef because its depth comes from technique, not a long list: a proper stock, a slow sofregit and a pounded finish that sets the sauce.
skills: a picada of almonds, garlic and bread
equipment: Large heavy pot for the stock
Wide, shallow casserole or a cazuela, about 12 inch (30 cm)
Mortar and pestle (or a small food processor)

ingredients.item: Whole white fish such as sea bass, hake or snapper
ingredients.note: you will fillet it and use the frame and head for stock
or more of the white fish
discard any that are open and do not close when tapped
heads and shells go into the stock
3 sliced for the sofregit, 2 whole for the picada

ingredients.item: Waxy potatoes such as Yukon Gold
ingredients.note: peeled and cut in 1/4 inch (6 mm) slices
or 2 ñora peppers soaked and scraped

ingredients.item: Fennel bulb trimmings, leek greens or celery

ingredients.note: half for the picada, half to finish

mise: Scrub the clams and leave them in cold salted water for 20 minutes to purge sand.
Peel the prawns, leaving the tails on; keep heads and shells for stock.
Fillet the whole fish, pin-bone it and cut the fillets and monkfish into 2 inch (5 cm) pieces; salt them lightly and chill.
Remove the gills from the head and rinse out any blood from the frame.
Grate the tomatoes on a box grater, discarding the skin; slice the potatoes and keep them in water.

timeline.do: Fillet the fish; purge the clams; peel the prawns.
Make the stock and simmer for 30 minutes; strain.
Cook the sofregit slowly for 20 minutes.
Make the picada.
Add stock and potatoes; simmer 15 to 18 minutes.
Stir in the picada; add fish, clams and prawns.
Rest 3 minutes, finish with parsley and serve.

steps.do: Fillet the whole fish as in the earlier lessons, using long strokes against the bones, then pin-bone the fillets and cut them and the monkfish into 2 inch (5 cm) pieces. Season with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and refrigerate.
steps.look: Neat, boneless pieces of even size so they cook in the same time.
steps.mistake: Cutting the pieces different sizes so the thin ones fall apart while the thick ones are raw.
steps.fix: Trim to even blocks; small trimmings go into the stock.

steps.do: Make the stock: heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat, add the prawn heads and shells and fry for 3 minutes, pressing the heads, then add the fish frame, head, fennel trimmings and bay. Pour in the 7 cups (1.7 litres) water, bring to a bare simmer, skim, and cook for 30 minutes without boiling.
steps.look: A pale gold, sweet-smelling stock with a red sheen from the prawn heads; small bubbles barely break the surface.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard or cooking longer than 40 minutes, which makes fish stock cloudy and bitter from the bones.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and strain at 30 minutes; a cloudy stock still tastes good, so carry on.

steps.do: Strain the stock through a fine sieve, pressing the prawn heads, and measure 5 cups (1.2 litres). Keep it hot.
steps.look: A clean, fragrant stock with no bone or scale fragments.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard on the frame, which forces cloudy fragments through.
steps.fix: Press the prawn heads only, and let the frame drain by itself.

steps.do: Make the sofregit: in the cazuela, warm 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the oil over medium-low heat, add the onion and a pinch of salt, and cook gently for 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and golden. Add the sliced garlic for 1 minute, then the grated tomato and paprika and cook 8 to 10 minutes more until the tomato darkens and the oil separates at the edges.
steps.look: A jammy, dark red-brown paste with oil shining around it, smelling sweet, not raw.
steps.mistake: Rushing the sofregit over high heat, which burns the onions and leaves a thin, sharp sauce.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a spoonful of water if it catches; the colour should deepen slowly.

steps.do: Make the picada: fry the bread in 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the small pan for 1 minute a side until golden, then fry the almonds 2 to 3 minutes until pale gold. Pound the 2 whole garlic cloves with a pinch of salt in the mortar, add the almonds and pound to a coarse meal, then add the bread and half the parsley and pound to a thick paste, loosening with 2 tbsp (30 ml) stock.
steps.look: A thick, grainy, green-flecked paste that smells of toasted almond and garlic.
steps.mistake: Browning the almonds too dark, which turns the picada bitter.
steps.fix: Take them off the heat as soon as they turn pale gold; they keep cooking in the pan.

steps.do: Pour the wine into the sofregit and boil 1 minute. Crumble in the saffron, add the drained potato slices, stir to coat, then pour in the hot stock. Simmer uncovered over medium heat for 15 to 18 minutes until the potatoes are just tender and the edges begin to soften into the broth.
steps.look: Potatoes that a knife slides into with slight resistance; the broth slightly thickened by their starch.
steps.mistake: Stirring the potatoes hard, which breaks them into mash.
steps.fix: Shake the pan rather than stirring; add a little more stock if the potatoes are not covered.

steps.do: Stir the picada into the broth and simmer 2 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly and turns creamy. Taste and season with salt.
steps.look: A broth with body, a slightly opaque, creamy look, and a nutty, garlicky smell.
steps.mistake: Adding the picada too early, so the almonds settle and catch.
steps.fix: Add it in the last minutes and shake the pan to mix it through.

steps.do: Nestle the monkfish into the broth first, then after 2 minutes add the white fish pieces skin side up, the clams and the prawns. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 5 to 7 minutes, shaking the pan gently, until the clams open, the prawns are pink and the fish is just opaque, 140 to 145°F (60 to 63°C) in the thickest piece.
steps.look: Clams opened wide, prawns curled into a loose C, fish flaking at the edges but moist in the middle.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, so the fish breaks up and the prawns curl tight and rubbery.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer; take out cooked pieces with a slotted spoon if others need longer. Discard clams that stay closed.

steps.do: Rest the stew off the heat for 3 minutes, scatter with the remaining parsley and a thread of olive oil, and take the cazuela straight to the table.
steps.look: Glossy broth just covering the potatoes, with fish, shells and prawns arranged on top.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on the heat while the table gathers, which overcooks the fish.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the fish is cooked; it stays hot for 10 minutes in a clay pot.

dishes.science: The broth's body comes from three sources. Fish frames are rich in collagen, which melts into gelatin within 30 minutes; longer boiling extracts calcium and bitter compounds and breaks fat into cloudy droplets. Potato starch leaches from the cut slices and swells in the hot liquid, giving viscosity. The picada finishes the job: ground almonds and fried bread are a starch and protein mixture that swells in the broth, thickening it, while the almond oils emulsify into the liquid with the olive oil, turning it creamy rather than greasy. A slow sofregit develops sweetness through caramelisation and Maillard browning of onion sugars, and the tomato's acids and glutamates add savoury depth. Fish proteins set between 120 and 140°F (49 and 60°C), so the fish goes in last.
dishes.plating: Serve in the cazuela at the table, or ladle into warm wide bowls: a layer of potato slices first, then a piece of each fish, two prawns and a few clams on top, with broth poured around rather than over so the fish stays visible. Finish with parsley and a thread of olive oil, and set out bread and a bowl for shells.

pairing.drink: A crisp Catalan white such as Penedès Xarel·lo or a Galician Albariño: bright acidity and a saline finish match the saffron and almond without overpowering the fish.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: a fresh Albariño from the Brennan's list that would sit perfectly with the stew's seafood and saffron.

variations: Add a spoon of allioli on top of each bowl at the table.
Use squid rings and mussels in place of clams and prawns.
Make it with salt cod, soaked for 36 hours, as in inland Catalan kitchens.
safety: Fish is cooked through at 145°F (63°C) or when it flakes and is opaque.
Discard clams that are open before cooking and do not close when tapped, and any that stay shut after cooking.
Keep raw seafood at or below 40°F (4°C) and use a separate board from vegetables.

dishes.title: Redfish Courtbouillon
dishes.summary: The Creole court-bouillon of south Louisiana: fillets of redfish poached in a tomato gravy built on a peanut-butter-coloured roux, the trinity and a stock made from the fish's own frame, served over rice. It is in the course because it unites two French ideas reshaped in New Orleans, a cooked roux and a stock from bones, into a dish that must be seasoned and timed by eye.
skills: filleting redfish and making stock from the head and frame
equipment: Heavy enamelled cast iron or stainless pot, 5 to 6 quart (5 to 6 litre), for the roux and gravy
Flat-edged wooden spoon or a roux paddle
Saucepan with lid for the rice

ingredients.item: Whole redfish (red drum), or snapper or black drum
ingredients.note: filleted, skin off; frame and head for stock

ingredients.item: Neutral oil or lard for the roux
Tinned whole plum tomatoes, crushed by hand
ingredients.note: or 2 lb (900 g) ripe tomatoes, peeled
juice of half, half sliced thin

mise: Fillet the redfish, skin the fillets, remove the pin bones and cut into 4 portions; season with 1 tsp (5 g) salt and the cayenne, cover and chill.
Remove gills from the head and rinse the frame of blood.
Dice the onion, pepper and celery into 1/4 inch (6 mm) pieces and keep them in one bowl beside the stove; the roux will not wait.
Crush the tomatoes by hand into a bowl.
Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear.

timeline.do: Fillet the fish; make and strain the stock (35 minutes).
Cook the roux to peanut butter colour (15 to 20 minutes).
Add the trinity, then tomatoes and stock; simmer 30 minutes.
Start the rice.
Season the gravy; slide in the fish and poach 8 to 10 minutes.
Finish with lemon, spring onions and parsley; serve over rice.

steps.do: Fillet the redfish: cut along the backbone from head to tail in long strokes, free the fillet over the ribs, then skin each fillet by holding the tail end and running the knife between flesh and skin at a low angle. Pin-bone and cut into 4 portions about 5 oz (140 g) each.
steps.look: Four even, clean white fillets; a frame with little meat left.
steps.mistake: Leaving the redfish's large scales on the frame for the stock, which makes it gritty.
steps.fix: Scale the fish first or rinse the frame thoroughly; strain the stock twice if needed.

steps.do: Make the stock: put the frame, head (gills removed), the onion and celery trimmings, a bay leaf and the 6 cups (1.4 litres) water into the stockpot. Bring to a simmer, skim the grey foam, and cook gently for 30 to 35 minutes. Strain through the fine sieve and measure 3 cups (720 ml).
steps.look: A clear, light stock that smells clean and of the sea.
steps.mistake: Boiling it hard, which clouds it and draws bitterness from the bones.
steps.fix: Keep it at a quiet simmer and stop at 35 minutes.

steps.do: Make the roux: heat the oil in the heavy pot over medium heat for 2 minutes, then whisk in the flour until smooth. Stir constantly with the flat spoon, scraping the whole base, for 15 to 20 minutes until it is the colour of peanut butter and smells of toasted nuts.
steps.look: A smooth, loose paste moving from blond to tan to peanut butter brown, with a toasted biscuit aroma.
steps.mistake: Turning the heat up to hurry, or stopping stirring for a moment, which gives black specks and a burnt smell.
steps.fix: If you see black specks or smell acrid smoke, throw it away and start again; a burnt roux ruins the whole dish.

steps.do: Add the onion, pepper and celery all at once to stop the roux cooking. Stir for 6 to 8 minutes over medium heat until the vegetables soften and the onion turns translucent, then add the garlic for 1 minute.
steps.look: A loud sizzle and a cloud of steam as the trinity goes in, then a sweet, toasty smell; the roux darkens slightly more from the vegetables.
steps.mistake: Adding the vegetables gradually, so the roux keeps cooking and scorches.
steps.fix: Have the trinity measured and ready before the roux starts; tip it in all at once.

steps.do: Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then add the crushed tomatoes, thyme, the second bay leaf, black pepper and Worcestershire. Whisk in the hot stock a ladle at a time so the roux dissolves smoothly. Bring to a simmer and cook uncovered over low heat for 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until it coats the back of a spoon.
steps.look: A brick-red gravy, thick enough to coat a spoon but still pouring, with a little oil shining at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock all at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk hard; if lumps remain, pass the gravy through a sieve and press the vegetables back in.

steps.do: Start the rice: bring the rinsed rice, 2 1/4 cups (540 ml) water and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt to a boil, cover tightly, turn the heat to its lowest setting and cook for 17 minutes, then rest off the heat, covered, for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Separate, tender grains with small steam holes on the surface.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking, which lets the steam out and leaves hard grains.
steps.fix: If grains are still firm, sprinkle 2 tbsp (30 ml) water over, cover and rest 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Taste the gravy and season with salt, cayenne and lemon juice until it tastes bright and well seasoned. It should be thin enough to come halfway up the fish; thin with a splash of stock if needed.
steps.look: A lively gravy with gentle heat at the back of the throat and no floury taste.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning, so the fish tastes flat.
steps.fix: Season the gravy boldly before the fish goes in, since the fish dilutes it.

steps.do: Slide the fish portions into the simmering gravy and spoon gravy over the top. Lay the lemon slices on top, cover and poach over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, without stirring, until the fish is opaque and flakes at the thickest point, 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: Fish turned white right through and beginning to flake; the gravy bubbling lazily around it.
steps.mistake: Stirring the pot, which breaks the fish into shreds.
steps.fix: Shake the pot gently instead; lift each portion out with a fish spatula to serve.

steps.do: Scatter the spring onions and parsley over the pot. Mound rice in warm shallow bowls, lift a portion of fish onto each, and ladle gravy around. Serve with hot sauce at the table.
steps.look: Bright green onions on a glossy red gravy; whole pieces of fish.
steps.mistake: Ladling the fish and gravy together, which breaks the fish.
steps.fix: Lift the fish first, then spoon over the gravy.

dishes.science: A roux thickens by starch gelatinisation, but cooking it longer changes what it does. As the flour toasts, its starch breaks down into shorter chains, which thicken less but bring deep, nutty flavours from Maillard reactions and caramelisation. A peanut-butter-coloured roux thickens perhaps half as much as a blond one, which is why a Creole gravy tastes rich yet stays loose. Adding the cool trinity drops the temperature at once and stops the browning. Fish stock adds gelatin and savoury depth from the frame, and tomato's acidity balances the roux's richness. Fish flesh holds little collagen and its proteins set at low temperatures, so poaching gently in the gravy at just below boiling keeps the fillets moist and whole.
dishes.plating: Use warm wide bowls. Pack rice into a small cup and turn out a neat mound slightly off centre, lean the fillet against it, and ladle the red gravy into the open side so the rice stays white at the top. Set a lemon slice on the fish and scatter spring onions and parsley over everything. Hot sauce goes on the table, not the plate.

pairing.drink: A dry Provence rosé or a light, chilled Beaujolais-Villages: enough fruit and acidity for the tomato, low tannin so the fish is not drowned, and freshness against the cayenne.
pairing.brennans: Redfish Véronique: compare Brennan's own refined redfish with this rustic home gravy and taste how the same fish carries a cream sauce versus a roux and tomato one.

variations: Use catfish or black drum, both traditional in Cajun country.
Add 1/2 lb (225 g) peeled Gulf shrimp for the last 3 minutes.
Make a Cajun version with a darker, chocolate roux and more cayenne, and fewer tomatoes.
safety: Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) or until opaque and flaking.
Hot roux reaches over 400°F (200°C) and sticks to skin: wear long sleeves, stir with a long spoon, and never splash it.
Add the vegetables carefully, as they steam violently; lean away from the pot.
Cool leftover rice within an hour and refrigerate; reheat until steaming.

dishes.title: Hor Mok Pla (Steamed Fish Curry Custard)
dishes.summary: Thai steamed fish curry custard: a red curry paste you pound yourself, beaten with coconut cream, egg and fish sauce, folded with fish and steamed in banana leaf cups over sweet basil, then capped with thick coconut cream and lime leaf. It is in the course because it marries pounding, beating and gentle steaming, and only patience gives the silky, aerated set.
skills: a red curry paste pounded by hand
fish and coconut beaten to a mousse with egg
equipment: Steamer basket or wok with rack and lid
8 banana leaf cups (krathong) or 8 small ramekins, 1/2 cup (120 ml) each
Stapler or cocktail sticks if making leaf cups
Large mixing bowl and a wooden spoon

ingredients.item: Dried long red chillies, seeded, soaked 20 minutes
Lemongrass, tender lower part, thinly sliced
Makrut lime zest, or 4 leaves finely shredded
Firm white fish fillet (snapper, cod or catfish)
Coconut cream (the thick top of an unshaken tin)
Thai sweet basil or holy basil leaves
Napa cabbage, shredded fine, blanched 30 seconds
Makrut lime leaves, cut into hair-fine strips

mise: Soak the dried chillies in warm water for 20 minutes; drain and squeeze dry.
Toast the shrimp paste wrapped in foil in a dry pan for 1 minute a side.
Make the banana leaf cups: cut two 6 inch (15 cm) circles per cup, layer them shiny sides out, make four 1 inch (2.5 cm) pleats round the edge and staple to form a square cup. Or oil the ramekins.
Slice half the fish into thin pieces 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) long; mince the other half finely with a knife.
Leave the coconut tin unshaken in the fridge for an hour so the cream separates.

timeline.do: Soak chillies; chill coconut cream; make leaf cups.
Pound the paste (20 to 25 minutes).
Beat paste, cream, fish and egg in one direction (10 minutes).
Start the rice; heat the steamer.
Fill cups over basil; steam 15 to 20 minutes.
Make the coconut topping; spoon on; steam 2 minutes more.
Garnish with lime leaf and chilli; serve with rice.

steps.do: Pound the paste: put the salt and the soaked chillies in the mortar and pound with a heavy, vertical action for 3 minutes until they break down. Add the hardest ingredients first, one at a time, pounding each to a paste before the next: lemongrass, galangal, lime zest, coriander root, then shallots and garlic, then fingerroot and the toasted shrimp paste.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, brick-red paste with no visible fibres of lemongrass, smelling intensely of citrus and chilli; about 1/3 cup (80 g).
steps.mistake: Adding everything at once, which leaves stringy lemongrass and a coarse paste.
steps.fix: Keep going; pound in the order of hardness and scrape down the sides; a few minutes in a small processor at the end is acceptable.

steps.do: In a large bowl, combine 3 tbsp (45 g) of the paste with 3/4 cup (180 ml) coconut cream and the minced fish. Stir in one direction only with a wooden spoon for 5 minutes until the mixture thickens and turns sticky.
steps.look: The mixture becomes pale, thick and glossy and clings to the spoon.
steps.mistake: Stirring back and forth, which stops the mixture thickening.
steps.fix: Keep to one direction and keep going; it will tighten at about the 4 minute mark.

steps.do: Add the fish sauce, palm sugar and the egg and keep stirring in the same direction for another 5 minutes until light and fluffy. Fold in the sliced fish.
steps.look: A light, mousse-like custard that holds soft peaks and holds the sliced fish evenly.
steps.mistake: Adding the egg too early, which makes the custard loose.
steps.fix: Add it once the mixture has thickened; if it seems runny, stir longer.

steps.do: Taste for seasoning by poaching 1 tsp (5 g) of the mixture in a little simmering water for 1 minute and tasting it. It should be salty, a little sweet, and hot.
steps.look: A small cooked dumpling that tastes balanced and holds together.
steps.mistake: Tasting raw custard, which is unsafe with raw egg and fish.
steps.fix: Always cook the test piece; adjust with fish sauce or sugar.

steps.do: Line each cup with basil leaves and a pinch of blanched cabbage. Spoon in the fish custard to 1/4 inch (6 mm) below the rim.
steps.look: Cups three-quarters full, the green basil peeking out at the edges.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the custard rises and spills.
steps.fix: Leave a small gap; it puffs as it steams.

steps.do: Set the cups in the steamer over boiling water, cover and steam over medium-high heat for 15 to 20 minutes until set and an inserted skewer comes out clean, 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
steps.look: Firm, puffed custard that springs back when touched; the surface turns from glossy to matte.
steps.mistake: Steaming too hard, which forms bubbles and a grainy texture.
steps.fix: Reduce to medium once boiling; a slightly grainy hor mok is still delicious.

steps.do: While it steams, simmer the remaining 1/2 cup (120 ml) coconut cream with the rice flour and a pinch of salt for 1 to 2 minutes, whisking, until thick enough to coat a spoon.
steps.look: A thick, glossy white cream.
steps.mistake: Boiling it hard, which splits the cream into oil.
steps.fix: Keep it at a simmer; whisk in a spoonful of cold cream if it begins to split.

steps.do: Spoon a tablespoon of the coconut cream over each set custard, scatter lime leaf strips and red chilli, and steam for 2 minutes more to set the top.
steps.look: A white cap with fine green threads and red strips of chilli.
steps.mistake: Adding the cream before the custard has set, so it sinks.
steps.fix: Wait until the custard is firm before adding the cream.

steps.do: Serve the cups hot or warm with jasmine rice. Unstaple the leaf cups at the table or serve them whole.
steps.look: Fragrant, warm cups with a firm but trembling set.
steps.mistake: Serving them straight from the steamer, too hot to eat.
steps.fix: Let them stand 2 minutes before serving.

dishes.science: Stirring the paste, coconut cream and minced fish in one direction works like making a fish ball: salt in the paste and fish sauce dissolve the muscle proteins myosin and actin, which unravel and link into a sticky network that traps fat and air. That network is what makes hor mok light rather than dense. The egg adds more protein that sets around 160°F (71°C), binding the custard as it steams. Coconut cream is an emulsion of fat in water held by proteins; heated hard it can split, so a little rice flour stabilises the topping. Steaming cooks gently, since steam cannot exceed 212°F (100°C); too much heat makes the proteins tighten fast and squeeze out liquid, leaving bubbles and graininess.
dishes.plating: Set two cups on a small plate or a banana-leaf-lined tray beside a neat dome of jasmine rice. The white coconut cap should be intact, with the green lime leaf and red chilli giving contrast. For a more formal plate, unmould a ramekin onto a basil leaf and spoon extra coconut cream around it.

pairing.drink: An off-dry German Riesling Kabinett: residual sugar soothes the chilli heat, high acidity lifts the coconut, and citrus aromas echo lemongrass and lime leaf.
pairing.brennans: J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Kabinett 2020: an off-dry Mosel Riesling on the Brennan's list whose sweetness and acidity would tame the curry's heat.

variations: Hor mok talay: use a mixture of prawns, squid and scallops in place of fish.
Steam it in a whole young coconut, the top cut off, for a dramatic centrepiece.
Use a good bought red curry paste if time is short, adding fresh lemongrass and lime leaf.
safety: Cook the custard to 160°F (71°C) in the centre, as it holds raw egg and fish; never taste it raw.
Steam can burn: lift the lid away from you and use tongs or gloves for the cups.
Wash hands well after handling chillies, and keep them away from your eyes.

dishes.title: Porterhouse with Bordelaise Sauce
dishes.summary: A thick porterhouse, dry-brined overnight, cooked slowly in a low oven and seared hard in cast iron, carved into strip and fillet and served with bordelaise, the Bordeaux red wine sauce finished with demi-glace and poached bone marrow. It is here because it is the steakhouse exam: two muscles that cook at different rates on one bone, a sauce reduced to a glaze, and a carve the guest can see.
skills: carving strip and fillet off the bone
a bordelaise from a red wine and shallot reduction, demi-glace and bone marrow
equipment: Wire rack set in a rimmed baking tray
Heavy 12 inch (30 cm) cast-iron frying pan
Instant-read probe thermometer, ideally a leave-in probe with an alarm
Small heavy saucepan for the sauce
Large carving board with a juice groove
Long carving knife and a boning knife
Tongs and a spoon for basting

ingredients.note: prime or choice with a large fillet side

ingredients.item: Kosher salt or coarse sea salt
ingredients.note: about 1 percent of the weight, for the dry brine

ingredients.item: Marrow bones, cut in 2 inch (5 cm) lengths (or ask the butcher to push out the marrow)
Dry red Bordeaux or Merlot blend
Demi-glace (made in the espagnole lesson, or good bought)
ingredients.note: or 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) beef stock reduced by half with 1 tsp (3 g) gelatin

ingredients.item: Cold unsalted butter, diced, to finish the sauce

mise: The day before, pat the steak dry, season every surface including the edges with the kosher salt, and leave it uncovered on the rack in the fridge for 12 to 24 hours.
Soak the marrow bones in cold salted water in the fridge for 2 hours (or overnight) to draw out the blood, then push the marrow out with your thumb and cut it into 1/2 inch (1 cm) dice.
Chop the shallots very finely and measure out the wine and demi-glace.
Take the steak out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking; heat the oven to 250°F (120°C).

timeline.do: Dry-brine the steak uncovered in the fridge; soak the marrow bones.
Oven to 250°F (120°C); start reducing the wine for the sauce.
Steak into the oven on its rack (45 to 70 minutes).
Finish the bordelaise base; poach the marrow.
Steak out at 115°F (46°C); rest 10 minutes; heat the iron pan.
Sear, baste and rest 5 minutes.
Mount the sauce with butter and marrow; carve and serve.

steps.do: Put the shallots, wine, bay and crushed peppercorns into the small heavy saucepan and boil over medium-high heat for 15 to 20 minutes until reduced to about 1/4 cup (60 ml) and syrupy.
steps.look: Large slow bubbles, shallots suspended in a glossy purple syrup; the sharp alcohol smell has gone.
steps.mistake: Reducing too fast and letting it catch, which tastes burnt and bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat in the final minutes and watch it; add a splash of water if it begins to stick.

steps.do: Add the demi-glace and simmer 5 to 8 minutes until it coats a spoon and a finger drawn across the back leaves a clean line. Strain through the fine sieve, pressing the shallots, back into the pan and set aside.
steps.look: A glossy, dark sauce with the body of warm honey that clings to the spoon.
steps.mistake: Reducing until it turns sticky and gluey.
steps.fix: Whisk in a little water or stock to loosen it to coating consistency.

steps.do: Put the steak on its rack in the 250°F (120°C) oven with a probe in the thickest part of the strip side, not touching bone. Cook until it reads 115°F (46°C) for medium-rare, 45 to 70 minutes, and check the fillet side, which cooks faster.
steps.look: An evenly pink-grey surface with no browning; the fillet a few degrees ahead of the strip.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fillet side pointing at the hottest part of the oven, which overcooks it.
steps.fix: Turn the steak so the fillet faces the cooler front of the oven; if the fillet races ahead, pull the steak when the fillet reaches 118°F (48°C).

steps.do: Rest the steak on the rack for 10 minutes while you heat the cast-iron pan over high heat for 5 minutes until it smokes lightly. Pat the steak dry and season with cracked pepper.
steps.look: A dry surface and a pan so hot that a drop of water vanishes instantly.
steps.mistake: Searing in a pan that is not hot enough, which slowly overcooks the outside before it browns.
steps.fix: Wait until the pan smokes; the sear should take about 2 minutes a side, no more.

steps.do: Add the oil, lay the steak in away from you and sear 1 1/2 to 2 minutes a side without moving it, then stand it on its edge with tongs to brown the fat strip for 1 minute.
steps.look: A loud, steady sizzle, a deep mahogany crust and rendered, golden fat on the edge.
steps.mistake: Moving the steak around constantly, which stops a crust forming.
steps.fix: Put it down and leave it; lift a corner after 90 seconds to check colour.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium, add the butter, thyme and garlic and baste for 1 minute by tilting the pan and spooning the foaming butter over the steak. Take it out at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) for medium-rare.
steps.look: Butter foaming and brown, smelling of garlic and thyme; the crust glistening.
steps.mistake: Letting the butter burn black.
steps.fix: Keep the heat at medium and baste quickly; the butter should be nutty, not acrid.

steps.do: Rest the steak on the board for 5 minutes. Meanwhile poach the diced marrow in barely simmering salted water for 1 to 2 minutes until it turns opaque, and drain.
steps.look: Marrow that turns from pink to creamy white and stays in cubes.
steps.mistake: Boiling it, which melts the marrow into fat.
steps.fix: Keep the water just trembling and lift the marrow out the moment it turns white.

steps.do: Reheat the sauce to a simmer, take it off the heat and whisk in the cold diced butter piece by piece, then fold in the marrow and parsley and season.
steps.look: A sauce that becomes glossy and slightly thicker as the butter goes in, with small cubes of marrow suspended.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce after adding butter, which splits it greasy.
steps.fix: Add an ice cube or a spoonful of cold stock and whisk hard to bring it back.

steps.do: Carve: run the boning knife along the T-bone to remove the strip in one piece, then the fillet. Slice both across the grain into 1/2 inch (1 cm) slices, holding the knife at a slight angle, and re-set them against the bone on a warm platter.
steps.look: Even, rosy pink slices edge to edge with a thin brown crust, and very little juice on the board.
steps.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which leaves long chewy fibres.
steps.fix: Look for the lines of muscle and cut across them; the strip and fillet run in different directions, so check each.

steps.do: Season the cut faces with flaky salt and spoon the bordelaise over or alongside, making sure each slice gets a little marrow.
steps.look: A glossy pool of sauce with marrow cubes beside rosy slices.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot sauce over the whole steak so the crust goes soggy.
steps.fix: Spoon the sauce beside the meat, or serve it in a warm jug.

dishes.science: A porterhouse holds two muscles: the strip, firm with more fat and connective tissue, and the tender fillet, which is smaller and cooks faster. A low oven heats the steak evenly, so the band of grey overcooked meat under the crust stays thin. The surface also dries in the oven, letting the sear reach Maillard browning temperatures, above about 285°F (140°C), quickly. Dry-brining overnight lets salt dissolve into the surface, then diffuse inward, seasoning the meat and changing proteins so they hold more juice. Resting lets heat even out and juice thicken a little as it cools. Bordelaise depends on reduction: water boils off, concentrating acids, sugars and gelatin, and cold butter whisked in creates an emulsion that gives gloss and body.
dishes.plating: Carve at the table or plate on a warm oval platter: stand the bone upright in the centre, set strip slices along one side and fillet slices along the other, each fanned in their original shape. Spoon a line of bordelaise across the base of each fan with marrow on top, scatter parsley and flaky salt, and serve the rest of the sauce in a warm jug.

pairing.drink: A Left Bank Bordeaux or a Napa Cabernet Sauvignon: firm tannin binds to the steak's fat and protein, and the cassis and cedar notes repeat the wine in the bordelaise.
pairing.brennans: Roasted Chateaubriand: Brennan's carves its own centre-cut fillet for two, so taste how this porterhouse's fillet side compares with that cut and its sauce.

variations: Use a bone-in rib-eye, cooked the same way to the same temperatures.
Make sauce marchand de vin, the New Orleans cousin, adding mushrooms and ham to the shallots.
Swap the bordelaise for béarnaise, built on the technique learned with steak béarnaise.
safety: Food safety guidance for whole cuts of beef is 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest; medium-rare at 130°F (54°C) is a common choice for whole steaks, as bacteria live on the surface, which the sear treats.
Keep the steak refrigerated at or below 40°F (4°C) while it dry-brines, on a rack over a tray on the bottom shelf, away from ready-to-eat foods.
Cast iron at searing heat smokes: turn on the extractor and keep a lid nearby in case the fat ignites. Never use water on a fat fire.

dishes.title: Wang Galbi (Butterflied Grilled Short Ribs)
dishes.summary: Korean royal galbi: thick English-cut short ribs butterflied into a long, thin sheet still attached to the bone, scored, marinated in pear, soy and sesame, and grilled over hot charcoal, then cut with scissors at the table. It is in the course because the knife work is pure butchery, unrolling a block of meat into one even ribbon, and the grilling rewards a cook who reads fire.
skills: butterflying short ribs into long ribbons on the bone
equipment: Sharp boning knife, 6 inch (15 cm), and a large chef's knife
Cutting board with a damp cloth under it
Charcoal grill (kettle or a tabletop Korean grill), lump charcoal and a chimney starter
Box grater or blender for the pear
Large non-reactive dish or zip bags for marinating

ingredients.item: English-cut beef short ribs, bone in, 3 to 4 inches (8 to 10 cm) long, at least 2 inches (5 cm) thick
ingredients.metric: 4 ribs, 8 to 10 cm long, 5 cm thick, about 1.4 kg

ingredients.item: Asian pear (or a ripe Bosc pear)
ingredients.note: grated; its enzymes tenderise the beef

ingredients.item: Lettuce leaves (red leaf or butter lettuce) and perilla leaves

mise: Soak the ribs in cold water for 30 minutes to draw out blood, changing the water once, then pat dry.
Grate the pear, onion, garlic and ginger and mix with the remaining marinade ingredients until the sugar dissolves.
Chill the ribs for 20 minutes before butterflying; firm meat cuts more cleanly.

timeline.do: Soak and butterfly the ribs; score; marinate 4 to 8 hours.
Light the charcoal; take the ribs out of the fridge.
Rice on; prepare the lettuce, ssamjang and kimchi.
Grill the ribs, 8 to 10 minutes.
Cut with scissors and serve with wraps.

steps.do: Stand a rib on its end with the bone to one side. With the boning knife, cut down alongside the bone, keeping 1/4 inch (6 mm) of meat on it, to within 1/2 inch (1 cm) of the bottom. Do not cut through: the meat must stay attached to the bone along that edge.
steps.look: A thick flap of meat hinged to the bone along one side.
steps.mistake: Cutting right through so the meat comes off the bone.
steps.fix: If it detaches, carry on butterflying the meat as a separate sheet; it will still taste wonderful.

steps.do: Lay the flap down and cut into the thick block parallel to the board, 1/4 inch (6 mm) above the board, stopping 1/2 inch (1 cm) from the far edge. Open it out like a book. Repeat, cutting into the new thick edge, turning and unrolling, until the meat is a single sheet 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and about 12 inches (30 cm) long.
steps.look: A long, even ribbon of meat still fixed to the bone, like a rolled carpet laid out.
steps.mistake: Uneven thickness, with thin holes and thick lumps that cook unevenly.
steps.fix: Go slowly with short strokes and keep the knife parallel to the board; a hole is fine, the sheet just has to hold together.

steps.do: Score the sheet on both sides in a crisscross pattern, 1/2 inch (1 cm) apart and about 1/8 inch (3 mm) deep, being careful not to cut through.
steps.look: A fine diamond pattern across the surface that opens the meat to the marinade.
steps.mistake: Scoring too deep, which makes the sheet fall apart.
steps.fix: Use the knife tip and light pressure; if a cut goes through, score more shallowly on that side.

steps.do: Lay the ribs in the dish, pour over the marinade and turn them so every surface is coated, folding each sheet back onto its bone. Cover and refrigerate for 4 to 8 hours, turning once.
steps.look: Ribs glossy and dark, the marinade clinging to every cut.
steps.mistake: Marinating more than 24 hours, which turns the surface mushy because of the pear enzymes.
steps.fix: Keep to 4 to 8 hours; if they must wait, lift them out of the marinade and keep them covered in the fridge.

steps.do: Light a full chimney of lump charcoal and when it is glowing and covered in white ash, about 20 minutes, spread it in a single even layer. The grill is ready when you can hold your hand 3 inches (8 cm) above the grate for only 2 to 3 seconds.
steps.look: Glowing coals with a light ash coating and very little smoke.
steps.mistake: Grilling over flames that are still licking up, which chars the sugary marinade black.
steps.fix: Wait until the flames have died back; keep a cooler zone with fewer coals for moving ribs to.

steps.do: Lift each rib out, let excess marinade drip off, and lay the sheet flat on the grate with the bone at one end. Grill 2 to 3 minutes a side until caramelised with charred edges, turning with tongs.
steps.look: A strong sizzle, sweet smoke, and a glossy, deep brown surface with crisp black edges.
steps.mistake: Leaving the ribs over the hottest part, so the sugars burn before the meat cooks.
steps.fix: Move them to the cooler zone if flare-ups start; brush with a little marinade only in the first minute.

steps.do: Grill the bone part for 2 minutes more, then check the thickest part of the meat near the bone: it should reach 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: Bone ends sizzling and browned, the meat firm but juicy.
steps.mistake: Undercooking the meat near the bone, which stays chewy.
steps.fix: Fold the sheet back onto the bone and grill 1 to 2 minutes more.

steps.do: At the table or on the board, cut the sheet off the bone with scissors and snip it into bite-sized pieces. Serve with lettuce and perilla leaves, rice, ssamjang and kimchi; eat by wrapping a piece of meat with a little rice and ssamjang in a leaf.
steps.look: Caramelised, glossy pieces; the bones still meaty enough to gnaw.
steps.mistake: Cutting the meat into large pieces that are hard to wrap.
steps.fix: Snip into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) squares.

dishes.science: Short rib is a hard-working muscle with lots of connective tissue. Grilled whole and fast it would be tough, but butterflying it to 1/4 inch (6 mm) turns it into thin meat that cooks in minutes, and scoring cuts the long collagen fibres so they cannot contract into chewiness. Asian pear contains an enzyme (a protease) that breaks down muscle proteins at the surface, tenderising the meat, which is why the marinade time is limited: too long and the surface turns mushy. Soy sauce salt seasons and dissolves proteins so the meat holds juice, while the sugars brown fast over charcoal through caramelisation and Maillard reactions. Charcoal's radiant heat is intense and dry, which builds char faster than a gas grill.
dishes.plating: Serve on a hot plate or a wooden board with the bones arranged at one side and the snipped meat heaped beside them, glistening and scattered with sesame seeds and spring onions. Surround it with small dishes: lettuce and perilla leaves stacked in a basket, a bowl of ssamjang, kimchi and steamed rice. Everyone builds their own wraps.

pairing.drink: A juicy, low-tannin red such as a Zinfandel or a cru Beaujolais: ripe fruit meets the sweet soy marinade, and the smoky char suits Zinfandel's spice.
pairing.brennans: Ridge Vineyards ‘Lytton Springs’ Dry Creek Valley 2021 (375 ml): the Zinfandel blend from the Brennan's list has the ripe fruit and spice to stand up to the char and sweet soy.

variations: LA galbi: use flanken-cut ribs, marinated the same way and grilled 2 minutes a side.
Make it in a very hot cast-iron griddle pan if you have no charcoal grill.
Use bone-in pork belly or pork shoulder butterflied the same way, cooked to 145°F (63°C).
safety: Cook whole cuts of beef to at least 145°F (63°C) with a rest; the thin sheets reach this quickly.
Marinate in the fridge, never on the counter, and discard used marinade or boil it for 1 minute before using it as a sauce.
Butterflying needs a stable board: put a damp cloth beneath it and keep your guiding hand flat on top of the meat, fingers clear of the blade.
Charcoal produces carbon monoxide: grill outdoors only, and let coals cool fully before disposing.
