dishes.title: Palm Nut Soup with Fufu
dishes.summary: Ghanaian palm nut soup: goat or chicken simmered with smoked fish in a broth of palm nut cream, tomato, onion and scotch bonnet, skimmed of its red oil and served with stretchy, pounded fufu. It is in the course because it trains skimming a rich soup to clarity, and pounding starch to an elastic dough by hand.
skills: extracting palm fruit cream by hand
a light soup with smoked fish and goat
equipment: Large pot for boiling cassava and plantain
Large mortar and pestle (asanka or wooden mortar) or a food processor
Bowl of cold water for wetting hands

ingredients.item: Goat meat on the bone, in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces (or bone-in chicken thighs)
Palm nut cream (tinned palm nut concentrate)
Smoked mackerel or smoked herring, flaked, bones removed
Garden eggs (African aubergines), or small aubergines
Cassava (yuca), peeled and cut into chunks, woody core removed

mise: Blend half the onion with the ginger and garlic into a paste.
Peel the cassava and plantains; cut into 2 inch (5 cm) chunks and keep them in cold water.

timeline.do: Steam the goat with onion paste and salt for 15 minutes.
Boil the tomatoes and onion, blend, add with palm cream and water.
Simmer 1 1/2 hours, skimming the oil.
Boil the cassava and plantain.
Pound the fufu.
Add smoked fish and garden eggs.
Shape fufu; ladle soup round it.

steps.do: Put the goat in the large pot with the onion paste, sliced onion and 1 tsp (5 g) salt. Cover and steam in its own juices over medium heat for 15 minutes, stirring, until the meat releases liquid and smells fragrant.
steps.look: The meat turning grey and releasing juices, and a strong aroma of onion and ginger.
steps.mistake: Adding water too early, so the meat does not absorb the seasoning.
steps.fix: Let it cook in its own juices first.

steps.do: Add the whole tomatoes, scotch bonnet and 2 cups (480 ml) water, cover and simmer for 10 minutes. Lift out the tomatoes and chilli, blend them smooth, and sieve back into the pot.
steps.look: A smooth red purée with no seeds or skins.
steps.mistake: Blending the scotch bonnet with the seeds if you want mild heat.
steps.fix: Leave the chilli whole and remove it later for less heat.

steps.do: Put the palm nut cream into a bowl with 2 cups (480 ml) hot water and work it with your hand for 2 minutes, squeezing the fibres as you would fresh pounded palm fruit. Pour it through the sieve into the pot, pressing the fibres with your hand until only dry strands remain. Add the remaining water and bring to a simmer.
steps.look: A deep orange-red broth and a small handful of pale, dry fibres left in the sieve.
steps.mistake: Not sieving the palm cream, so fibres stay in the soup.
steps.fix: Sieve it well, squeezing the fibres by hand; they hold a surprising amount of cream.

steps.do: Simmer uncovered for 1 1/2 hours, stirring occasionally. As red oil rises to the surface, skim it off with a ladle into a bowl, leaving a thin film.
steps.look: A layer of bright red oil gathering on the surface, and a broth that thickens and turns glossy.
steps.mistake: Leaving all the oil on, so the soup is greasy and heavy.
steps.fix: Skim regularly; keep some oil for flavour.

steps.do: Meanwhile, boil the cassava and plantain in salted water for 20 to 25 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Drain.
steps.look: Soft, tender chunks that crush under a fork.
steps.mistake: Undercooking them, so the fufu is lumpy.
steps.fix: Boil 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Pound the cassava and plantain while hot in the mortar, a few pieces at a time, folding with a wet hand between strokes, for 10 to 15 minutes until smooth, stretchy and elastic. Or process in a food processor for 3 minutes, then knead with wet hands.
steps.look: A smooth, stretchy, slightly glossy dough that pulls in strands.
steps.mistake: Pounding when it has cooled, which makes it lumpy.
steps.fix: Pound while hot; return to a warm pan with a splash of water if it stiffens.

steps.do: Add the smoked fish and garden eggs to the soup and simmer 10 minutes. Check that the meat is tender and season with salt.
steps.look: Tender goat, flakes of smoked fish, and a rich, smoky, peppery broth.
steps.mistake: Adding the fish too early, so it breaks up and disappears.
steps.fix: Add it only in the last 10 minutes.

steps.do: Wet your hands and shape the fufu into smooth balls the size of a large orange. Set each in a deep bowl and ladle the soup round it, with meat and fish.
steps.look: Smooth, white balls surrounded by a glossy orange soup.
steps.mistake: Shaping with dry hands, so it sticks.
steps.fix: Keep a bowl of cold water to wet your hands.

dishes.science: Palm nut cream is an emulsion of red palm oil, water and plant fibre. As the soup simmers, the emulsion breaks and the oil rises because it is less dense than water; skimming it controls richness while leaving some for flavour and colour from carotenoids. The goat's collagen turns to gelatin during the long simmer, giving body. Fufu is stretchy because cooked cassava and plantain starch gelatinise when boiled, and pounding while hot aligns and bonds the swollen starch molecules into an elastic network, much like kneading. If it cools, the starch begins to set and the dough turns lumpy. Smoked fish adds savoury, smoky depth from compounds made during smoking.
dishes.plating: Set a smooth ball of fufu in the centre of a deep, wide bowl. Ladle the soup round it so the fufu stands like an island, with pieces of goat, smoked fish and a garden egg arranged in the broth. Serve with a bowl of water for rinsing fingers, as fufu is eaten by hand.

pairing.drink: A cold, crisp lager or a fruity, chilled Beaujolais: the beer refreshes against the scotch bonnet, and the light red handles the smoky, rich broth.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): a chilled, fruity Beaujolais from the Brennan's list with freshness to cut the rich palm soup.

variations: Use beef, chicken or snails instead of goat.
Serve with omo tuo (rice balls) or banku instead of fufu.
Make abenkwan from fresh palm fruit, boiled and pounded.
safety: Cook goat or chicken to at least 165°F (74°C); after the long simmer it will be far above this.
Cassava must be peeled, cored and boiled thoroughly; never eat it raw.
Wear gloves for scotch bonnets; wash hands thoroughly afterwards.
Pounding hot starch: keep fingers clear of the pestle and wet your hands only with cold water.

dishes.title: Hamam Mahshi (Stuffed Squab)
dishes.summary: Egyptian stuffed squab: whole pigeons filled with freekeh cooked with onions and warm spices, trussed, poached gently in spiced stock and roasted until crisp. It is in the course because it brings together preparing small birds, stuffing them safely and trussing them neatly, with a two-stage cook that keeps the breast moist.
skills: poaching then roasting to a crisp skin
equipment: Sharp boning knife and kitchen scissors
mise: Pat the squabs dry; pull out any remaining feathers with tweezers.
Remove the wishbone so the breast carves cleanly: lift the neck skin, scrape along the wishbone with the knife tip and twist it out.

timeline.do: Salt the squabs; remove wishbones; chill 1 hour.
Cook the freekeh stuffing halfway; cool slightly.
Stuff and truss.
Poach at 185°F (85°C) for 35 minutes.
Roast at 425°F (220°C) for 8 to 10 minutes.
Rest; serve with lemon.

steps.do: Season the squabs inside and out with 1 1/2 tsp (7 g) salt and refrigerate for an hour.
steps.look: Lightly seasoned, dry skin.
steps.mistake: Leaving them wet, which stops the skin crisping.
steps.fix: Pat dry again before cooking.

steps.do: Fry the chopped onion in 4 tbsp (60 g) samna over medium heat for 8 minutes until golden. Add the freekeh, spices and remaining salt and toast for 2 minutes until it smells smoky.
steps.look: Golden onions and a toasty, green wheat smell.
steps.mistake: Burning the freekeh.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium and stir.

steps.do: Add 1/2 cup (125 ml) of the stock and cook gently for 12 minutes until absorbed. The freekeh should be half cooked, still firm at the centre. Spread it out to cool slightly.
steps.look: Grains plump but still chewy.
steps.mistake: Cooking it soft, so it turns mushy inside the birds.
steps.fix: Stop while it still has bite; it finishes in the bird.

steps.do: Fill each squab two-thirds full with the warm stuffing, as the freekeh will swell. Close the vent with a cocktail stick.
steps.look: Birds filled but not packed tight.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the stuffing bursts out.
steps.fix: Remove some stuffing; cook extra in a dish alongside.

steps.do: Truss: tie the legs together with string, then loop the string round the body and tie it to hold the wings close.
steps.look: Compact birds with legs and wings tucked in.
steps.mistake: Loose trussing, so the birds lose their shape.
steps.fix: Retie more tightly.

steps.do: Put the remaining stock in the narrow pot with the halved onion, cardamom and bay. Bring to 185°F (85°C), lower in the squabs, cover and poach for 35 minutes, keeping the temperature steady, until the thigh and the centre of the stuffing read 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: A trembling, steaming liquid with no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Boiling, which toughens the birds.
steps.fix: Check the temperature often and lower the heat if it rises.

steps.do: Lift the squabs out, pat dry, brush with the remaining samna and roast on the rack at 425°F (220°C) for 8 to 10 minutes until the skin blisters and browns.
steps.look: Crisp, golden-brown skin.
steps.mistake: Roasting too long, so the breast dries.
steps.fix: Take them out as soon as they are browned.

steps.do: Rest for 5 minutes, snip off the string, and serve one bird per person with lemon wedges and the extra stuffing. Strain the broth and serve it in cups alongside.
steps.look: Glossy birds with crisp skin and a cup of fragrant broth.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to remove the string and cocktail stick.
steps.fix: Snip and pull them out before serving.

dishes.science: A stuffed bird has two cooking problems: the stuffing in the centre heats last, and the breast meat overcooks quickly. Putting half-cooked, warm freekeh in the cavity starts the centre warm, and filling it only two-thirds full leaves room for the grain to swell. Poaching at 185°F (85°C) heats the bird gently and evenly, so the breast stays moist while the stuffing reaches a safe temperature; at a boil, the muscle fibres contract and squeeze out moisture. Roasting at the end dries the skin and browns it through Maillard reactions. Freekeh is wheat harvested green and smoked, which gives its toasty flavour.
dishes.plating: Set each bird on a warm plate on a spoon of the extra freekeh, breast up, with a lemon wedge beside it. Serve a small cup of the strained broth on the side, as in Cairo, and a simple salad of tomato, cucumber and parsley.

pairing.drink: A Lebanese red such as Château Musar, or a red Burgundy: earthy, spiced reds suit gamey squab and the warm spices in the freekeh.
pairing.brennans: Château Musar Bekaa Valley 2003: an aged Lebanese red on the Brennan's list whose earthy spice is made for squab and freekeh.

variations: Use poussins, poaching for 45 minutes.
Stuff with spiced rice instead of freekeh.
Grill the poached birds over charcoal instead of roasting.
safety: Both the bird and the centre of the stuffing must reach 165°F (74°C).
Stuff the birds just before cooking, never in advance, and keep raw birds refrigerated.
Wash hands and boards after handling raw poultry.

dishes.title: Agnolotti del Plin with Sugo d'Arrosto
dishes.summary: Piedmont's tiny pinched pasta: a golden egg-yolk dough rolled almost transparent, filled with roast veal and pork and greens, pinched between your fingers into little pillows and served in the roasting juices, the sugo d'arrosto. It is in the course because it unites a fine fresh pasta, a filling built from a roast and a sauce made from that roast's own pan.
equipment: Pasta machine (hand-cranked or stand mixer attachment)
Roasting tin and a heavy casserole
Piping bag with a plain 1/2 inch (1 cm) tip, or a zip bag
Fluted pasta wheel (or a sharp knife)
Two floured trays and clean tea towels

ingredients.item: Veal shoulder, in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces
Pork shoulder, in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces
Spinach or escarole, cooked, squeezed dry and chopped

mise: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C).
Cook the spinach, cool and squeeze out every drop of water in a cloth.
Dust two trays with semolina.

timeline.do: Roast the veal and pork with wine and herbs (1 1/2 to 2 hours).
Make the pasta dough; rest it 30 minutes.
Grind the meats for filling; strain and reduce the roasting juices.
Roll, fill and pinch the agnolotti (40 to 50 minutes).
Boil the pasta 2 to 3 minutes; warm the sugo.
Toss in the sugo and serve with Parmigiano.

steps.do: Season the veal and pork with 1 tsp (5 g) salt. Brown them in the oil and 2 tbsp (30 g) butter in the casserole over medium-high heat for 10 minutes, then add the garlic, rosemary and sage. Pour in the wine, let it bubble for 2 minutes, add 1 cup (240 ml) stock, cover and roast at 325°F (160°C) for 1 1/2 to 2 hours until very tender.
steps.look: Deep brown meat, tender enough to break with a spoon, in a dark, fragrant juice.
steps.mistake: Not browning the meat well, so the sugo is pale and weak.
steps.fix: Brown in batches; the colour in the pan is the flavour of the sauce.

steps.do: Make the dough: mound the flour on a board, make a well, add the yolks, whole egg and oil, and beat with a fork, drawing in flour gradually. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and silky. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A firm, bright yellow dough that springs back slowly when pressed.
steps.mistake: A dough too dry to come together, or sticky.
steps.fix: Add water by the teaspoon if dry; a dusting of flour if sticky.

steps.do: Lift out the meat. Strain the juices into a saucepan, skim the fat, add the remaining stock and reduce over medium heat to about 3/4 cup (180 ml), until it coats a spoon. Keep this sugo.
steps.look: A dark, glossy juice with concentrated flavour.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so it turns salty and sticky.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water or stock.

steps.do: Grind the meats with the garlic and spinach, then beat in the Parmigiano, egg, nutmeg, pepper and 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the sugo. Season and put into the piping bag.
steps.look: A smooth, moist filling that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: A filling that is too dry or crumbly.
steps.fix: Add a little more sugo.

steps.do: Roll a quarter of the dough through the machine, starting at the widest setting and working down to the second thinnest, about 1/32 inch (1 mm), until you can see your hand through it. Keep the rest covered.
steps.look: A long, smooth, nearly translucent sheet about 4 inches (10 cm) wide.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thick, so the agnolotti are doughy.
steps.fix: Go one more setting thinner.

steps.do: Pipe the filling in small dots the size of a hazelnut, 1/2 inch (1 cm) from the long edge of the sheet and 1/2 inch (1 cm) apart.
steps.look: A neat line of evenly spaced dots.
steps.mistake: Dots too large, so the pasta cannot close.
steps.fix: Keep them small; you will make many.

steps.do: Fold the near edge of the dough over the filling and press it down along the far side of the dots. Pinch the dough between each dot firmly with thumb and forefinger to seal and form the little pockets (the plin).
steps.look: A row of tiny, plump pillows joined by pinched seams.
steps.mistake: Leaving air pockets, which burst in the water.
steps.fix: Press out the air with your fingertips as you pinch.

steps.do: Cut along the length with the fluted wheel to trim the edge, then cut between each pocket with a quick forward roll so each one folds over on itself. Lay them on the semolina-dusted tray.
steps.look: Little pinched pillows, each with a fluted edge.
steps.mistake: Letting them touch, so they stick together.
steps.fix: Space them out; mist the dough with water if it dries before sealing.

steps.do: Bring a large pot of water to the boil with 1 tbsp (15 g) salt. Warm the sugo in a wide pan with the remaining butter. Cook the agnolotti for 2 to 3 minutes until they float and the edges are tender.
steps.look: Pasta rising to the surface, the dough just tender at the folded edge.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, so the delicate dough tears.
steps.fix: Taste one at 2 minutes.

steps.do: Lift the agnolotti with a slotted spoon into the sugo and toss gently with a splash of pasta water until glossy. Serve at once with grated Parmigiano.
steps.look: Glossy pasta coated in a dark, buttery sauce.
steps.mistake: Draining in a colander, which breaks them.
steps.fix: Use a slotted spoon or spider.

dishes.science: An egg-yolk dough is rich and tender because yolk fat coats the flour proteins, limiting gluten and giving a silky bite, while the yolk proteins set on cooking and hold the thin sheet together. Rolling thin means the pasta cooks in the same time as the filling heats through. The pinch seals the dough by pressing the moist surfaces together so they bond. Sugo d'arrosto is flavour developed by the Maillard reaction in browned meat, dissolved into wine and stock and concentrated by reduction; gelatin from the shoulder gives the sauce body. Butter whisked in at the end emulsifies with the juices and gives gloss.
dishes.plating: Use warm, shallow bowls. Spoon in twelve to fifteen agnolotti in a loose mound, spoon over the glossy sugo so it pools around them, and finish with a fine snowfall of Parmigiano and a crisp sage leaf. In Piedmont they are also served plain in a napkin to show the pasta.

pairing.drink: A Barbera d'Asti or a young Nebbiolo: Barbera's bright acidity and low tannin cut the butter and roast juices, the classic Piedmont match.
pairing.brennans: La Miraja ‘Le Masche’ Barbera d’Asti 2023: a Piedmont Barbera on the Brennan's list, exactly the local wine for agnolotti.

variations: Fill with leftover braised beef (brasato) instead of roast veal and pork.
Serve with butter and sage, or in a rich clear broth.
Use a filling of roasted squash, amaretti and Parmigiano for a vegetarian version.
safety: The filling uses raw egg, so it must be cooked through; the agnolotti cook to well above 160°F (71°C) in boiling water.
Roast meats should reach at least 145°F (63°C); after 2 hours they are well above that.
Keep filled pasta covered and cool, and cook within 2 hours or freeze it on the tray.

dishes.title: Mole Negro Oaxaqueño
dishes.summary: Oaxaca's black mole: four chillies toasted almost black, their seeds burnt to charcoal, nuts, seeds, fruit and bread fried, tomatoes charred, all blended, sieved and fried in lard until thick and glossy, then finished with chocolate and simmered with chicken. It is in the course because it is the deepest sauce in the Mexican kitchen, built in layers that each need judgement.
equipment: Comal or heavy dry frying pan
Large heavy pot or cazuela for frying the mole
Large frying pan for frying nuts and fruit
Large pot for poaching the chicken

ingredients.item: Chicken pieces, bone in (or turkey legs)
Chilhuacle negro chillies (or extra mulato), stemmed and seeded, seeds kept
Pasilla chillies, stemmed and seeded, seeds kept
Mulato chillies, stemmed and seeded, seeds kept
Stale bread (pan de yema or brioche), torn

mise: Open windows and turn on the extractor; burning chilli seeds makes strong, choking smoke.
Stem and seed the chillies, keeping the seeds in a small bowl.
Have all fried ingredients weighed in separate bowls beside the stove.

timeline.do: Poach the chicken in stock 40 minutes; keep the stock.
Toast chillies; burn the seeds; soak 30 minutes.
Fry nuts, seeds, fruit, bread; char tomatoes, onion, garlic.
Blend and sieve the two pastes.
Fry the pastes in lard 25 to 30 minutes.
Thin with stock; add chocolate; simmer 30 minutes; add chicken.
Serve with sesame, rice and tortillas.

steps.do: Poach the chicken in the hot stock at a gentle simmer for 35 to 40 minutes until the thighs reach 175°F (79°C). Lift out and keep the stock.
steps.look: Tender chicken and a flavourful stock.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the chicken.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer.

steps.do: Toast the chillies on the dry comal over medium heat, pressing them flat with a spatula, about 30 seconds a side, until they blister and turn almost black but not burnt to ash.
steps.look: Blistered, darkened chillies with a smoky, fruity smell.
steps.mistake: Burning them to ash, which turns the mole acrid.
steps.fix: Take them off as soon as they darken; throw away any that turn grey.

steps.do: Toast the chilli seeds in the dry pan, stirring, until completely black, like charcoal, about 5 minutes. Put the seeds and chillies in hot water and soak for 30 minutes. Drain and discard the soaking water.
steps.look: Black seeds, softened chillies.
steps.mistake: Using the bitter soaking water.
steps.fix: Always discard it; use fresh stock to blend.

steps.do: Heat the lard in the frying pan over medium heat and fry, separately, the almonds, peanuts, sesame, raisins, plantain, bread and tortilla, each until golden, lifting each out to a bowl. Keep the lard.
steps.look: Golden nuts, puffed raisins, caramelised plantain and crisp bread.
steps.mistake: Frying everything at once, which burns some and leaves others raw.
steps.fix: Fry each separately; sesame takes only 30 seconds.

steps.do: Char the tomatoes, tomatillos, onion and garlic on the comal until blackened in patches and soft, about 10 minutes. Peel the garlic.
steps.look: Blistered, slumping vegetables with black patches.
steps.mistake: Leaving them pale, which gives a flat mole.
steps.fix: Keep charring; the black spots add depth.

steps.do: Blend the chillies and seeds with 1 cup (240 ml) stock until smooth, then push through the sieve. Blend the fried ingredients, charred vegetables, spices and avocado leaves with 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) stock until smooth, then sieve.
steps.look: Two smooth, thick pastes, one black-red, one brown.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, so the mole is gritty.
steps.fix: Sieve both and press firmly.

steps.do: Heat 3 tbsp (40 g) of the reserved lard in the large pot until shimmering. Pour in the chilli paste carefully, as it spits. Stir for 10 minutes, then add the second paste and continue frying, stirring, for 15 to 20 minutes until thick and dark, the fat showing at the edges.
steps.look: A thick, shiny, near-black paste that holds a channel when you drag a spoon through it.
steps.mistake: Not frying long enough, so the mole tastes raw and harsh.
steps.fix: Keep going until it darkens and smells rich and roasted.

steps.do: Stir in hot stock gradually until the mole is the thickness of pouring cream. Add the chocolate, piloncillo and salt and simmer gently for 30 minutes, stirring often.
steps.look: A glossy, velvety, dark sauce with a thin layer of fat on top.
steps.mistake: Burning the base because it is not stirred.
steps.fix: Stir often and scrape the bottom; lower the heat.

steps.do: Add the chicken to the mole and simmer for 10 minutes to heat through. Taste and season.
steps.look: Chicken coated in a thick, glossy, deeply flavoured mole.
steps.mistake: Boiling the chicken in the mole until it falls apart.
steps.fix: Keep it at a bare simmer.

steps.do: Serve the chicken with plenty of mole, sprinkled with toasted sesame seeds, with rice and warm tortillas.
steps.look: A glossy black sauce scattered with pale sesame.
steps.mistake: Serving too little sauce.
steps.fix: Mole is the dish; be generous.

dishes.science: The colour of mole negro comes from charring chillies and burning their seeds to carbon. Carbon is bitter, so it is balanced by the sugars in raisins, plantain, chocolate and piloncillo, and the fats in nuts and lard. Frying the blended paste in lard is the step that changes everything: the high heat drives off water, caramelises sugars, creates Maillard flavours and blends the fat-soluble chilli compounds into the sauce. The paste is cooked until the fat separates, a sign that the water has gone. Nuts, seeds and bread add starch and protein that thicken the sauce once stock is added, and sieving removes skins and seed fragments.
dishes.plating: Serve on a wide, warm plate: a piece of chicken in the centre, the mole spooned over until it covers most of the plate in a glossy black pool, and a scattering of toasted sesame seeds. Serve rice and warm tortillas on the side.

pairing.drink: A ripe Zinfandel or a Grenache-based red: ripe dark fruit and spice match the chillies and chocolate without clashing.
pairing.brennans: Ridge Vineyards ‘Essence’ Zinfandel Sonoma 2014 (375 ml): a rich Zinfandel from the Brennan's list with the dark fruit and spice to meet mole negro.

variations: Mole coloradito: use ancho and guajillo chillies and less charring.
Enmoladas: fold tortillas round shredded chicken and cover with mole.
Use pork ribs instead of chicken.
safety: Cook chicken to 165°F (74°C); thighs are better at 175°F (79°C).
Frying the paste spits violently: wear long sleeves, use a long spoon and a pot with high sides.
Burning chilli seeds makes choking smoke; ventilate well and keep children and pets away.

dishes.title: Peking Duck with Mandarin Pancakes
dishes.summary: Peking duck at home: a whole duck whose skin is loosened, scalded, glazed with maltose and dried for two days, then roasted until the skin is crisp and lacquered, carved into slices of skin and meat and wrapped in thin mandarin pancakes with sweet bean sauce, cucumber and spring onion. It is in the course because it is a lesson in drying, glazing and carving that only works with planning.
equipment: Kettle and a large pot for scalding
Bicycle pump with a needle or ball adapter, cleaned, or a straw (optional)
S-hook or a sturdy rack and roasting tray
Rolling pin, heavy frying pan and a clean tea towel

ingredients.item: Whole duck, with head and neck skin if possible
Spring onions, white parts in fine strips

mise: Clear a fridge shelf and allow two days for drying.
Trim excess fat from the neck and cavity opening.
Make the glaze by dissolving the maltose in the hot water with the vinegar and wine.

timeline.do: Separate skin from meat; scald; glaze; dry in the fridge uncovered.
Glaze again; continue drying.
Make pancake dough; rest 30 minutes.
Roast the duck (about 1 1/2 hours).
Roll and cook the pancakes; prepare sauce, cucumber and onions.
Rest the duck; carve the skin, then the meat.
Serve with warm pancakes and garnishes.

steps.do: Loosen the skin from the meat: slide your fingers under the neck skin and work gently over the breast and down to the legs, without tearing. If using a pump, insert the needle under the neck skin, hold the skin tight round it and inflate until the skin balloons away from the meat.
steps.look: Skin loose over the whole body, like a jacket.
steps.mistake: Tearing the skin, which lets fat run out and leaves gaps in the crispy skin.
steps.fix: Go slowly; small tears are fine, but avoid large ones.

steps.do: Season the cavity with the salt and five spice and fill with spring onion and ginger. Close the cavity with a skewer.
steps.look: A sealed, seasoned bird.
steps.mistake: Getting salt on the skin, which draws moisture.
steps.fix: Wipe the skin clean.

steps.do: Hold the duck over the sink and pour boiling water from the kettle slowly over every part of the skin, about 8 cups (2 litres) in total.
steps.look: The skin tightening, shrinking and turning paler.
steps.mistake: Pouring too quickly, so some areas are missed.
steps.fix: Go slowly and turn the duck as you pour.

steps.do: Dry the duck with paper, then brush the warm glaze evenly all over the skin. Hang it on the hook or set it on the rack breast up, and refrigerate uncovered with a fan blowing gently at it if possible, for 24 to 48 hours. Brush with glaze again after 24 hours.
steps.look: Skin taut, dry, and feeling like parchment with a slight sheen.
steps.mistake: Covering the duck, which keeps the skin moist.
steps.fix: Leave it uncovered; dry longer if it still feels damp.

steps.do: Make the pancake dough: stir the boiling water into the flour with chopsticks, then knead for 5 minutes into a smooth dough. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough.
steps.mistake: A sticky dough.
steps.fix: Knead in a little more flour.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C). Set the duck breast up on the rack over a tray with 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water in it. Roast for 1 hour, then raise the oven to 400°F (200°C) and roast 20 to 30 minutes more, turning the tray, until the skin is deep mahogany and crisp, and the thighs reach 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Glossy, deep brown, crisp skin and clear juices.
steps.mistake: Glaze burning black in spots.
steps.fix: Cover dark patches with foil; lower the oven temperature.

steps.do: While the duck roasts, roll the dough into a log and cut into 16 pieces. Flatten two pieces, brush one with sesame oil and press the other on top. Roll the pair into a thin round 6 inches (15 cm) across. Repeat.
steps.look: Sixteen thin rounds of dough in pairs.
steps.mistake: Rolling them unevenly, so they tear.
steps.fix: Roll from the centre outwards, turning the dough.

steps.do: Cook each pair in the dry frying pan over medium heat for 45 seconds to 1 minute a side until they puff and show faint brown spots. Peel the pair apart while hot and stack under a tea towel.
steps.look: Thin, soft pancakes that separate cleanly.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, which makes them stiff.
steps.fix: Take them off as soon as spots appear; steam briefly if they become stiff.

steps.do: Simmer the sweet bean sauce with the sugar, 1 tbsp (15 ml) sesame oil and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water for 2 minutes until glossy. Cut the cucumber and spring onion.
steps.look: A glossy, dark, sweet sauce.
steps.mistake: Burning the sauce.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low.

steps.do: Rest the duck for 10 minutes. Carve the skin first: slice the crisp skin off the breast in pieces 2 inches (5 cm) square. Then slice the meat thinly and carve the legs.
steps.look: Crisp shards of skin and juicy slices of meat.
steps.mistake: Carving the skin and meat together, so the skin softens.
steps.fix: Carve skin first, serve it at once.

steps.do: To eat, spread a pancake with a little sauce, add a slice of skin and meat, cucumber and spring onion, and roll it up.
steps.look: A neat roll with crisp skin and fresh garnish.
steps.mistake: Too much filling, so it falls apart.
steps.fix: Keep each wrap small.

dishes.science: The crisp skin depends on drying and on separating the skin from the meat. Loosening the skin lets fat render out from underneath and lets hot air reach both sides. Scalding tightens the skin's proteins and makes the surface smooth so the glaze sticks. Maltose is a sugar that browns more slowly and evenly than honey, giving a lacquered, mahogany colour through caramelisation and Maillard reactions. Days of drying in cold air evaporate water from the skin, so when it hits the oven, the skin crisps instead of steaming. The tray of water under the duck catches dripping fat and stops it smoking.
dishes.plating: Arrange the skin pieces in overlapping rows on a warm platter, with the meat slices on another plate. Serve the pancakes folded in a steamer basket, with small dishes of sauce, cucumber batons and spring onion strips. Show guests how to build the first wrap.

pairing.drink: A Pinot Noir or a Grand Cru Champagne: Pinot's acidity and red fruit cut the rich skin and suit the sweet sauce; bubbles clean the palate.
pairing.brennans: Roasted Rohan Duck Breast: compare Brennan's French approach to duck with this Beijing roast, both depending on rendered fat and crisp skin.

variations: Use duck legs, glazed and roasted, if a whole duck is too large.
Serve the carcass as a broth with cabbage and tofu, as in Beijing restaurants.
Use bought pancakes if time is short, steaming them for 3 minutes.
safety: Duck legs and thighs must reach at least 165°F (74°C); many prefer 175°F (79°C) for tender legs.
Dry the duck on the bottom shelf of the fridge away from ready-to-eat food, below 40°F (4°C).
If using a pump, clean it thoroughly first; use a dedicated adapter.
Boiling water for scalding: work over the sink and keep a firm grip on the duck.

dishes.title: Chicken Ballotine with Mushroom Mousseline
dishes.summary: A whole chicken boned out through the back with its skin intact, filled with a mushroom mousseline of puréed chicken, cream and duxelles, rolled, wrapped and poached gently in a water bath, then browned and sliced. It is in the course because boning a whole bird without tearing the skin is one of the trade's defining knife skills, and a mousseline is the base of a classical cold kitchen.
skills: boning a whole chicken through the back
equipment: Frying pan for the duxelles and browning
Large pot or roasting tin for the water bath
Instant-read thermometer, ideally a leave-in probe

ingredients.item: Chicken breast meat for the mousseline, from the bird, cold

mise: Put the food processor bowl and blade in the freezer for 20 minutes.
Cook the duxelles: soften the shallots in 2 tbsp (30 g) butter, add the mushrooms and thyme and cook until all the liquid evaporates and the mixture is dry, about 12 minutes; cool completely.
Fill a large pot with water and heat it to 170°F (77°C).

timeline.do: Bone the chicken (30 to 45 minutes); chill the meat.
Make duxelles; chill. Make the mousseline.
Fill, roll and wrap tightly.
Poach in the water bath until 165°F (74°C), about 60 minutes.
Unwrap, dry and brown in butter; rest.
Make the pan sauce.
Slice and serve.

steps.do: Place the chicken breast down. Cut down the length of the backbone through the skin, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) deep. Working one side at a time, scrape the knife against the carcass, pulling the meat away with your fingers, until you reach the leg and wing joints.
steps.look: The meat and skin pulling away from the carcass in one piece.
steps.mistake: Cutting through the skin, especially along the breastbone where it is thinnest.
steps.fix: Keep the blade against the bone; small holes can be patched with mousseline.

steps.do: Cut through the hip and wing joints where they meet the carcass, about 2 inches (5 cm) from the backbone. Continue scraping over the breastbone until the carcass lifts away, being careful not to cut the skin over the top of the breastbone.
steps.look: A flat sheet of meat and skin with the carcass removed.
steps.mistake: Tearing the skin along the keel of the breastbone.
steps.fix: Scrape slowly with the blade, and lift the carcass gently.

steps.do: Remove the thigh bones by scraping the meat down from the bone and cutting round the joint. Remove the drumstick bone the same way, cutting the tendons at the end. Cut off the wing tips and middle sections at the 2 joints, leaving the first wing bone or removing it.
steps.look: Boneless legs turned inside out, with skin intact.
steps.mistake: Leaving pieces of cartilage, which are hard to eat.
steps.fix: Feel for hard spots and cut them out.

steps.do: Lay the boned chicken skin side down. Cut 8 oz (225 g) of breast meat from the thickest parts for the mousseline, so the meat layer is even, about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Season the meat with 1 tsp (5 g) salt and chill.
steps.look: An even rectangle of meat on the skin, with no thick lumps.
steps.mistake: Uneven thickness, so it cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Move pieces of meat to fill gaps.

steps.do: Make the mousseline: cut the reserved breast into cubes and pulse in the cold food processor with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt for 30 seconds into a paste. Add the egg white and pulse. With the motor running, pour in the cold cream in a thin stream. Stop as soon as it is smooth.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, thick paste that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: A warm mixture that splits and looks greasy.
steps.fix: Keep everything cold; set the bowl over ice and beat by hand to recover.

steps.do: Push the mousseline through the fine sieve with a scraper, then fold in the cooled duxelles, tarragon and white pepper. Poach 1 tsp (5 g) in simmering water for 1 minute to test the seasoning.
steps.look: A smooth, light, mushroom-studded mousseline; the test dumpling springy and well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Tasting it raw.
steps.fix: Always cook the test; adjust salt.

steps.do: Spread the mousseline down the centre of the boned chicken, leaving 1 inch (2.5 cm) of meat on each side. Fold the sides over to form a roll, then tie at intervals of 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) with string.
steps.look: A neat cylinder about 3 inches (8 cm) wide.
steps.mistake: Overfilling so the roll will not close.
steps.fix: Remove some mousseline and poach it separately.

steps.do: Roll the ballotine tightly in several layers of cling film, twisting the ends to compress it into a firm sausage, then wrap in foil.
steps.look: A tight, compact roll with no air pockets.
steps.mistake: Loose wrapping, which lets water in.
steps.fix: Twist the ends more tightly; add another layer.

steps.do: Lower it into the 170°F (77°C) water bath, weighting it to keep it submerged. Poach for about 60 minutes, keeping the water between 165 and 175°F (74 and 79°C), until a probe in the centre reads 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: A water bath steaming but not bubbling.
steps.mistake: Letting the water boil, which makes the mousseline grainy.
steps.fix: Watch the thermometer and lower the heat.

steps.do: Unwrap the ballotine, pat it dry and brown it in the remaining butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until golden all over. Rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: Crisp, golden skin all round.
steps.mistake: Not drying it, so it spits and does not brown.
steps.fix: Pat dry thoroughly.

steps.do: For the sauce, pour off the fat, add the wine and boil until reduced by half, add the stock and reduce by half again, then add the cream and simmer until it coats a spoon. Season with salt and lemon juice.
steps.look: A glossy, ivory sauce.
steps.mistake: A thin sauce.
steps.fix: Simmer a few minutes more.

steps.do: Remove the string and slice the ballotine into rounds 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick with a sharp knife. Serve with the sauce.
steps.look: Neat slices showing a ring of white meat around the mushroom mousseline.
steps.mistake: Using a blunt knife, which squashes the slices.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife and one long stroke per slice.

dishes.science: Boning the bird lets you control the thickness of the meat so it cooks evenly around the filling. The mousseline works like a forcemeat: salt dissolves the muscle proteins, creating a sticky protein network that traps the cream's fat and water. Egg white adds more protein that sets on heating. Keeping everything cold stops the fat melting and the emulsion breaking. Poaching in a water bath below boiling cooks the mousseline gently so it stays light and smooth instead of grainy. The final browning develops Maillard flavours on the skin. Duxelles is cooked dry so the mushroom water does not loosen the mousseline.
dishes.plating: Use warm plates. Lay two slices slightly overlapping in the centre so the ring of meat and the mushroom mousseline show clearly. Spoon a pool of sauce at the base, and add a few sautéed mushrooms and a small bundle of green beans or a spoon of potato purée at the side.

pairing.drink: A white Burgundy such as Meursault: its richness and nutty oak match the cream sauce and mushroom, and its acidity cuts the butter.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Meursault 2022 (375 ml): a Meursault from the Brennan's list whose richness and nuttiness suit chicken, cream and mushroom.

variations: Use boned chicken legs as individual ballotines, poaching for 30 minutes.
Fill with spinach and ricotta instead of mushroom mousseline.
Serve it cold, sliced, as a galantine with a herb salad.
safety: Cook to 165°F (74°C) in the centre of the mousseline, the coolest point.
Keep raw chicken and mousseline below 40°F (4°C) while working; work in stages.
Wash hands, knives and boards thoroughly after boning raw poultry.
Boning knife: always cut away from your hand and keep the blade against the bone.

dishes.title: Beef Wellington
dishes.summary: Beef Wellington: a seared centre-cut fillet brushed with mustard, wrapped in mushroom duxelles and prosciutto, encased in homemade rough puff pastry, glazed and baked until the pastry is crisp and the beef rosy pink. It is the capstone of the dinner course because it combines searing, duxelles, lamination and precise roasting in one parcel you cannot open to check.
skills: resting and slicing to a perfect pink
equipment: Rolling pin and a cool work surface
Instant-read thermometer, ideally a leave-in probe
Small non-stick frying pan, 8 inch (20 cm), for the crêpes

ingredients.item: Cold unsalted butter, in 1/2 inch (1 cm) cubes
Egg yolks, beaten with 1 tsp (5 ml) milk

mise: Make the rough puff pastry the day before or at least 3 hours ahead.
Take the beef out of the fridge 30 minutes before searing.

timeline.do: Make rough puff pastry with 4 folds; chill.
Sear the beef; brush with mustard; chill.
Make the duxelles and the crêpes; cool.
Wrap beef in duxelles and prosciutto; chill 30 minutes.
Encase in pastry; egg wash; chill 30 minutes.
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 30 to 40 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes; finish sauce.
Slice and serve.

steps.do: Make rough puff: mix the flour and salt in a bowl, add the cold butter cubes and toss. Add the iced water a little at a time, mixing with a knife, until it comes together into a rough dough with visible lumps of butter.
steps.look: A shaggy dough streaked with lumps of butter the size of a fingernail.
steps.mistake: Rubbing in the butter, which makes shortcrust instead of puff.
steps.fix: Leave the butter in lumps.

steps.do: Roll the dough into a rectangle 12 by 6 inches (30 by 15 cm). Fold the top third down and the bottom third up like a letter. Turn 90 degrees and roll and fold again. Wrap and chill 20 minutes. Repeat for 4 folds in total.
steps.look: A smooth dough with streaks of butter, becoming more layered with each fold.
steps.mistake: Letting the butter get warm and greasy.
steps.fix: Chill for longer between folds if the butter softens.

steps.do: Season the beef with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in the frying pan over high heat and sear the fillet for 1 to 2 minutes on each side, including the ends, until browned all over. Brush with mustard while hot, then cool.
steps.look: A brown crust all round and a raw centre.
steps.mistake: Searing too long, so the beef is overcooked before baking.
steps.fix: Sear quickly and cool immediately.

steps.do: Make duxelles: process the mushrooms, shallots and garlic finely. Cook in the butter with thyme over medium-high heat, stirring, for 10 to 15 minutes until all the liquid has evaporated and the mixture is dry and holds together. Season and cool.
steps.look: A dark, dry paste that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Leaving moisture in the duxelles, which makes the pastry soggy.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until dry; it should not release liquid.

steps.do: Make the crêpes: whisk the 1/3 cup (40 g) flour, the egg, the 1/2 cup (120 ml) milk and a pinch of salt to a smooth batter. Cook 3 thin crêpes 8 inches (20 cm) across in a lightly buttered non-stick pan over medium heat, about 1 minute a side, and cool them flat.
steps.look: Thin, pale crêpes with a few golden freckles that bend without tearing.
steps.mistake: Thick crêpes, which add a doughy layer under the pastry.
steps.fix: Use about 3 tbsp (45 ml) batter per crêpe and swirl it to the edge at once.

steps.do: Lay a large sheet of cling film on the board and overlap the prosciutto slices to make a rectangle large enough to wrap the beef. Spread the duxelles over it in an even layer 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Lay the beef at one edge and roll it up tightly in the prosciutto, using the film to pull it tight. Twist the ends and chill for 30 minutes.
steps.look: A tight, even cylinder.
steps.mistake: Gaps in the prosciutto, which let the duxelles touch the pastry.
steps.fix: Patch gaps with extra prosciutto.

steps.do: Roll the pastry into a rectangle 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, large enough to wrap the beef. Lay the crêpes overlapping in the centre, unwrap the beef, set it on them and fold the crêpes up and over it as a jacket. Brush the edges with egg wash and fold the pastry round, trimming excess so there is only one overlap. Seal and turn seam side down. Fold the ends under.
steps.look: A neat parcel with the seam underneath.
steps.mistake: Too much pastry at the seams and ends, which stays raw.
steps.fix: Trim to a single overlap.

steps.do: Brush with egg wash, chill 10 minutes, brush again, then score a pattern lightly with the back of a knife without cutting through. Sprinkle with flaky salt and chill 20 minutes.
steps.look: A glossy, scored parcel.
steps.mistake: Scoring too deep, so it splits.
steps.fix: Score with the back of the blade only.

steps.do: Bake on a parchment-lined tray at 425°F (220°C) for 30 to 40 minutes until the pastry is deep golden and a probe in the centre reads 120°F (49°C) for medium-rare.
steps.look: Golden, risen pastry and a rich smell.
steps.mistake: Underbaking the pastry while waiting for the beef.
steps.fix: Choose a fillet of even thickness so both finish together.

steps.do: Rest for 10 minutes; the centre rises to about 130°F (54°C). Meanwhile, reduce the wine by two-thirds, add the stock and reduce to a glossy sauce.
steps.look: A glossy, dark sauce.
steps.mistake: Cutting it immediately, so juices flood the pastry.
steps.fix: Rest it.

steps.do: Slice into thick slices 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) wide with a serrated knife, using gentle sawing strokes. Serve with the sauce.
steps.look: Rosy pink beef, a ring of duxelles and prosciutto and crisp pastry.
steps.mistake: Pressing down hard, which squashes the pastry.
steps.fix: Saw gently.

dishes.science: Rough puff pastry rises because lumps of cold butter are flattened into thin layers between layers of dough as you roll and fold. In the hot oven, water in the butter and dough turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the fat keeps them separate. The duxelles must be cooked dry, because mushrooms are about 90 percent water, and any moisture turns the pastry soggy. The prosciutto and the crêpes act as moisture barriers between duxelles and pastry. Searing creates flavour through the Maillard reaction. Chilling the wrapped beef keeps it cold, so the pastry can bake through before the centre overcooks.
dishes.plating: Set two thick slices on a warm plate, cut face forward, showing the pink centre, mushroom ring and golden pastry. Spoon the red wine sauce beside the slices, never over the pastry. Add a few green beans or roast carrots on the side.

pairing.drink: A mature Bordeaux or a Napa Cabernet: firm tannin and dark fruit match the rich beef, mushrooms and pastry.
pairing.brennans: Château Talbot Saint-Julien 4ème Cru Classé 2019: a classic Saint-Julien from the Brennan's list, a natural partner for beef in pastry.

variations: Use bought all-butter puff pastry to save time.
Make individual Wellingtons with fillet steaks, baking for 20 minutes.
Venison Wellington: a venison loin wrapped the same way, out of the oven at 120°F (49°C).
safety: Food safety guidance for whole cuts of beef is 145°F (63°C) with a rest; medium-rare at 130°F (54°C) is a common choice for fillet.
Keep the beef refrigerated between stages and never leave it out for more than 2 hours in total.
Use a stable board and a sharp knife; keep fingers clear of the blade when slicing.

dishes.title: Christmas Pudding with Brandy Butter
dishes.summary: The British Christmas pudding: dried fruit soaked in brandy, bound with suet, breadcrumbs, dark sugar, treacle and spice, steamed for hours in a basin until dark and dense, then reheated, flamed with brandy and served with brandy butter. It is in the course because a long, steady steam is a skill of patience and safety, and the flaming is a piece of service theatre a server must master.
equipment: Large pot with lid and a trivet or upturned saucer
Baking parchment, foil and kitchen string
Large mixing bowl and wooden spoon
Kettle for topping up boiling water
Small saucepan or ladle for warming brandy, and long matches
Electric whisk or wooden spoon for brandy butter

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, soft, for brandy butter

mise: Soak the dried fruit and peel in the brandy, covered, overnight.
Butter the basin and put a small circle of parchment in the base.
Cut a circle of parchment and foil 4 inches (10 cm) wider than the top of the basin and fold a pleat across the middle.

timeline.do: Soak the fruit overnight in brandy.
Mix, fill the basin and steam 5 hours; cool; re-cover; store.
Feed with 1 tbsp (15 ml) brandy through holes in the top (optional).
Reheat by steaming 1 1/2 hours; make brandy butter.
Turn out; warm brandy.
Flame at the table and serve with brandy butter.

steps.do: In the large bowl, mix the soaked fruit and any liquid with the suet, sugar, breadcrumbs, flour, spice, zests, lemon juice, grated apple and carrot. Add the egg and treacle and stir well for 2 minutes until evenly mixed.
steps.look: A dark, moist, sticky mixture that drops heavily from the spoon.
steps.mistake: A dry mixture that will crumble.
steps.fix: Add 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) milk or stout.

steps.do: Pack the mixture into the buttered basin, pressing down, leaving 1 inch (2.5 cm) space at the top for expansion. Level the surface.
steps.look: A basin filled to just below the rim.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the pudding pushes off the cover.
steps.fix: Remove a little; bake the extra in a ramekin.

steps.do: Cover with the pleated parchment and foil, tie string tightly under the rim with 2 turns, and make a handle of string over the top.
steps.look: A tight, waterproof cover with a pleat for rising.
steps.mistake: No pleat, so the cover splits.
steps.fix: Always fold a pleat across the middle.

steps.do: Place the basin on the trivet in the pot and pour boiling water to come halfway up its sides. Cover and steam at a gentle simmer for 5 hours, topping up with boiling water every 45 minutes.
steps.look: Steady steam and a gentle simmer; the kitchen smells of spice.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry, which can crack the basin and burn the pudding.
steps.fix: Set a timer and check the water level every 45 minutes.

steps.do: Lift out the basin and cool. Remove the cover and replace with fresh parchment and foil. Store in a cool, dark cupboard for up to 2 months.
steps.look: A dark, firm pudding.
steps.mistake: Storing it with the damp steaming cover, which can grow mould.
steps.fix: Always re-cover with fresh paper.

steps.do: To serve, steam again for 1 1/2 hours until heated through, at least 165°F (74°C) in the centre.
steps.look: A hot pudding with steam rising when the cover is removed.
steps.mistake: Serving it lukewarm.
steps.fix: Steam longer and check the centre.

steps.do: Make the brandy butter: beat the soft butter until pale, about 3 minutes, then beat in the icing sugar a little at a time, followed by the brandy a spoonful at a time.
steps.look: A pale, fluffy, smooth butter.
steps.mistake: Adding the brandy too fast, so it curdles.
steps.fix: Add a spoonful of icing sugar to bring it back.

steps.do: Run a knife round the pudding and turn it out onto a warm, heatproof plate. Dim the lights.
steps.look: A dark, glossy dome.
steps.mistake: Turning it out onto a cold plate, so it cools.
steps.fix: Warm the plate first.

steps.do: Warm the 3 tbsp (45 ml) brandy gently in a small pan or ladle for 30 seconds, without boiling. Off the heat and away from the stove, light it with a long match, and pour the flaming brandy over the pudding.
steps.look: Blue flames dancing over the pudding for 30 to 60 seconds.
steps.mistake: Overheating the brandy, so the alcohol evaporates and will not light.
steps.fix: Warm it only until it is just warm to the touch.

steps.do: Once the flames die down, after about a minute, cut into 4 wedges and serve each with 2 tbsp (30 g) brandy butter.
steps.look: A rich, dark slice and melting brandy butter.
steps.mistake: Cutting before the flames are out.
steps.fix: Wait until the flames have died completely.

dishes.science: The long steaming turns the pudding dark through slow Maillard reactions and caramelisation of the fruit and dark sugar, while the steady 212°F (100°C) heat cooks the flour and egg without drying. Suet melts slowly, coating the flour and keeping the texture moist and tender. Soaking the fruit in brandy plumps it, and the alcohol and sugar help preserve the pudding, which is why it can mature for weeks. Brandy lights because at about 40 percent alcohol it gives off flammable vapour; warming it increases that vapour, while boiling drives the alcohol away before you can light it. Brandy butter is an emulsion of butter, sugar and spirit beaten into a light, airy cream.
dishes.plating: Bring the whole flaming pudding to the table on a warm plate, topped with a sprig of holly (removed before cutting, as holly berries are not edible). Serve each wedge on a warm plate with a generous spoon of brandy butter melting at its side, or a pool of custard.

pairing.drink: A tawny or vintage port, or a Pedro Ximénez sherry: dried fruit and caramel flavours match the pudding, and sweetness balances the spice.
pairing.brennans: Graham’s Vintage Port 2000: a rich vintage port from the Brennan's list with the dried fruit and spice to match a Christmas pudding.

variations: Use stout instead of brandy for soaking.
Make individual puddings in small basins, steaming 2 hours.
Serve with custard, rum sauce or clotted cream instead of brandy butter.
safety: Flaming brandy: warm it off the heat, light it away from the stove, keep hair and sleeves clear, never pour from the bottle, and keep a lid nearby to smother flames.
Steam burns: lift the basin with oven gloves and the string handle.
If you hide a coin or charm, wrap it in parchment and warn every guest; it is a choking hazard.

dishes.title: Bastani Sonnati (Saffron and Rosewater Ice Cream)
dishes.summary: Persian saffron and rosewater ice cream: a rich custard infused with saffron, scented with rosewater, churned and folded with frozen shards of cream and pistachios, then served between thin wafers. It is in the course because it combines tempering a custard with churning, and teaches how to perfume without overpowering.
skills: a saffron custard base cooked to 180°F (82°C)
equipment: Ice cream maker, with its bowl frozen for 24 hours
Small tray lined with parchment, for the cream
mise: Freeze the ice cream maker bowl for 24 hours.
Grind the saffron with a pinch of sugar and steep in the hot water for 20 minutes.
Spread the 1/3 cup (80 ml) cream on the parchment-lined tray in a thin layer and freeze until solid.

timeline.do: Freeze the churn bowl; freeze the cream sheet.
Make the custard, cool and chill 4 hours.
Churn; fold in cream shards and pistachios.
Freeze 2 hours to firm.
Scoop between wafers.

steps.do: Warm the milk and 1 cup (240 ml) cream with the salt in the saucepan over medium heat until steaming and bubbles form at the edge, about 180°F (82°C).
steps.look: Steam rising and tiny bubbles round the edge.
steps.mistake: Boiling it, which can make the custard taste cooked.
steps.fix: Take it off just before it boils.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks, sugar and salep in a bowl for 2 minutes until pale and thick.
steps.look: A pale, thick mixture that falls in ribbons.
steps.mistake: Leaving lumps of salep.
steps.fix: Sift the salep with the sugar first.

steps.do: Temper: pour a ladle of the hot milk into the yolks while whisking, then another, then pour the yolk mixture back into the pan.
steps.look: A smooth, warm mixture with no scrambled egg.
steps.mistake: Pouring the hot milk in all at once, which scrambles the eggs.
steps.fix: Add slowly; strain if lumps form.

steps.do: Cook over low heat, stirring constantly with the spatula, until the custard coats the back of a spoon and a line drawn with your finger stays clear, 175 to 180°F (79 to 82°C).
steps.look: A custard that thickens slightly and coats the spatula.
steps.mistake: Overheating past 185°F (85°C), so it curdles.
steps.fix: Pour at once into a cold bowl and blend with a stick blender.

steps.do: Strain into the bowl set in iced water, stir in the saffron water, and cool, stirring. Cover and chill for at least 4 hours.
steps.look: A golden-yellow custard, smelling of saffron.
steps.mistake: Churning a warm custard, which never freezes properly.
steps.fix: Chill thoroughly; overnight is best.

steps.do: Stir in rosewater to taste, starting with 1 tsp (5 ml). Churn according to the machine's instructions, about 20 to 25 minutes, until thick like soft-serve.
steps.look: A thick, creamy ice cream that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Too much rosewater, so it tastes like soap.
steps.fix: Add a little at a time.

steps.do: Break the frozen cream sheet into small shards and fold them and the pistachios into the ice cream quickly. Transfer to the container and freeze for 2 hours.
steps.look: Pale yellow ice cream with white chips of cream and green pistachios.
steps.mistake: Folding too long, so the shards melt.
steps.fix: Work quickly with a cold spatula.

steps.do: Let the ice cream soften for 5 minutes, then scoop between wafers to make sandwiches, or serve in bowls.
steps.look: A firm ice cream with flecks of white and green.
steps.mistake: Serving it rock hard.
steps.fix: Soften briefly at room temperature.

dishes.science: The custard is thickened by egg yolk proteins, which set between about 160 and 180°F (71 and 82°C); above that, they tighten into curds. Tempering raises the temperature of the yolks gradually so they do not set too fast. Sugar lowers the freezing point of the base, keeping the ice cream scoopable, and fat from the cream and yolks coats ice crystals and gives a smooth texture. Churning beats air into the base while freezing it fast, so the ice crystals stay small. Salep, from orchid tubers, contains a starch-like substance that adds chew and slows melting. Saffron's colour comes from water-soluble crocin.
dishes.plating: Sandwich a thick slab of ice cream between two thin wafers and roll the edges in chopped pistachios. Or serve two small scoops in a chilled glass with a few crushed pistachios and dried rose petals on top.

pairing.drink: A Sauternes or a late harvest Riesling: honeyed sweetness and floral notes echo saffron and rosewater.
pairing.brennans: Château Suduiraut Sauternes 2016 (375 ml): a Sauternes from the Brennan's list whose honeyed sweetness suits saffron and rose.

variations: Make it with cardamom instead of rosewater.
Fold in chopped dried figs instead of pistachios.
Make faloodeh, a rose and lime sorbet, to serve alongside.
safety: Cook the custard to at least 160°F (71°C), which this method passes, to make the egg yolks safe.
Cool custard quickly over ice and keep it refrigerated.
Salep may be hard to find; cornflour is a safe substitute.

dishes.title: Eight Treasure Rice Pudding
dishes.summary: Eight treasure rice pudding: sweet glutinous rice steamed in a bowl lined with a pattern of dried fruits, nuts and lotus seeds around a heart of red bean paste, turned out like a jewelled dome and glazed with osmanthus syrup. It is in the course because it trains steaming in stages, building a design that only shows when you turn it out, and a clean syrup.
skills: arranging dried fruits in a pattern
equipment: Steamer large enough for a bowl, or a wok with a rack and lid
Heatproof bowl, 5 to 6 inches (13 to 15 cm) across, 3 cups (720 ml) capacity
Muslin or a clean cloth for steaming the rice

ingredients.item: Lotus seeds, dried, soaked and cooked (or tinned)
Dried apricots or candied winter melon
Rock sugar or caster sugar, for syrup
Dried osmanthus flowers (or a few drops of vanilla)
Cornflour mixed with 1 tbsp (15 ml) water

mise: Rinse the glutinous rice and soak overnight in cold water.
Soak the dates, lotus seeds and goji berries in warm water for 30 minutes.
Generously grease the bowl with lard.

timeline.do: Soak the glutinous rice overnight.
Steam the rice 30 to 35 minutes; mix with lard and sugar.
Arrange fruit in the bowl; layer rice and bean paste.
Steam the pudding 45 minutes.
Make osmanthus syrup.
Turn out and glaze.

steps.do: Drain the rice and spread it in a muslin-lined steamer basket. Steam over boiling water for 30 to 35 minutes until the grains are translucent and tender.
steps.look: Shiny, translucent grains that stick together.
steps.mistake: Steaming dry rice that has not been soaked, which stays hard.
steps.fix: Always soak overnight; sprinkle with water and steam longer if needed.

steps.do: While the rice is still hot, mix in the 2 tbsp (25 g) lard and the 3 tbsp (40 g) sugar with a wet spatula until every grain is glossy.
steps.look: Glossy, sweet, sticky rice.
steps.mistake: Letting it cool first, so the lard does not mix in.
steps.fix: Mix while hot.

steps.do: Arrange the fruits and nuts in a pattern in the base and 2 inches (5 cm) up the sides of the greased bowl, placing the most colourful in the centre. Press them in firmly.
steps.look: A colourful mosaic covering the base and sides.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps, so the pattern looks sparse.
steps.fix: Fill gaps with raisins and goji.

steps.do: Spread a layer of rice about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick carefully over the fruit and up the sides, pressing gently with a wet spoon so you do not disturb the pattern.
steps.look: An even layer of rice holding the fruits in place.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, which moves the fruit.
steps.fix: Press with a wet spoon.

steps.do: Flatten the red bean paste into a disc 3 inches (8 cm) across and put it in the centre, then cover with the remaining rice and press firmly to level.
steps.look: A compact bowl with the paste hidden in the middle.
steps.mistake: Paste touching the sides, so it shows when turned out.
steps.fix: Keep it in the centre.

steps.do: Cover the bowl with foil or a plate and steam for 45 minutes over medium heat.
steps.look: A firm, set pudding.
steps.mistake: Letting water drip into the bowl.
steps.fix: Cover tightly.

steps.do: Make the syrup: simmer the water, rock sugar and osmanthus for 3 minutes, then stir in the cornflour mixture and simmer 1 minute until clear and slightly thick.
steps.look: A clear, glossy syrup with golden flowers.
steps.mistake: Cloudy syrup from too much cornflour.
steps.fix: Use only a little.

steps.do: Run a knife round the edge, place a plate on top and turn it out. Pour the syrup over.
steps.look: A jewelled dome, glossy with syrup.
steps.mistake: Turning out too soon, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Rest 5 minutes first.

dishes.science: Glutinous rice is almost all amylopectin, a branched starch that becomes very sticky when cooked and does not set hard as it cools, so the pudding holds together and stays soft. Soaking lets water into the grains so they cook through in steam without boiling, which would make them mushy. Lard coats the grains, adding richness and helping them release from the bowl. Steaming keeps the temperature steady at 212°F (100°C), so the pudding sets evenly. The syrup is thickened by a little cornflour, which turns clear when it gelatinises, giving a glossy glaze.
dishes.plating: Turn the pudding out onto a round plate with a slight lip to catch the syrup. Spoon over the glossy osmanthus syrup so it runs down the sides and pools around the base. Cut into wedges at the table so each guest sees the red bean centre.

pairing.drink: A jasmine or oolong tea, or a lightly sweet Moscato d'Asti: floral notes meet the osmanthus without overpowering the delicate rice.
pairing.brennans: Castello Banfi ‘Florus’ Moscadello di Montalcino 2011: a late harvest Moscato from the Brennan's list whose floral sweetness suits osmanthus and red dates.

variations: Use black sesame paste instead of red bean paste.
Make individual puddings in small cups, steaming 25 minutes.
Add chestnuts or dried longan to the pattern.
safety: Steam burns: lift the bowl out with oven gloves or a plate lifter.
Cool leftover rice quickly and refrigerate; reheat by steaming until hot.

dishes.title: Jalebi with Rabri
dishes.summary: Jalebi with rabri: coils of fermented batter fried crisp in ghee and soaked in saffron syrup, served warm on rabri, milk slowly reduced with its skins until thick, sweet and scented with cardamom. It is in the course because it brings together fermentation, deep frying, a sugar syrup at an exact stage, and the patience of reducing milk.
skills: rabri reduced from milk for hours
equipment: Heavy, wide kadai or deep pan for frying
Wide, heavy pan for the rabri
Squeeze bottle or a piping bag with a 1/8 inch (3 mm) tip
mise: Start the batter the day before.
Set a wire rack over a tray next to the stove.

timeline.do: Make the batter and ferment 12 to 24 hours.
Make the rabri (1 to 1 1/2 hours); chill or keep warm.
Make the syrup and keep it warm.
Fry the jalebis and soak them.
Serve warm on rabri.

steps.do: Whisk the flour, yoghurt and warm water to a smooth batter the thickness of double cream, beating hard for 3 minutes. Cover and leave in a warm place, 77 to 86°F (25 to 30°C), for 12 to 24 hours until bubbly and slightly sour.
steps.look: A domed, bubbly batter with a sour smell.
steps.mistake: Leaving it somewhere cold, so it does not ferment.
steps.fix: Move it somewhere warmer; give it more time.

steps.do: Make the rabri: bring the milk to the boil in the wide pan, then lower the heat to keep it at a steady simmer. As a skin forms, push it to the side of the pan with a spatula. Continue for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, stirring the base and scraping the skins from the sides into the milk, until reduced to about a quarter, 1 cup (240 ml).
steps.look: Thick, creamy milk with layers of skin (malai).
steps.mistake: Letting the base scorch.
steps.fix: Stir the base often and keep the heat low.

steps.do: Stir the sugar, cardamom and saffron into the rabri and simmer 2 minutes. Cool and chill, or keep warm.
steps.look: A thick, sweet, golden rabri.
steps.mistake: Adding sugar too early, which makes it scorch.
steps.fix: Add it at the end.

steps.do: Make the syrup: boil the sugar, water and cardamom until a drop between finger and thumb forms one thread, 223 to 226°F (106 to 108°C). Add saffron, lemon juice and rose water. Keep warm, about 140°F (60°C).
steps.look: A clear, golden syrup that pulls a single thread.
steps.mistake: Boiling too long, so the syrup crystallises.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water and reheat.

steps.do: Whisk the batter for 30 seconds and pour into the squeeze bottle. Heat the ghee to 350°F (180°C).
steps.look: A smooth batter that flows in a steady ribbon.
steps.mistake: Overbeating, which knocks out the bubbles.
steps.fix: Whisk briefly.

steps.do: Squeeze the batter into the hot ghee in spirals, 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) across, starting from the outside and working in. Fry 45 seconds a side until crisp and pale gold.
steps.look: Crisp, light coils that float.
steps.mistake: Ghee too cool, so the jalebis absorb fat.
steps.fix: Check the temperature; fry fewer at once.

steps.do: Lift out, drain briefly, and drop into the warm syrup for 30 seconds, turning once. Lift onto the rack.
steps.look: Glossy, syrup-filled coils that stay crisp.
steps.mistake: Leaving them too long in the syrup, so they go soft.
steps.fix: Keep to 30 seconds.

steps.do: Spoon rabri onto plates and arrange warm jalebis on top. Sprinkle with pistachios and almonds.
steps.look: Crisp, glossy jalebis on thick, creamy rabri.
steps.mistake: Serving cold, soggy jalebis.
steps.fix: Fry just before serving.

dishes.science: Fermentation fills the batter with gas from yeasts and lactic acid bacteria, which gives the jalebi a hollow, lacy texture and slight sourness. Frying at 350°F (180°C) turns water in the batter to steam, puffing it and setting a crisp shell. When the hot jalebi meets warm syrup, the steam inside condenses and pulls syrup into the hollow centre. Syrup at one-thread stage is concentrated enough to stay on the jalebi without crystallising, and lemon juice inverts some sucrose to stop crystals forming. Rabri thickens as water evaporates from the milk, concentrating its proteins and sugars, while the skins add a chewy texture.
dishes.plating: Spoon a pool of rabri into a shallow bowl and lay two or three warm jalebis on top, glistening with syrup. Scatter slivered pistachios and almonds and a few saffron threads over the rabri.

pairing.drink: A masala chai, or a late harvest Gewurztraminer: spice and sweetness echo the cardamom and saffron.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007: a late harvest Alsace wine from the Brennan's list with rose and spice to meet saffron and cardamom.

variations: Serve jalebi alone, hot from the syrup, with milk.
Make imarti with a lentil batter for a firmer coil.
Flavour the rabri with rose petals.
safety: Hot ghee at 350°F (180°C) burns: keep the pan on a back burner, never fill it more than one-third full, and keep children away.
Sugar syrup at 226°F (108°C) sticks to skin; never touch it.
Keep a lid nearby in case the ghee catches fire; never use water.

dishes.title: Halawet el Jibn
dishes.summary: Syrian halawet el jibn: a dough of melted cheese and semolina cooked in syrup until it stretches, rolled thin, filled with ashta cream, rolled up and finished with syrup, pistachio and rose. It is in the course because it is all about temperature control: too hot and the cheese turns greasy, too cool and the semolina stays raw.
skills: melting cheese into a semolina dough
equipment: Small saucepan for syrup and ashta
Smooth work surface or a large tray
mise: If using akkawi, cube and soak it in cold water for about 8 hours, changing the water several times, until most of the salt is gone.
Make the ashta and syrup ahead so they are cool.

timeline.do: Desalt the akkawi.
Make syrup and ashta; cool.
Melt the cheese and make the dough.
Roll, fill and roll up.
Chill briefly; slice.
Dress with syrup, pistachio and rose.

steps.do: Make the syrup: boil the sugar, water and lemon juice for 5 minutes until it runs in a thread, about 220°F (104°C). Add orange blossom water. Cool, and set half aside for serving.
steps.look: A clear, slightly thick syrup.
steps.mistake: Boiling too long, which makes a toffee.
steps.fix: Add water and reheat.

steps.do: Make the ashta: whisk the milk, cream, cornflour and sugar in the small saucepan over medium heat until it boils and thickens, about 4 minutes. Add the rose water. Cool with film on the surface, then put into the piping bag.
steps.look: A thick, smooth cream that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Lumps from not whisking.
steps.fix: Whisk constantly; sieve if needed.

steps.do: Drain and dry the cheese. Warm half the syrup in the wide pan over low heat, add the cheese and stir until it melts into stretchy strings, about 3 minutes.
steps.look: Melted, stretchy cheese.
steps.mistake: Using high heat, so the cheese turns greasy and rubbery.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low.

steps.do: Add the semolina gradually, stirring constantly, until the mixture comes together into a smooth, glossy mass that leaves the sides of the pan, 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, elastic dough that pulls away from the pan.
steps.mistake: Cooking too long, which tightens the cheese.
steps.fix: Take it off as soon as it comes together.

steps.do: Turn the dough onto a surface brushed with syrup and knead briefly with syrup-wetted hands. Roll it out to a rectangle about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick.
steps.look: A smooth, thin sheet of dough.
steps.mistake: Letting it cool too much, so it tears.
steps.fix: Work quickly while warm.

steps.do: Cut into strips about 4 inches (10 cm) wide. Pipe a line of ashta along one edge of each strip and roll up into a log.
steps.look: Neat logs with ashta in the centre.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the ashta squeezes out.
steps.fix: Use a thin line of ashta.

steps.do: Chill the logs on a tray for 10 minutes, then cut them with a sharp, wet knife into pieces 2 inches (5 cm) long.
steps.look: Neat rolls showing a white centre.
steps.mistake: Cutting warm rolls, which squash.
steps.fix: Chill first.

steps.do: Arrange on a plate, drizzle with the reserved syrup and sprinkle with pistachios and rose petals.
steps.look: Glossy rolls dusted green and pink.
steps.mistake: Too much syrup, so they become soggy.
steps.fix: Drizzle lightly and serve more on the side.

dishes.science: Cheese melts when heat loosens the casein proteins, allowing them to stretch. Semolina starch absorbs water from the syrup and gelatinises, setting the stretched cheese into a pliable dough. Too much heat makes the casein tighten and squeeze out fat, leaving a greasy, rubbery texture. Ashta is a starch-thickened cream: cornflour granules swell when heated and thicken the milk. Syrup made with lemon juice resists crystallising, because the acid splits some sucrose into glucose and fructose. Desalting akkawi removes salt so the dessert stays sweet.
dishes.plating: Arrange the rolls cut side up on a plate so the white ashta centres show. Drizzle with syrup, scatter ground pistachio over the top and a few rose petals. Serve the rest of the syrup in a small jug.

pairing.drink: A Turkish coffee or a sweet Muscat: rich coffee cuts the sweetness, and Muscat's floral notes match orange blossom and rose.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: a sweet fortified wine from the Brennan's list whose richness balances the cheese and syrup.

variations: Use ricotta and cream instead of ashta.
Serve with a scoop of rose ice cream.
Shape into small cones and fill with ashta.
safety: Hot syrup and melted cheese can burn: wet your hands with cool syrup before handling the dough.
Keep filled rolls refrigerated and eat within a day.

video.search: halawet el jibn sweet cheese rolls ashta

dishes.title: Ekmek Kataifi
dishes.summary: Greek ekmek kataifi: a crisp base of shredded kataifi pastry baked in butter and soaked in lemon syrup, covered with a thick vanilla custard and crowned with lightly sweetened whipped cream and pistachios. It is in the course because it layers three textures that each need a different skill: a syrup-soaked pastry that stays crisp, a starch custard that sets firm, and cream whipped to exactly soft peaks.
skills: layering in a dish to slice clean
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) square baking dish, at least 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) deep
Electric mixer or a large balloon whisk
mise: Make the syrup first so it is completely cool: boil the sugar, water, lemon peel and cinnamon for 5 minutes, add the lemon juice and cool.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C).
Chill the bowl and whisk for the cream.

timeline.do: Make the syrup; cool.
Bake the kataifi base 25 to 30 minutes; pour over cool syrup.
Make the custard; spread over the base; chill 4 hours.
Whip the cream; spread on top.
Scatter pistachios and cut.

steps.do: Pull the kataifi strands apart gently with your fingers to fluff them, then toss with the melted butter until every strand is coated.
steps.look: Loose, buttery strands with no dry patches.
steps.mistake: Leaving clumps, which bake soggy.
steps.fix: Separate the clumps and toss again.

steps.do: Press the kataifi evenly into the dish to a layer about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. Bake at 350°F (180°C) for 25 to 30 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
steps.look: Golden, crisp strands and a toasty smell.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the base is pale and goes soggy under syrup.
steps.fix: Bake 5 minutes more until deep gold.

steps.do: Pour the cool syrup evenly over the hot pastry and leave it to absorb for 30 minutes.
steps.look: A sizzle as the syrup hits the hot pastry, then all the syrup absorbed.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot syrup on hot pastry, which turns it soggy.
steps.fix: Always one hot and one cool.

steps.do: Make the custard: heat the milk until steaming. Whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour in a bowl until smooth, then whisk in a ladle of the hot milk. Pour back into the pan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it boils and thickens; keep it bubbling for 1 minute.
steps.look: A thick custard with large, slow bubbles.
steps.mistake: Taking it off before it boils, so it thins later.
steps.fix: Bring it back to the boil and hold 1 minute.

steps.do: Off the heat, whisk in the vanilla and butter. Spread the hot custard evenly over the syrup-soaked base, smooth the top, cover with cling film touching the surface, and chill for at least 4 hours.
steps.look: A smooth, level custard layer about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick.
steps.mistake: Not covering the surface, so a skin forms.
steps.fix: Press the film onto the surface.

steps.do: Whip the cold cream with the icing sugar to soft peaks that just hold their shape, about 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: Billowy cream that holds a soft peak that curls over.
steps.mistake: Overwhipping, so it turns grainy.
steps.fix: Fold in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of liquid cream by hand to smooth it.

steps.do: Spread the cream over the set custard in soft swirls with a palette knife. Scatter with pistachios and a pinch of cinnamon.
steps.look: White, soft cream, green pistachios.
steps.mistake: Spreading on warm custard, so the cream melts.
steps.fix: Chill the custard fully first.

steps.do: Cut into 4 squares with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped between cuts.
steps.look: Clean slices showing three distinct layers.
steps.mistake: Using a cold, dry knife, which drags the cream.
steps.fix: Dip and wipe between cuts.

dishes.science: Kataifi stays crisp under syrup because the pastry is baked dry and golden first, and the cool syrup meets hot pastry: the temperature difference lets the pastry absorb syrup while the outside stays firm. The custard is thickened by cornflour, whose starch granules swell and burst above about 203°F (95°C), so it must boil; that also destroys an enzyme in yolks that would otherwise thin it. Butter adds gloss. Whipping cream traps air in a network of fat globules partly broken by the whisk; at soft peaks the network holds air but stays smooth, while further whipping clumps the fat into butter.
dishes.plating: Lift each square with a palette knife and set it on a plate so the three layers face the guest: golden crunchy base, yellow custard, white cream. Add a few more pistachios on top and a light dusting of cinnamon.

pairing.drink: A Greek Vinsanto or a Muscat of Samos: honeyed, raisined sweetness and acidity match the syrup and cut the cream.
pairing.brennans: Hexamer ‘Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg’ Riesling Spätlese 2010: a sweet, lively Riesling from the Brennan's list whose acidity cuts the custard and cream.

variations: Add a layer of chopped pistachios or walnuts under the custard.
Flavour the custard with mastic for a more traditional taste.
Make individual servings in glasses.
safety: The custard boils, which makes the egg yolks safe.
Keep the finished dessert refrigerated and eat within 2 days.
Hot syrup and pastry: pour carefully to avoid splashing.
