dishes.title: Baked Alaska
dishes.summary: Baked Alaska: a dome of homemade vanilla ice cream frozen rock hard on a disc of sponge, armoured in thick Italian meringue and browned in a blazing oven or with a torch, so it arrives hot outside and frozen within. It is in the course because it draws together churning, a cooked meringue and split-second timing, and because it is a piece of dining room theatre worth understanding.
skills: homemade ice cream frozen hard in a dome
an Italian meringue piped and torched
equipment: Ice cream maker with its bowl frozen for 24 hours
Heavy saucepan, whisk and an instant-read thermometer
Bowl 5 inches (13 cm) across, about 2 1/2 cups (600 ml), lined with cling film
Small heavy saucepan and a sugar thermometer
Piping bag with a large star or plain tip, or a palette knife
Ovenproof serving plate or a baking tray lined with parchment
Long knife and a jug of hot water

ingredients.item: Vanilla pod, split (or 2 tsp (10 ml) extract)

mise: Freeze the ice cream maker bowl for 24 hours.
Clear space in the freezer for the bowl and then the finished dessert on a flat tray.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C) for the sponge.

timeline.do: Make and churn the ice cream; pack into the lined bowl and freeze overnight.
Bake the sponge; cool and wrap.
Unmould the ice cream onto the sponge; freeze 1 hour.
Make the Italian meringue; cover completely; freeze at least 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 475°F (250°C).
Bake 3 to 4 minutes or torch.
Serve at once, cutting with a hot knife.

steps.do: Make the ice cream base: heat the milk, cream, salt and vanilla pod and seeds until steaming, about 180°F (82°C). Whisk the yolks and sugar until pale, temper with a ladle of the hot milk, return to the pan and cook over low heat, stirring, until it coats a spoon at 175 to 180°F (79 to 82°C).
steps.look: A smooth custard that coats the spatula and holds a clean line drawn through it with a finger.
steps.mistake: Overheating past 185°F (85°C), which scrambles the yolks into flecks.
steps.fix: Pour at once into a cold bowl and blend with a stick blender, then strain.

steps.do: Strain the custard into a bowl set in iced water, stir until cool, then cover and chill for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Churn in the ice cream maker for 20 to 25 minutes until thick, like soft-serve.
steps.look: Thick, creamy ice cream that holds a ribbon.
steps.mistake: Churning a warm base, which never thickens.
steps.fix: Chill longer; the base should be below 40°F (4°C).

steps.do: Pack the ice cream into the film-lined bowl, pressing out air pockets with the back of a spoon, level the top, cover and freeze overnight until rock hard.
steps.look: A solid, smooth dome of ice cream.
steps.mistake: Leaving air pockets, which make the dome collapse when cut.
steps.fix: Press firmly in layers as you fill.

steps.do: Make the sponge: whisk the eggs and sugar on high speed for 6 to 8 minutes until pale and thick. Fold in the flour in three additions, then the melted butter, and bake in the lined 6 inch (15 cm) tin at 350°F (180°C) for 18 to 20 minutes until springy. Cool.
steps.look: A light, golden sponge about 1 inch (2.5 cm) tall.
steps.mistake: Deflating the batter by stirring instead of folding.
steps.fix: Fold gently with a large spatula; the next one will rise better.

steps.do: Set the sponge on the ovenproof plate and brush it with the liqueur, if using. Dip the ice cream bowl in warm water for 5 seconds, turn the dome out onto the sponge, peel off the film, and trim the sponge to leave a 1/2 inch (1 cm) border. Freeze 1 hour.
steps.look: A frozen dome sitting neatly on its sponge base.
steps.mistake: Letting the ice cream soften, so it slumps.
steps.fix: Work fast and return it to the freezer at once.

steps.do: Make the Italian meringue: boil the sugar and water without stirring to 244°F (118°C). When the syrup reaches 230°F (110°C), start whipping the whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks. Pour the hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl into the whites with the mixer running, then whip on high for 8 to 10 minutes until glossy, stiff and cool.
steps.look: A thick, glossy meringue that stands in stiff peaks and feels barely warm.
steps.mistake: Pouring syrup onto the whisk, which spins it into sugar threads.
steps.fix: Pour down the side; if threads form, pick them out.

steps.do: Working quickly, pipe or spread the meringue over the frozen dome in a layer at least 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick, sealing it right down to the plate so no sponge or ice cream shows. Pull the surface into peaks or pipe rosettes.
steps.look: A complete, thick shell of meringue with no gaps, swirled into peaks.
steps.mistake: Leaving a gap at the base, where the heat gets in and melts the ice cream.
steps.fix: Run the palette knife round the base to seal it to the plate.

steps.do: Freeze the finished dessert, uncovered, for at least 1 hour, or up to 2 days.
steps.look: A firm, frozen meringue shell.
steps.mistake: Covering it with film, which sticks to the meringue.
steps.fix: Freeze uncovered; once frozen, cover loosely with a tall box.

steps.do: To serve, bake in the 475°F (250°C) oven on the top shelf for 3 to 4 minutes until the peaks are golden brown, or torch the surface evenly, holding the flame 3 inches (8 cm) away.
steps.look: Golden tips and pale valleys, a smell of toasted marshmallow.
steps.mistake: Baking too long, so the ice cream melts inside.
steps.fix: Watch it every 30 seconds; take it out as soon as the tips colour.

steps.do: Cut at once into 4 wedges with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped between each cut, and serve.
steps.look: A hot, toasted meringue shell, cold ice cream and soft sponge in every slice.
steps.mistake: Waiting at the table, so the ice cream softens.
steps.fix: Have plates and the hot knife ready before it comes out of the oven.

dishes.science: The trick is insulation. Meringue is mostly air trapped in a network of egg protein and sugar, and air conducts heat very poorly, so a thick, sealed meringue shell protects the frozen ice cream for the few minutes the oven browns the surface. Italian meringue is made with syrup at 244°F (118°C), which partly cooks the whites and dissolves the sugar, giving a dense, stable foam that does not weep. The sponge at the base insulates the ice cream from the plate. Ice cream stays smooth because churning freezes it quickly while beating in air, keeping ice crystals small, and the sugar and fat lower its freezing point.
dishes.plating: Bring the whole Alaska to the table on its plate, golden and smoking slightly, and cut it there. Lay each wedge on its side on a cold plate so the browned shell, white meringue, vanilla ice cream and sponge show, and add a spoon of fruit sauce or a few berries.

pairing.drink: A demi-sec Champagne or a sweet sparkling Moscato: gentle sweetness and bubbles refresh after rich meringue and ice cream.
pairing.brennans: Cherries Jubilee: another Brennan's dessert built on table-side theatre, flamed in the dining room just as a Baked Alaska can be.

variations: Flambé it at the table with warmed rum poured over and lit.
Use two layers of ice cream, such as raspberry sorbet and vanilla.
Make individual Alaskas on rounds of sponge.
safety: Syrup at 244°F (118°C) does not fully pasteurise the whites, so use pasteurised egg whites; the ice cream custard is cooked to a safe 160°F (71°C) or above.
Hot sugar syrup causes serious burns: pour carefully and keep children away.
A 475°F (250°C) oven and a blowtorch are both fierce: use oven gloves and keep the torch flame away from your hand and anything flammable.

dishes.title: Sachertorte
dishes.summary: Vienna's Sachertorte: a dense, fine-crumbed chocolate sponge split and filled with apricot jam, painted with more jam and enrobed in a glossy chocolate glaze cooked with sugar syrup, served with unsweetened whipped cream. It is in the course because it requires folding a whisked batter into melted chocolate without losing air, a glaze cooked to the right point, and the precision of tempering chocolate for its decoration.
skills: a chocolate sponge raised with meringue
a cooked chocolate glaze poured in one motion
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) springform tin, lined and buttered
Heatproof bowls and a pan for melting chocolate
Small saucepan and a sugar thermometer
Small piping cone or a zip bag

ingredients.item: Dark chocolate, 60 to 70 percent, for cake

mise: Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C).
Melt the cake chocolate over barely simmering water and cool to about 95°F (35°C).
Have the butter and eggs at room temperature.

timeline.do: Bake the cake 40 to 45 minutes; cool upside down overnight.
Split, fill and coat with warm jam; let it set 1 hour.
Cook and pour the glaze; set 2 hours.
Temper chocolate and pipe the decoration.
Slice with a hot knife; serve with whipped cream.

steps.do: Beat the butter and icing sugar for 3 minutes until pale and creamy. Beat in the yolks one at a time, then the cooled melted chocolate, vanilla and salt.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, chocolate-brown mixture.
steps.mistake: Adding hot chocolate, which melts the butter and makes the batter greasy.
steps.fix: Cool the chocolate to about 95°F (35°C) first.

steps.do: In a clean bowl, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, then add the caster sugar gradually and whip to firm, glossy peaks that bend slightly at the tip, about 4 minutes.
steps.look: Glossy peaks that hold but curl over at the tip.
steps.mistake: Overwhipping to dry, grainy peaks that will not fold in.
steps.fix: Fold in a spoonful of liquid white and whisk briefly to loosen.

steps.do: Fold a third of the whites into the chocolate mixture to loosen it, then fold in the rest in two additions alternately with the flour, cutting down through the centre and turning the bowl.
steps.look: A smooth, airy batter with no streaks of white.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which knocks out the air and makes a heavy cake.
steps.fix: Fold gently with a large spatula, about 30 strokes in all.

steps.do: Pour into the tin, level the top and bake for 40 to 45 minutes until a skewer comes out with a few moist crumbs. Turn out upside down on the rack and cool overnight for a flat top.
steps.look: A risen cake with a slightly cracked top that settles as it cools.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven in the first 25 minutes, so the cake sinks.
steps.fix: Keep the door closed until a skewer test at 35 minutes.

steps.do: Trim the top flat if needed and split the cake into two layers with the serrated knife. Spread half the warm jam on the bottom layer and set the top on it.
steps.look: Two even layers with a thin line of jam.
steps.mistake: Splitting a warm cake, which crumbles.
steps.fix: Cool it completely, overnight is best.

steps.do: Brush the warm jam over the top and sides in a thin, even layer, and leave to set for 1 hour.
steps.look: A shiny, tacky coat of apricot over the whole cake.
steps.mistake: Using cold jam, which tears the crumb.
steps.fix: Warm it until runny and sieve it.

steps.do: Make the glaze: boil the sugar and water to 225°F (107°C). Take it off the heat, add the chopped chocolate and stir until smooth. Keep stirring as it cools to about 100°F (38°C), when it thickens and coats a spoon in an even, opaque layer.
steps.look: A glossy, thick glaze that coats a spoon like pouring cream.
steps.mistake: Pouring it too hot, so it runs off thin and dull; or too cool, so it sets in ridges.
steps.fix: Reheat gently or cool longer, testing on a spoon.

steps.do: Set the cake on the rack over a tray. Pour all the glaze over the centre in one motion and spread it once over the top with the palette knife so it flows down the sides. Do not touch it again. Leave to set for 2 hours.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy coat with no bare spots.
steps.mistake: Going back to smooth it, which leaves marks.
steps.fix: Scrape the excess from the tray and keep it for decoration.

steps.do: Temper the decoration chocolate: melt two-thirds of it to 115 to 120°F (46 to 49°C), stir in the remaining chopped chocolate until it cools to 81 to 82°F (27 to 28°C), then warm it gently to 88 to 90°F (31 to 32°C).
steps.look: Glossy chocolate that sets crisp with a snap on the tip of a knife in 3 minutes.
steps.mistake: Letting it go above 90°F (32°C), which loses the temper and leaves it dull and streaky.
steps.fix: Cool it again with more chopped chocolate and rewarm.

steps.do: Put the tempered chocolate into the piping cone and pipe the word Sacher or a simple design on the cake.
steps.look: Glossy, crisp lettering.
steps.mistake: Piping with untempered chocolate, which smears.
steps.fix: Practise first on parchment.

steps.do: Whip the cream to soft peaks without sugar. Slice the cake with a hot knife and serve each slice with a spoon of cream.
steps.look: Clean slices showing the jam line, with soft cream alongside.
steps.mistake: Sweetening the cream, which makes the plate too sweet.
steps.fix: Keep the cream plain; it balances the cake.

dishes.science: Sachertorte is a whisked chocolate sponge: the air in the whipped whites lifts it, and folding preserves the bubbles while the melted chocolate and butter make the crumb dense and fine. The jam acts as a moisture barrier and glue, keeping the cake moist under the glaze. The glaze is a sugar syrup cooked to 225°F (107°C) and blended with chocolate; stirring as it cools encourages fine sugar crystals and gives the glaze its glossy, slightly firm finish. Tempering aligns the cocoa butter into its stable crystal form (form V), which sets with a snap and a shine; untempered chocolate sets soft and streaky.
dishes.plating: Set a slice on a plate, glossy top and cut face showing the thin line of apricot, with a generous spoon of unsweetened whipped cream beside it. Serve with a cup of coffee, the Viennese way.

pairing.drink: A Viennese melange coffee, or a Banyuls: the coffee cuts the richness, and the sweet red wine matches chocolate and apricot.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: a sweet red wine from the Brennan's list, the classic partner for dark chocolate.

variations: Use raspberry jam instead of apricot.
Make individual Sacher cubes for a buffet.
Use a simple ganache glaze if a cooked glaze seems daunting.
safety: Sugar syrup at 225°F (107°C) burns: stir with a long spoon and keep children away.
Keep the cake at cool room temperature and eat within 4 days.

dishes.title: Macarons
dishes.summary: French macarons: smooth, domed almond meringue shells with ruffled feet, made by the Italian meringue method, folded to the exact consistency, piped, rested, baked and filled with dark chocolate ganache. It is in the course because few things in pastry are as unforgiving: a few strokes too many or too few in the folding and the shells crack, spread or stay hollow.
equipment: Small heavy saucepan and a sugar thermometer
Piping bag with a 1/2 inch (1 cm) plain tip
Two heavy baking trays lined with parchment or silicone mats

ingredients.item: Egg whites, aged 24 to 48 hours in the fridge, divided
ingredients.metric: about 75 g, as two 37 g portions

ingredients.item: Dark chocolate, 60 to 70 percent, chopped, for ganache

mise: Separate the egg whites a day ahead, cover and keep them in the fridge, then bring them to room temperature for 1 hour before using; weigh them into two equal portions.
Pulse the ground almonds and icing sugar in the food processor for 15 seconds, then sift; discard any coarse bits left in the sieve.
Place the template under the parchment.

timeline.do: Separate and age the whites.
Make the shells; rest 30 to 60 minutes; bake; cool.
Make the ganache; fill the shells.
Mature the filled macarons in the fridge for 24 hours.
Bring to room temperature.
Serve.

steps.do: Mix the sifted almond and icing sugar with the first portion of egg white to a thick paste.
steps.look: A thick, stiff almond paste.
steps.mistake: Lumps of almond.
steps.fix: Press them out with the spatula.

steps.do: Boil the caster sugar and water to 244°F (118°C). When it reaches 230°F (110°C), start whipping the second portion of white to soft peaks.
steps.look: A clear syrup reaching temperature as the whites hold soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Starting the whites too late or too early.
steps.fix: Lower the heat under the syrup if the whites are behind.

steps.do: Pour the hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl into the whipping whites. Whip on high for 5 minutes until glossy and stiff, and cooled to about 120°F (49°C).
steps.look: A thick, glossy meringue holding stiff peaks.
steps.mistake: Pouring onto the whisk.
steps.fix: Pour down the side.

steps.do: Fold a third of the meringue into the almond paste to loosen it, then fold in the rest. Continue folding (macaronage), pressing the batter against the side of the bowl, until it flows off the spatula in a thick, unbroken ribbon and a figure of eight drawn with it sinks back in about 10 seconds.
steps.look: A glossy batter like slow-flowing lava, holding a ribbon.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, so it runs thin and the shells spread; or undermixing, so they crack and have peaks.
steps.fix: Test often; stop as soon as it ribbons.

steps.do: Pipe 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) rounds onto the template, holding the bag straight up 1/2 inch (1 cm) above the tray and stopping pressure before lifting.
steps.look: Smooth, round discs with small peaks that settle within 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Piping at an angle, which makes oval shells.
steps.fix: Hold the bag vertically.

steps.do: Tap the trays firmly on the counter 3 or 4 times to release bubbles, and pop any remaining with a toothpick.
steps.look: Smooth, flat discs with no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Skipping this, so the shells crack.
steps.fix: Tap firmly.

steps.do: Rest the piped shells at room temperature for 30 to 60 minutes until a skin forms and they are no longer sticky to a light touch.
steps.look: A matte, dry skin.
steps.mistake: Baking before a skin forms, which makes them crack.
steps.fix: Wait longer in a humid kitchen.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time at 300°F (150°C) for 13 to 15 minutes until the feet are risen and the tops do not move when gently pushed.
steps.look: Smooth, domed shells with ruffled feet.
steps.mistake: Oven too hot, so they brown or crack.
steps.fix: Use an oven thermometer and adjust.

steps.do: Cool the shells completely on the tray, about 20 minutes, then peel the parchment away from the shells rather than lifting the shells off the paper.
steps.look: Shells that release cleanly.
steps.mistake: Peeling warm shells, which stick.
steps.fix: Cool fully.

steps.do: Make the ganache: heat the cream until steaming, pour over the chocolate, stand 2 minutes, stir until smooth, add the butter. Cool until thick enough to pipe, about 30 minutes.
steps.look: A glossy, thick ganache.
steps.mistake: Using it while runny.
steps.fix: Cool longer, or chill 10 minutes.

steps.do: Pair shells by size. Pipe a ganache mound on one shell of each pair and sandwich with the other, pressing gently. Chill for 24 hours before serving.
steps.look: Even sandwiches with the filling just visible.
steps.mistake: Serving the same day, when the shells are crisp and dry.
steps.fix: Mature them for 24 hours.

dishes.science: A macaron shell is a meringue stabilised with ground almonds and sugar. The Italian method cooks the whites with hot syrup, making a stable, glossy meringue. Macaronage deflates the meringue just enough that the batter flows and levels itself, but still holds enough air to rise. Resting forms a dry skin on top, so that in the oven the steam escapes from the base, lifting the shell and forming the ruffled feet. Aged egg whites have lost some water, making a stronger foam. Maturing the filled macarons lets moisture from the ganache soften the shells into a chewy centre.
dishes.plating: Arrange the macarons on a white plate in a neat row or a small pyramid, the feet facing outward. Serve with coffee or a glass of Champagne.

pairing.drink: A Champagne, or a strong espresso: the bubbles cleanse the palate, and the coffee balances the sweet shells.
pairing.brennans: Krug ‘Grand Cuvée’ Brut NV (375 ml): a rich Champagne from the Brennan's list with toasty depth for chocolate macarons.

variations: Raspberry macarons with raspberry jam and white chocolate ganache.
Pistachio macarons with pistachio buttercream.
Salted caramel macarons.
safety: Age the egg whites covered in the fridge, never at room temperature, and bring them up to temperature only for the hour before use.
The shells contain raw egg white that is cooked by the syrup and the oven.
Hot sugar syrup causes serious burns: pour carefully.

dishes.title: Gâteau Opéra
dishes.summary: Gâteau Opéra: thin layers of almond joconde sponge soaked in strong coffee syrup, layered with coffee buttercream and dark chocolate ganache, covered with a glossy chocolate glaze. It is in the course because it is the summit of the layered cake: six thin, perfectly level layers that need every pastry skill learned so far, from folding and syrups to buttercream and glazing.
equipment: Two baking trays 10 by 14 inches (25 by 35 cm), lined
6 inch (15 cm) square cake frame or tin with removable base
Long, sharp knife and hot water
mise: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Make the coffee syrup by heating the coffee and sugar until dissolved; cool.
Dissolve the espresso powder in 1 tsp (5 ml) hot water.

timeline.do: Bake the joconde; make the buttercream and ganache; assemble and chill overnight.
Glaze; chill 1 hour.
Trim the edges; slice with a hot knife.

steps.do: Make the joconde base: in the stand mixer with the whisk, beat the ground almonds, icing sugar and whole eggs on high for 5 minutes until the mixture is pale, has nearly doubled and falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon. Sift the 3 tbsp (25 g) flour over and fold it in with a large spatula in about 10 strokes.
steps.look: A thick, pale beige batter that holds a ribbon on its surface for 2 to 3 seconds and smells of almond.
steps.mistake: Whisking for only a minute or two, so the batter stays heavy and the thin sponge bakes dense and rubbery.
steps.fix: Keep whisking until it ribbons; the almonds slow it down, so 5 full minutes is normal.

steps.do: In a spotlessly clean bowl, whip the 2 egg whites to soft peaks, about 90 seconds, add the 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar and whip to firm, glossy peaks that bend at the tip. Fold a third into the almond batter to loosen it, fold in the rest in one addition, then fold in the cooled melted butter.
steps.look: A light, airy batter with no white streaks, slightly glossy from the butter.
steps.mistake: Pouring the butter onto the batter in one place, where it sinks and knocks out the air.
steps.fix: Drizzle the butter round the edge of the bowl and fold it in with a few broad strokes; lighten it first with a spoonful of batter if you prefer.

steps.do: Divide the batter between the two lined trays and spread it with the offset palette knife into even layers about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, reaching the corners. Bake one tray at a time on the middle shelf at 425°F (220°C) for 5 to 7 minutes until pale gold and springy.
steps.look: Thin, evenly golden sheets that spring back when touched and just start to shrink from the paper.
steps.mistake: Spreading thick in the centre and thin at the edges, so the edges burn before the centre sets.
steps.fix: Spread from the centre outwards and check the depth at the corners; trim any dark edges after baking.

steps.do: Slide each sponge on its paper onto a rack and cover with a clean tea towel so it stays supple while it cools, about 15 minutes. Then turn it over onto fresh parchment and peel off the baking paper.
steps.look: Soft, flexible sheets that bend without cracking.
steps.mistake: Leaving the sponge uncovered, so it dries and cracks when cut and moved.
steps.fix: Brush a dried sheet with extra coffee syrup when building; it will soften.

steps.do: Make the coffee buttercream: boil the 1/3 cup (65 g) sugar and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water without stirring to 240°F (116°C). Meanwhile whip the 2 yolks on high until pale. Pour the syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl, then whip for 6 to 8 minutes until the bowl feels cool. Beat in the soft butter a tablespoon at a time, then the dissolved espresso.
steps.look: A smooth, satiny, pale coffee-coloured buttercream that holds soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Adding butter while the yolk foam is warm, so it melts into a soup; or using cold butter, so it looks curdled.
steps.fix: If soupy, chill the bowl 10 minutes and whip again; if curdled, keep whipping or warm the outside of the bowl briefly with a hot towel.

steps.do: Make the ganache: heat the 1/3 cup (80 ml) cream until steaming, about 175°F (79°C), pour it over the 3 oz (85 g) chopped chocolate, stand 2 minutes, then stir from the centre outwards until glossy. Leave at room temperature for 20 to 30 minutes until it is thick enough to spread like soft butter.
steps.look: A dark, glossy ganache that holds a soft shape when spread.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard before the chocolate has melted, which traps air bubbles and leaves lumps.
steps.fix: Stand the full 2 minutes, then stir gently; set the bowl over warm water for a few seconds if lumps remain.

steps.do: Cut three squares of joconde exactly 6 inches (15 cm) with a sharp knife and a ruler, using the frame as a guide. Set the frame on a flat board lined with parchment and lay the first square inside, best side down. Brush it with a third of the coffee syrup until it is moist all the way through.
steps.look: A square that fills the frame exactly, dark with syrup but not swimming.
steps.mistake: Cutting squares too small, so the layers slip and the sides are uneven.
steps.fix: Cut them a fraction large and press them into the frame; trim the edges at the end anyway.

steps.do: Spread half the buttercream over the soaked sponge in a level layer about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, smoothing it into the corners. Lay on the second square, press gently with a flat tray to level, soak with syrup, and spread all the ganache in a thin, level layer. Chill 10 minutes.
steps.look: Two smooth, level fillings with no domes or dips.
steps.mistake: Building on soft fillings, so the layers squeeze and bulge.
steps.fix: Chill for 10 minutes between layers to firm each one before the next goes on.

steps.do: Lay on the third square, press it level with the tray, soak it with the remaining syrup, and spread the remaining buttercream over the top in a very thin, perfectly flat layer, scraping across once with the long palette knife. Chill overnight, or freeze for 1 hour.
steps.look: A flat, smooth top with the buttercream just covering the sponge.
steps.mistake: A thick top layer of buttercream, which makes the glaze sit on a soft, uneven base.
steps.fix: Scrape off excess; the top layer is only a surface for the glaze.

steps.do: Make the glaze: melt the 3 oz (85 g) chocolate with the 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil over barely simmering water, then cool, stirring, to 90°F (32°C). Pour it over the cold cake inside the frame and spread it in one pass with the palette knife. Chill 1 hour until set.
steps.look: A thin, mirror-like, dark top with no knife marks.
steps.mistake: Pouring the glaze hot, which melts the buttercream and leaves streaks.
steps.fix: Check with a thermometer; pour at 88 to 90°F (31 to 32°C) onto a cake straight from the fridge.

steps.do: Warm the sides of the frame with a hot towel and lift it off. Trim 1/4 inch (6 mm) from each side with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut, then cut into 4 neat rectangles. Finish each with a fleck of gold leaf.
steps.look: Sharp, straight edges showing six clean, even stripes of sponge, buttercream and ganache.
steps.mistake: Sawing with a cold knife, which drags chocolate across the layers.
steps.fix: Press straight down in one stroke and wipe the blade clean each time.

dishes.science: Joconde is an almond sponge lifted by whipped whole eggs and whites; ground almonds add flavour and moisture, so the thin layers soak up syrup without falling apart. Coffee syrup moistens and flavours the sponge. The buttercream is a French buttercream, an emulsion of butter with a yolk and syrup foam. Ganache is an emulsion of chocolate in cream. The glaze is chocolate thinned with a little oil, which keeps it soft enough to cut. Chilling overnight sets every layer so the cake slices cleanly.
dishes.plating: Set a rectangle on a plate, glossy top and six thin layers facing the guest, with a fleck of gold leaf on top. Add a small quenelle of coffee cream or a few coffee beans.

pairing.drink: A strong espresso, or a tawny port: coffee echoes the cake, and the port matches chocolate and almond.
pairing.brennans: Dow’s Vintage Port 2000 (375 ml): a rich vintage port from the Brennan's list with the dark fruit to stand up to coffee and chocolate.

variations: Use a pistachio buttercream.
Make a white chocolate glaze.
Make individual small squares for a buffet.
safety: Hot sugar syrup causes serious burns: pour carefully.
Yolks heated by syrup are not fully pasteurised; use pasteurised eggs for anyone vulnerable.

dishes.title: Paris-Brest
dishes.summary: Paris-Brest: a ring of choux pastry baked crisp with flaked almonds, split and filled with a hazelnut praline mousseline made from your own caramelised nut paste and pastry cream beaten with butter. It is the capstone of the dessert course because it joins choux, a dry caramel taken to the right colour, a starch custard and a butter emulsion, each needing a different discipline.
equipment: Saucepans, including a heavy one for caramel
Piping bags with a 1/2 inch (1 cm) star tip
Baking tray lined with parchment, with a 7 inch (18 cm) circle drawn on it
Silicone mat or oiled tray for the caramel
mise: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Toast the hazelnuts at 350°F (180°C) for 10 minutes; rub off the skins.
Make the pastry cream first so it can chill.

timeline.do: Make the praline paste and the pastry cream; chill.
Make and pipe the choux ring; bake 40 to 45 minutes; cool.
Make the mousseline.
Split and fill the ring; chill 1 hour.
Dust with icing sugar and serve.

steps.do: Make the praline: melt the sugar in the heavy pan over medium heat, swirling without stirring, until it turns a deep amber, about 340°F (170°C). Stir in the warm hazelnuts and pour onto the silicone mat. Cool completely.
steps.look: A hard, glossy amber brittle with whole nuts.
steps.mistake: Burning the caramel, which makes the praline bitter.
steps.fix: Take it off at deep amber.

steps.do: Break the brittle and blitz in the food processor for 5 to 8 minutes, scraping down, until it turns into a smooth, runny paste.
steps.look: A glossy, fluid praline paste.
steps.mistake: Stopping too early, so it stays sandy.
steps.fix: Keep blending; the oils will release.

steps.do: Make the pastry cream: heat the milk until steaming. Whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour; temper with the milk; return to the pan and boil, whisking, for 1 minute. Cover the surface and chill.
steps.look: A thick, glossy custard.
steps.mistake: Not boiling long enough.
steps.fix: Boil 1 full minute.

steps.do: Make the choux: bring the water, milk, butter, salt and sugar to a full boil. Off the heat, add the flour all at once and beat until smooth. Return to medium heat and beat for 2 minutes until a film forms on the base.
steps.look: A smooth ball of dough and a film on the pan.
steps.mistake: Not drying the dough enough, so the choux is heavy.
steps.fix: Cook 1 minute more.

steps.do: Transfer to the mixer and beat for 1 minute to cool slightly. Add the eggs gradually, beating well, until the dough is glossy and falls from the spatula in a V shape.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy dough that holds a V.
steps.mistake: Adding all the eggs at once, so the dough is too runny.
steps.fix: Add slowly; you may not need all.

steps.do: Pipe a ring round the circle, then a second ring inside touching it, and a third on top of the seam. Scatter with flaked almonds.
steps.look: A neat, triple ring of choux.
steps.mistake: Uneven rings that bake lopsided.
steps.fix: Pipe with steady pressure.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 15 minutes, then lower to 350°F (180°C) and bake 25 to 30 minutes more without opening the door, until deep golden and rigid.
steps.look: A puffed, golden, crisp ring.
steps.mistake: Opening the door early, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Keep the door shut for the first 30 minutes.

steps.do: Make the mousseline: bring the pastry cream and butter both to 68°F (20°C). Beat the pastry cream smooth, then beat in the butter a little at a time, then 1/3 cup (100 g) of the praline paste. Whip for 3 minutes until light.
steps.look: A smooth, light, nutty cream.
steps.mistake: Different temperatures, so the cream splits.
steps.fix: Warm the bowl gently or chill it briefly until it comes together.

steps.do: Split the cooled ring horizontally with the serrated knife. Pipe the mousseline in tall rosettes all round the base. Put the top back on and dust with icing sugar. Chill 1 hour.
steps.look: A ring filled with tall rosettes of cream.
steps.mistake: Filling the ring warm, so the cream melts.
steps.fix: Cool the choux completely.

dishes.science: Choux pastry rises on steam: the water in the cooked flour paste turns to vapour in the oven, inflating it, and the egg and gelatinised starch set into a crisp shell around the hollow centre. Drying the paste on the stove removes excess water so the shell holds its shape. Praline is caramelised sugar ground with toasted nuts until the nut oils release and turn the mixture into a paste. The pastry cream must boil so the cornflour gelatinises. Mousseline is butter emulsified into pastry cream: both must be at the same temperature, about 68°F (20°C), or the emulsion breaks.
dishes.plating: Set the whole ring on a cake stand, dusted with icing sugar, the rosettes of praline cream peeking out. Cut wedges with a serrated knife and serve each on its side.

pairing.drink: A sweet Vouvray or a Madeira: honeyed Chenin or nutty Madeira match the hazelnut praline.
pairing.brennans: Broadbent ‘Single Cask’ Malvasia Madeira 500 ml 2009: a rich Madeira from the Brennan's list with caramel and nut flavours for praline.

variations: Make individual small Paris-Brest rings.
Use almond praline instead of hazelnut.
Add a hidden centre of pure praline paste in the cream.
safety: Caramel at 340°F (170°C) causes severe burns: pour carefully and never touch it.
The pastry cream boils, which makes the yolks safe; keep the finished pastry refrigerated.
